We call these graphons, as they can be seen as the limit of typical large graphs. We demonstrate how the extremal weights of these cycle structures in graphs and their graphon equivalents converge in a probabilistic sense, applying the method of equivariant diagonalization. Additionally, this investigation confirms an existing conjecture by Kolmos, Sokólski, and Vesztergombi that the convergence of these cycle structures in graphs to their graphon equivalent holds in an asymptotic probabilistic framework. We also employ analysis of eigenvectors to demonstrate how converging cycles in graphs leads to converging eigenvalues and eigenvectors in its associated Laplacian-based operators. Furthermore, this analysis enables us to examine how the convergence of these cycle structures in graphs results in convergent distributions of lengths of walks within these graphons. We also extended our analysis to consider random covering acycles in these graph structures. We observed that as as these graph structures converge to their graphon equivalents, the k-acycles and covering acycles also exhibit convergent patterns in their cycle lengths and weights, as well as the weights of the cycles and walks in these graphon equivalents displayed emergent sinusoidal patterns in their eigenfunctions. We also derived an explicit formula for computing these eigenfunctions given the graphon's probability distribution. We used these analysis to investigate a particular aspect of these graph structures, specifically how the extremal cycles in these graphs where edges have unequal weights exhibit convergent patterns in their lengths and weights that reflect a mix of jump and persistence behaviors. This research outlines various sampling techniques employed by Wikipedia, utilizing a bag sampling algorithm that enhances long document ranking efficiency. Furthermore, we examine the influence of the hyperparameter 'num_BITS' on ranking performance in the general ranking task. We also analyze bag sampling's performance in top k lists, utilizing both synthetic and real query sets. Finally, we review other compression methods implemented by Wikipedia. The proposed compression methods resulted in an overall 7.8% decrease in recall, primarily due to 'prefix trie' compression, which accounts for 1.1% of the loss, while 'position caching' accounts for 4.4%. Nonetheless, incorporating 'prefix trie' for top k lists enables faster generation of candidate lists. It's also observed that in scenarios where a large number of documents are not candidates, 'prefix trie' can recapture the lost recall. Conversely, when a large number of documents are candidates despite the lack of relevance, 'prefix trie' cannot recapture the lost recall. A proposed new method 'index-iterator' outperforms both 'prefix trie' and 'position caching' compression. Interestingly, while 'index-iterator' may not offer substantial speed gains for large top k lists, it's more efficient than 'prefix trie' for smaller top k lists. Moreover, 'index-iterator' performs notably better than 'prefix trie' with large top k lists. Lastly, we identify areas for future research and a potential strategy for utilizing compressed indices to speed up approximation methods. As a result, semi-supervised node classification with GNNs has become increasingly challenging. To address this issue, researchers have turned to pseudo-labeling as a means to increase the size of the labeled data set. However, the effectiveness of pseudo-labeling depends largely on the quality of pseudo labels, and when applied to GNNs, these methods often produce subpar results. To improve pseudo labeling's effectiveness, we introduce a new technique called supervised pseudo labeling, which uses the model's initial parameters and high-quality pseudo labels to train a separate classifier. This classic supervised learning method allows the model to focus on optimizing its parameters for improved initial results. Moreover, when combined with elastic weight consolidation, our approach effectively increases the size of the labeled data set while reducing overfitting, resulting in improved overall performance. Our experiments demonstrate that supervised pseudo labeling significantly outperforms pseudo labeling and elastic weight consolidation when employed in semi-supervised GNN node classification. Additionally, our approach has been successfully adapted to semi-supervised unsupervised graph clustering, yielding impressive improvements in performance. Our results confirm that a classic supervised learning method such as supervised pseudo labeling can significantly enhance the accuracy of semi-supervised GNN node classification and graph clustering. Our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/swkwong/Supervised-Pseudo-Labeling. Our research results reveal that a simple yet efficient method like supervised pseudo labeling can effectively enhance the accuracy of semi-supervised GNN node classification and graph clustering when applied to labeled nodes with high confidence. However, when the model's predictions lack confidence, our approach tends to yield mixed results. To address this issue, we developed a new method called confidence guided pseudo labeling, which aims to eliminate noisy pseudo labels by selecting only high-confidence nodes for the training data set. Our experiments demonstrate that CG-CREC successfully eliminates noisy pseudo labels and significantly improves the model's overall accuracy. A single field, the Einstein tensor, provides a unified explanation for both dark energy and dark matter. The model effectively reunites two components, allowing them to coexist or separately vary in density. However, adhering to cosmic inflation requirements poses a challenge: the field must be non-interacting and possess a minimal mass, leading us to propose the use of Generalized Einstein Structures as a framework for study. Our research focuses on an inflationary regime corresponding to an anisotropic flat band, and we have discovered that the model's interaction can be significant, despite cosmic constraints remaining compatible with observational data from the Planck satellite. We have also identified the model's stability during inflation and verified that the field's behavior corresponds to a stable attractor solution. Our research contributes to the model's overall appeal, suggesting that the model could be a competitor to alternative single-field inflation models currently under consideration. Our study is currently the only in-depth examination of the model's inflationary properties to date. Our research also includes a discussion on the model's potential stability during the band's instability and transition to the stable attractor. Our work establishes a connection between the PE models and theories involving ghost fields, representing a distinct class of models designed to stabilize a ghost. We've created a statistical model that uses a simple hierarchical framework to  understand how students select courses, taking into account students' preferences for particular courses and course similarities. By integrating this model into an online student course scheduling system, we show that inferring the model's key parameters yields accurate and relevant information about course structures and student interests. The project also revealed interesting insights into student preferences, highlighting distinct course groups and individual student interests within those categories. By showing how student attraction to particular courses can be explained by their shared characteristics, we were able to identify meaningful patterns in student behavior. Ultimately, the model produced a range of other desirable outcomes, including optimized course loads for individual students and course pairs, allowing instructors to identify areas where their courses are most relevant and gauging the level of student interest in unscheduled courses. The model can be applied to various domains such as book clubs, software adoption, and educational pathways, enabling a deeper understanding of complex selection mechanisms. The model's full source code and a live Chronos system are available online for further research.

Despite the widespread use of social media for sharing user-generated content, social media platforms are often hindered by various barriers, such as technical issues, laws, and regulations, and purposeful censorship. As a result, a growing number of people are using tools to bypass these restrictions and access a wider range of content. However, the effectiveness and implications of using these tools, known as anti-censorship tools, are not well understood. This study aims to investigate how ordinary people use these tools to bypass censorship and access a wider range of content. The researchers conducted in-depth interviews with 17 participants who relied on anti-censorship methods to access social media, including Twitter and TikTok. The results reveal that these users employ diverse strategies to access the content they want, often mixing informal techniques, such as using virtual private networks, with online guidance that highlights accessible social media platforms. The participants' motivations for using these methods varied, including avoiding tracking by governments or companies, circumventing content restrictions such as Twitter's ban on posting news via link, and enhancing their online privacy. However, the researchers also found that using these methods was complex and often required seeking advice from others, which they were willing to do, even though they were not always successful in accessing the content they wanted. The study highlights the growing significance of using social media despite facing censorship, as well as the potential risks and challenges involved. The participants' stories emphasize the necessity of addressing the technical issues related to accessibility, such as the detection of anti-censorship tools by social media platforms, and highlight the need for clear justifications and explanations for the content that is blocked or removed. The researchers' analysis suggests that even though an extensive system is in place to handle content reported by users, a large number of social media users lack awareness of this system and the reasons behind removal or blocking of content. The study's findings provide valuable insights for policymakers, researchers, and social media platform developers, and highlight the potential for misuses of anti-censorship tools to bypass legitimate content restrictions. The researchers' research may guide platform developers in enhancing their systems to make it simpler for users to access the content they need, as well as address the growing concern about the potential for anti-censorship tools to be detected by social media platforms. The study's conclusions serve as a call to action for further investigation into the various methods of censorship and their impact on users' experiences. In the treatment of cancer, individual patient data meta-analysis plays a vital role in evaluating the effectiveness of new treatments and combining data from multiple studies for more accurate comparisons. When analyzing continuous outcomes from clinical trials, conventional methods often rely on assumptions that may not hold true, such as normal distribution of residuals. To address this limitation, we've developed and applied a constrained longitudinal data analysis using natural cubic splines to estimate mean profiles in patient survival data. This approach enables control of the mean profile at specific time points, such as when patients might be undergoing treatment changes or when data collection ends. To showcase the method's potential, we performed a meta-analysis of individual patient data on peginterferon beta-1a in multiple sclerosis patients from seven clinical trials. Using the constrained longitudinal data analysis, we've estimated mean profiles at relevant time points, such as treatment end or off-treatment at six weeks. Results from this analysis show that patients receiving peginterferon beta-1a experience notable changes in disease progression compared to a control group, particularly during treatment. This approach has broad applications in various fields, including clinical trials for treatments involving frequent measurements over time. Present research has primarily concentrated on generating a safety buffer based on geometrically derived estimates of escape time. Consequently, the proposed AceDA achieves superior dialogue state tracking performance across two benchmark datasets and sets a new baseline for future research. The proposed method's effectiveness is attributed to its ability to distill information from the confusion network, which aids individual model performance. A crucial aspect of access structures, known as universal structures, involves measuring the least number of minimal qualified sets they contain. Research has shown that the minimum universal access structures with n minimal qualified sets are densely packed in a specific coordinate space and have an almost universal nature. Specifically, this class of structures in 2^n-1 coordinates has an asymptotic size of n with a significant gap from the optimal, increasing at a lower rate of n/c log n. Consequently, lower bounds are found for the optimal size of universal structures in this class. Conversely, upper bounds are placed on the size of access structures in 2^n-1 coordinates that have a specific property called "almost universality." Furthermore, it was discovered that the minimum universal access structures with n qualified sets in 2^n-1 coordinates can be created for all n values, including those that exist below a specific, normal-distributed range. Specifically, this range falls below 1.44 log n. The findings also implied the presence of a significant gap between the information-theoretic bounds and achievable rates in a related problem known as wiretap channel coding. Ultimately, computational methods were used to calculate the size of universal structures in 2^n-1 coordinates for n equal to 31, 32, and 33. The results revealed that these sizes fluctuate between two distinct patterns: some n values having an asymptotic size of n with a significant log n gap, while others had an almost universal nature with a substantial n log n gap. Specifically, this last scenario occurs when n equals 33, resulting in an asymptotic size of n with a significant 4 log n gap. The findings also confirmed the presence of "plateaus" in access structures at certain n values, including those with an asymptotic size of 5 with a 2 log n gap, observed for n equal to 33. The research introduced the concept known as "reversal structures," featuring access structures in which their minimal qualified sets in the primary structure are maximal in a related reverse structure. Notably, this concept has an almost dual nature, featuring a significant gap between the information-theoretic bounds and achievable rates in the reverse structure. The research found that reversal structures do not affect the size of access structures in the zone of complexity 2^n-1. However, specific patterns were observed in the reversal structures for n equal to 33, resulting in an asymptotic size of n with a significant 4 log n gap. To study decoherence in entangled systems, we investigate several key events 
such as the sudden change in entanglement, the loss of quantum correlations, and 
entanglement's collapse. These events are examined using the hydrodynamic model, 
which draws from linear irreversibility and optimal kinematics principles. This 
model leverages the leading order of the von Neumann entropy rate and optimal 
estimators to analyze different decoherence phenomena. Analyzing the sudden 
change in entanglement, we explore the hydrodynamic model's applicability to the 
Boston, Beijing, Shanghai, and Moscow networks, considering 20 pairs of qubits. 
Meanwhile, we examine the hydrodynamic model's predictions on the Mubin and GHZ 
states within the Hamburg network and Munich universe. Furthermore, we investigate 
the hydrodynamic model's diagnosis of the GHZ state's collapse and compare its results 
to those of a different model derived from stochastic quantum dynamics. In addition, 
we use the hydrodynamic model to study quantum correlations in the Hamburg and Shanghai 
networks, focusing particularly on the GHZ state. Lastly, we explore the hydrodynamic 
model's predictions on entanglement's collapse in several network scenarios and compare 
its results to those of a different model based on stochastic quantum dynamics and 
supported by numerical simulations. To facilitate easy replication of our research, 
all our code is openly available on GitHub. This study demonstrates that understanding 
decoherence patterns in quantum systems requires a data-driven approach, where 
estimators play a pivotal role in creating a predictive framework for different 
phenomena. Accordingly, we suggest adopting an empirical strategy to analyze quantum 
system data, especially when such data is limited, to produce reliable predictions. 
Although our research focuses on hydrodynamic models applicable to both bosonic and 
fermionic systems, the principles discussed here are universally applicable to various 
spatially distributed quantum systems, whether based on a different physical structure 
or not. Moreover, we uncover substantial agreement between the hydrodynamic model's 
predictions and optimal estimators' estimates on multiple real-world network datasets 
and emphasize the importance of both simulations and real-data analysis in advancing 
our understanding of complex quantum phenomena. Ultimately, we hope this research 
will inspire interest in the study of hydrodynamic models in quantum systems, 
sparking fresh approaches to explaining decoherence's manifestations and the resultant 
loss of quantum properties. By elucidating the underlying physical principles, 
this study paves the way for leveraging hydrodynamic modeling

Most current research in continuous learning assumes the absence of a training set, yet still uses labeled data from previous tasks to adjust to new tasks. In contrast, our Continual Learning Benchmark focuses on the more practical scenario in which models are maintained across multiple domains without needing to retrain on past tasks and without having access to old data. We instead use old data points' mean values in the Nearest Mean Classifier, requiring no past task data. Remarkably, our classifier's performance compares favorably to state-of-the-art continuous learning methods that utilize old data, especially when evaluating both unlabeled old data and unlabeled new test observations equally. We further reveal that existing continuous learning methods that adjust weights in conjunction with old data points' features suffer from hyperparameter sensitivity, particularly in scenarios with a large number of old data points. A set of 6 new anisotropic flow coefficients is proposed to facilitate a comprehensive investigation of angular correlations in the transverse momentum plane beyond elliptic, triangular, and pentadic flows. These coefficients don't depend on the specific characteristics of the initial conditions but are influenced by the locations and magnitudes of the particles. In order to examine the individual effects of the transverse momentum and initial anisotropy on the angular correlations, a specific model, the one-dimensional Gaussian-uncorrelated model, is constructed. This model consists of single-particle initial conditions with uniform distribution in the initial angle and Gaussian distribution in the initial momentum, and the subsequent hydrodynamic evolution is disregarded. The model can successfully reproduce the measurements from Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV. Furthermore, the model suggests that the pentadic and higher-order flow coefficients may serve as sensitive indicators of the early-stage anisotropies in heavy-ion collisions. In addition, the connections between the flow coefficients and the initial conditions are discussed through numerical examples. These findings provide a basis for a more precise extraction of the information about the initial conditions from these observables with enhanced precision. Lastly, the model offers a simple method to deduce the anisotropy of the initial momentum from the measured flow coefficients, which may be used to deduce the viscosity of the system if the hydrodynamic behavior is well established in the future studies. These findings were presented at the 20th Advanced Research Workshop on Nuclear Physics and Murray Gell-Mann Meeting on Quantum Chromodynamics.

Decentralized machine learning holds great promise for improving predictions in wireless settings. Graph neural networks, a type of machine learning algorithm, is particularly well-suited for problems with underlying structural connections. When trained in a fully decentralized manner, these models lack critical information about their own structural connections, which hampers their predictive power. This paper addresses this limitation by integrating local graph information into fully decentralized graph neural networks, while maintaining their decentralized properties. A new method is developed to improve the robustness of their predictions under noisy conditions, and the performance benefits of this approach are confirmed through simulations on three real-world datasets. Notably, the proposed method achieves up to a 25% increase in test accuracy across these datasets. This work is further future-proofed by outlining a strategy for adaptively decoding messages from the network, even when the underlying labels are correlated. As a result, decentralized GNNs trained under the proposed scheme exhibit enhanced resistance to correlated label noise, and their predictions remain robust in this context. The research is thus relevant to correlated label noise and can be extended to other challenges. Furthermore, the proposed decoding strategy offers a general solution that can be applied beyond GNNs to various problems. The findings suggest that centrally aggregating the network's structural code and using this information to decode the message may be an effective approach. Based on these insights, a new method is developed to improve the robustness of decentralized GNN predictions under correlated label noise, and the approach achieves up to a 100% improvement in test accuracy across the datasets. The results are further corroborated by baseline comparisons to other decentralized machine learning approaches. A complete, open-source framework is provided to facilitate the deployment of the proposed methods in real-world settings. Moreover, the research includes suggestions for further improving the performance of decentralized GNNs. As an extension of this work, a new method is developed to enable fair competition between centralized and decentralized models by centrally aggregating the network's structural code and using it to decode the model parameters. Notably, the approach achieves up to a 25% increase in combined test accuracy and fairness, and the approach can be generalized to other challenges. The research outlines strategies for further enhancing the performance of decentralized GNNs. As an example of this, a new method is developed to enable adaptation to new domains using a combination of central aggregation and decoding operators. Notably, the approach achieves up to an 8% increase in test accuracy and can be extended to other problems. The results are further confirmed by baseline comparisons to other approaches. We develop a comprehensive, efficient global search strategy to identify neutral, strongly interacting narrow resonances produced through the decay of top quarks. This method is specifically designed for detecting axions or ALPs with mass within a few hundred MeV to approximately one GeV, a region of interest for understanding dark matter in cosmology. As a key advantage of our approach, any width in the resonance can be accommodated, offering flexibility in the analysis. Furthermore, we present simulated search outcomes from existing LHC experiments, specifically focusing on the 13 TeV proton-proton collisions and expressing the sensitivity in terms of production cross-sections and decay widths. For the ATLAS experiment, we present results for 36.1 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity, while for the CMS experiment, we present results for 12.9 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. These findings highlight the CMS experiment as more sensitive to resonances with smaller widths and the ATLAS experiment more sensitive to those with larger widths. Finally, we present next-generation prospects for both experiments, aiming for luminosities of 300 fb$^{-13}$, 1000 fb$^{-13}$, and 3000 fb$^{-13}$, respectively. Both current and future sensitivity bounds are presented, serving as standard references for theoretical models to reference against. This work marks the first analysis of this nature for both ATLAS and CMS, offering improvements of two orders of magnitude in sensitivity over their respective previous results. This analysis has been made available to the respective experiments for future consideration.

The fundamental bosonic oscillator has been reimagined in two distinct contexts: as a quantum quantum harmonic oscillator with variable mass and frequency; and as a classical system comprising a nonlinear pendulum with variable length and frequency, capable of oscillating in an infinite number of modes. Building on the legacy of Louis de Broglie, Albert Einstein and Niels Bohr, a review of the bosonic oscillator's quantum model highlights its far-reaching implications in describing infinite sets of oscillating states observed in various physical systems, from traditional harmonic oscillators to more complex systems, including granular media and bacterial flagella, which often exceed the quantum classical divide. The review also sheds light on pioneering researchers who influenced the development of the bosonic oscillator's quantum model. Furthermore, the quantum oscillator's classical analog is compared to a nonlinear self-oscillating system, which has implications in explaining phenomena observed in traditional harmonic oscillators and other complex systems, thus blending quantum and classical approaches. The reviews' conclusions offer new insights into contemporary research trends and future potential areas of exploration, including quantum biology, the quantum Clausius heat equation, topological effects and entanglement in quantum engineering. As such, the reviews may appeal to anyone with an interest in fundamental science, particularly those following developments in quantum biology, nanotechnology, and quantum information theory. The reviews may also prove useful for undergraduate and graduate students looking to delve into research opportunities in interdisciplinary fields. Lastly, the reviews' human perspective offers a unique insight into the lives of renowned scientists, including Louis de Broglie, Albert Einstein and Niels Bohr, providing a captivating read for readers interested in figures and histories of science. resulting from their inability to assess the stability of formed grasps. To overcome
this limitation, we introduce DexGraspNet, a novel method that uses synthetic data
networks to generate diverse, stable grasps on complex objects. Unlike traditional
approaches, DexGraspNet directly optimizes a policy employing object-oriented
features, thereby circumventing the need for time-consuming grid-search optimization
in object-space. Furthermore, by leveraging object-orientation, we enforce parametric
stability during policy training, ensuring that the learned grasp is robust and
predictive. To achieve this, we adapt the Lagrangian method and propose a dual
training regimen. Firstly, training GraspNet with Diversity Loss helps overcome
grasp hyper-parameter ambiguity. Secondly, training GraspNet with Stability Loss aids
in minimizing variance in object-centered grasp orientation. Our results show that
DexGraspNet yields grasps that are 81% stable in simulation and 75% stable in real-world settings. Notably, our GraspNet outperforms prior methods in terms of grasp diversity by a significant margin. Moreover, an additional network, GraspNet, is used to project any grasp to a stable, diverse, and transferable form. The collective framework, comprising GraspNet, GreedNet, and DexGraspNet, unlocks the potential of robotic dexterous manipulation, ultimately yielding an impressive 90% success rate in simulation and 85% in real-world applications. Through simulations utilizing a comprehensive model that accounts for various physical factors, rCASPR's potential in producing high-quality images while reducing radiation exposure and acquisition time is investigated and compared with traditional linear sampling. This process often relies on distillation, which can be heavily influenced by distiller model architecture, specifically the number of channels in each layer. We have found that by eliminating unimportant channels during training, the distiller's output closely mimics the original model's, allowing for more effective knowledge transfer. This process is known as channel pruning and is further utilized in this study to improve student-model performance. We have also discovered an algorithm that efficiently identifies optimal channel elimination strategies, utilizing the gradient magnitude as a key performance indicator. Our method not only requires less computation but also eliminates parameters that are less crucial to the teacher model. We have tested this approach on the distillation of ResNet-50 to MobileNet-V2 and observed that the mobile version performs better at higher image resolutions and also achieves better results at lower image resolutions when compared to the original model. We have publicly made available our code at https://github.com/ziyimorgan/fixedchanneldistillation. We have found that certain pruning algorithms, such as evolution-based methods, may lead to over-pruning, whereas our method avoids this issue and enables priests to efficiently eliminate parameters while still achieving better student-model performance. To better understand how ecosystems respond to environmental changes, researchers have been developing various mathematical and computational models to study how grasslands respond to climate change, particularly increased aridity. By using complex systems made of interconnected nodes that adapt and evolve over time, researchers have been able to create a framework for understanding how ecosystems behave in different scenarios. In a new study, researchers have taken a novel approach by accounting for the influence of spatial non-locality, where the behavior of one node can affect its neighboring nodes. Interestingly, when spatial non-locality was incorporated, it had the effect of making grazing ecosystems more resilient to increased aridity, but this result came at a cost: it led to more frequent and frequent adaptions in individual nodes, which in turn could lead to individual nodes becoming disconnected from their local environments. When considering the dynamic interplay between scales, researchers have been able to create a new mathematical framework for understanding how grazing ecosystems respond to climate change. This new framework, based on concepts from renormalization group theory, provides a mathematical tool for understanding how physical systems become unstable at different scales, which in turn could lead to a deeper understanding of how grazing ecosystems respond to climate change. In a new study, researchers have used this framework to identify two distinct regimes in grazing ecosystems, characterized by either spatially non-local mean-field behavior or fragmented dynamics. When aridity is low, this regime transition occurs at a critical point, but when spatial non-locality is incorporated, this result is shifted due to increased feedbacks. Most surprisingly, when individual nodes become disconnected from their local environments, it led to more frequent noise bursts and chaotic behavior, but this effect is characterized by patches of spatially correlated dynamics, which in turn could lead to more complex and resilient ecosystems. In particular, this result could lead to more effective strategies for managing and preserving more resilient and diverse ecosystems. The majority of methods suggesting adaptive inputs have them randomly assigned across examples, yet our research examines what occurs when inputs are given strategically in terms of classification errors. This investigation comes from thinking about Randomized Projections, a technique that has been shown to be an effective method for dimensionality reduction, about whether or not it can be learned by a machine. This question leads to an analysis of how different learners deal with Randonized Projections as a classifier in various settings, including binary linear classification problems, noise-based scenarios, and real-world applications. Our key findings reveal that, in most cases, strategic input can result in much weaker guarantees compared to using random inputs, and that some learning algorithms may not be able to learn Randonized Projections unless the input is truly random. This leads to an exploration of the general properties that new classifiers should have in order to handle adaptive inputs effectively in high dimensionality settings. Our last contribution is to show that, in many of our analyzed scenarios, these strategic input methods can result in significantly worse classification errors compared to using random inputs. A novel approach to quantum financial research called quasi-quantum communication has the potential to launch a quantum network-enabled era of quantum financial trading. To examine how this technology could be used in high-frequency trading, our study uses real market data to compare the performance of conventional and quantum random number generators based on the Bernoulli and Gaussian distributions. By selecting the optimal threshold to convert the generated bits into trade signals, our results demonstrate that the quasi-quantum random number generator can generate profitable trading strategies similar to those produced by the quantum random number generator and significantly outperform the random control. The underlying reason for this profit comes from the QRRG's smaller entropy per bit compared to the quantum random number generator. This finding highlights an unexpected benefit of quantum technology for high-frequency trading: even in a near-term, uncompleted state, it can provide an advantage over conventional methods. Nonetheless, the profit generated by the quasi-quantum method is ultimately subject to disappear over time due to the conventional law of entropy. To ensure continuous profit, our study also suggests incorporating both quantum and classical information to make trading decisions. As an alternative strategy to avoid profit disappearance over time, our results also demonstrate the efficacy of the quasi-quantum method in high-frequency trading by combining the QRRG with a moving average method. Furthermore, the advantage of the quasi-quantum method over the quantum method becomes apparent under market conditions similar to random scenarios. In conclusion, the applications of quantum science in finance hold numerous possibilities for investigation and exploration. Furthermore, the quasi-quantum communication technology has the potential to launch an early quantum communication-enabled era of quantum financial trading. A significant problem with summarization that has not been thoroughly investigated is the propagation of errors. Current top-performing models suffer from poor overall performance when relying on recall-based evaluation methods. We present a new approach called ErrOrbit, a system designed to mitigate errors that impact summarization output. We first identify common error patterns that occur in summarization, which take the form of specific entity mistakes. These mistakes often stem from a single initial error, resulting in a chain of incorrect entity references. To address this, we developed an error control mechanism that exploits the structure of these mistake chains. Our model employs sequence-to-sequence networks, which generate summary chains consisting of reference chains to mitigate errors. During inference, our model predicts a summary chain by selecting one optimal chain from various possible combinations. Our results indicate that ErrorOrbit outperforms other systems that utilize post-processing methods to correct errors in summarization. When tested on the CopyME dataset, ErrorOrbit demonstrated substantial gains over its competitors, achieving a 44.3% reduction in errors. Notably, our model also performed better under human evaluation of output quality, receiving scores of 43.6% compared to 31.3% for the best competing system. When tested on the SummEval dataset, ErrorOrbit demonstrated consistent performance improvements across various error metrics. Our findings suggest that incorporating sequence-to-sequence networks for error control can lead to significant gains in output quality. Our model also outperformed current top-performing systems that use transformer architecture on various metrics by up to 4.3 points. Notably, our model's performance improvements were most pronounced when evaluating output quality using the coverage and consistency metrics, which are often overlooked in recent summarization research. For robots to adapt to new situations without having enough information, they can use what they know about similar situations and apply that to new ones through training in similar environments. Currently, many methods for teaching robots rely on the size of the data set and the complexity of the problems being different, which can lead to over-emphasis on simple tasks and problems that are easy to picture. Instead of focusing on basic object recognition, robots should learn about the three-dimensional layout of the scene in which they will be operating. Learning the geometry of a scene can be more effective than traditional methods of visual learning in preparing robots for new situations. To learn about scene geometry, robots can use data from surveys, but it is often lacking in important details, such as distances and metrics, which are crucial for scene-based learning. To address this lack of data, we have developed a new method of visual learning that makes the most of data from surveys by creating a more detailed, interactive 3D layout of the scene. By using 3D point clouds with metrics that can be manipulated, our approach enables the training of robots to adapt to new situations based on the geometry of the scene, even when the data set is limited. The underlying technique uses a matrix representation of the dataset to determine the tau value through a series of matrix multiplications and divergences. This method outperforms previous methods which were based on algorithms utilising O(n^2) iterations to compute the tau value. The overall time complexity of the process remains unchanged at O(n^2) but with a significant reduction in memory usage when compared to previous methods that required the storage of auxiliary arrays. The reliability of the algorithm has also been tested with random datasets of varying sizes, showcasing its efficiency in time and memory usage. This method has also been further expanded to offer solutions for synthetic datasets consisting of different dimensions and sizes. The validity of the results has also been verified using the tests from the ksd package in R. In addition to this, an alternative version of the algorithm has been introduced which has a reduced time efficiency of O(nQ(n-1)) due to its implementation of the Greedysort algorithm. This method has also been proven to be stable and efficient in its in-situ operations. In order to further showcase its efficiency, a comparison between the O(n^2) time-efficient algorithm and its counterparts has been introduced, highlighting the over-substantiation of the time complexity of the original implementation by Bargallies et al. in their paper "A linear-time-complexity algorithm for computing Kendall's tau from an array of numbers". This comparison involved utilising the time-efficient version to calculate the tau value for datasets of varying sizes and then comparing its results with those of its counterparts. In addition to this, an alternative version of the algorithm has been introduced which calculates the tau value for datasets consisting of percentages and results in its adherence to the original definition of the tau value as noted by its original implementers in their paper "A linear-time-complexity algorithm for computing Kendall's tau from an array of numbers". In further testing of the algorithm's reliability and validity, a cross-sectional and longitudinal analysis of the algorithm's reliability and validity were introduced, highlighting its consistency in its results across synthetic datasets consisting of different dimensions and sizes. In addition to this, an alternative version of the algorithm has been introduced which calculates the tau value for datasets of any size and results in its consistency with other measures of correlation such as the Pearson and Spearman correlation coefficients. This research focuses on integrating Local Differential Privacy with Federated Learning to create a secure, user-centric model that balances privacy and minimization errors. By combining the core principles of Local DP and FL without requiring explicit methods, this paper develops a general framework based on optmized utility functions and proves its robustness. Unlike existing approaches that rely on explicit learning algorithms, this model is versatile and applicable to various learning techniques, including stochastic gradient descent and neural networks. Furthermore, we propose a new learning algorithm that converges to an accurately decentralized mean, with theoretical proof confirming its applicability to convex loss functions and optimal convergence at a rate of $O(1/t)$, despite the presence of noise. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated through simulations with real-world data sets, which reveal the significant impact of privacy levels on model accuracy. This paper is further enhanced by its presentation of relevant challenges and potential areas for future exploration. Multi-parameter topological data analysis has been increasingly utilized in recent times. A key concept in this analysis is the Euler characteristic, used to derive insights from persistent homology across various dimensions. The construction of a multi-parameter Euler characteristic function in this study relies on a generalized form of the combinatorial formula for single-parameter Euler characteristic, and it is theoretically validated for spaces with triangable boundaries and further extended to apply to any metric space through its underlying combinatorial structure. The advantages and flexible modularity of this analysis are discussed with relevant applications and it is demonstrated how it can be applied using high-dimensional data from the NIST dataset involving diamond-scintillator detectors. The study's findings indicate that multi-parameter Euler characteristic functions are capable of capturing trends inherent in data while it approaches a state of topological transition. The study also reveals that multi-parameter Euler characteristic functions are insensitive to minor changes but sensitive to larger variations, thereby making them useful for detecting subtle patterns in data. The study further utilizes the NIST dataset to evaluate the performance of multi-parameter Euler characteristic functions in distinguishing samples of different diamond-scintillator ratios and further identifies potential limitations of these methods, such as data classification biases towards the parameters being analyzed. The study makes available an open-source implementation of multi-parameter Euler characteristic functions in Python for data analysis. The study concludes by highlighting the scope and capability of multi-parameter Euler characteristic functions for data analysis. The study further makes recommendations for utilizing these methods in data analysis and expresses interest in exploring these methods further for data analysis. The study points out the possibility of combining multi-parameter Euler characteristic methods with other techniques for data analysis and it discusses the particular applications of multi-parameter Euler characteristic methods to undirected graphs, giving insights into the methods' behavior and providing further optimization and directions for open exploration. The study specifically identifies the following as areas for open exploration: (i) multi-parameter applications to datasets, particularly to distinguish samples of different parameter values, and multi-parameter data analysis using machine learning techniques; (ii) multi-parameter data analysis using other techniques such as persistent trajectories and localized cohomology; (iii) multi-parameter data analysis using other techniques such as persistence spectra and flow morphology matrices. The study expresses interest in exploring these methods for data analysis and comments on the particular applications of multi-parameter Euler characteristic methods to undirected graphs, persistent trajectories and diamond-scintillator data analysis. The study points out the demonstrations and novel demonstrations provided for multi-parameter data analysis and topological data analysis. The study expresses interest in further topological data analysis and multi-parameter data analysis

In this research, we revisit the discrete-time dynamical system devised by Friesen and Venturino (2005) to model biological phenomena, similar to Zeng and Wu's (2015) model. Our analysis, however, reveals that the system can be simplified into a linear system component and a nonlinear part, whose dynamics are separated. By applying this distinction, we revisit the parameters' domain for which the system's dynamic behavior was originally analyzed and identify various types of bifurcations, notably those resulting in stable periods of two and three years. Furthermore, it becomes evident that the system exhibits a unique, nonlinear relationship, contradicting a preceding linear hypothesis (Zeng and Wu, 2015). Our findings, therefore, yield comprehensive information on the system's dynamic behavior, encompassing data on the maximum population in 3-year cycles, as well as scenarios leading to system collapse. To facilitate the investigation, we created an interactive web-based visualization tool that displays the system's dynamic behavior in response to different parameter adjustments. This approach enables the exploration of various parameter sets and dynamics, including attractors, bifurcations, and various orbit types. Moreover, the tool allows users to input their own sets of parameter values for analysis. As an extension of the research, we also identified and analyzed the system's three-dimensional volume occupation dynamics, revealing distinct phases resulting from different parameter combinations, such as those resulting in stable and unstable equilibrium states. Ultimately, the paper confirms the existence of unique, coexisting stable populations, encompassing various length cycles, thus validating the effectiveness of the proposed discrete-time dynamical system for modeling the interactions between three species in predator-prey frameworks. All of the analysis's codes and interactive visualization tools have been made publicly available on the GitHub platform. Specifically, the tool used to display the system's dynamic behavior was written using the programming language Python, whereas the core analysis was conducted using the libraries Eigen and ARB, renowned for their capabilities in the field of symbolic dynamics. As for the parameter set simulations, we utilized the ARb library's ability to perform parameter set simulations based on the system's elementary polynomial equations. This approach proved to be particularly efficient in terms of computational resource utilization. A comprehensive documentation of the code has also been prepared and included in the repository. This research provides novel insights into the system's dynamic behavior, offering potential applications in the modeling of pre-transitional phenomena within climate change research. Researchers proposed the Facet Pivot algorithm as an enhancement to the Vertex Pivot algorithm for efficiently solving linear programming problems. Facet Pivot algorithms, which utilize advanced technologies like parallel computing, excel particularly in solving problems with sparse constraints that exhibit a shallow degree of generality. Initially, the algorithm was implemented using a topological ordering method to identify feasible improvements, but later variants utilize pre-analysis techniques to achieve significant performance gains. Notably, the algorithm's efficacy was demonstrated in the context of a parallel computing framework utilized by industry leaders in the aerospace sector, specifically for solving a specific sub-class of network flow problems characterized by low ranks. In this paper, the underlying principles and implementation details of the Facet Pivot algorithm are discussed based on its application in the Bosco optimizer, which has been successfully integrated with Apache Optimizer Framework Incubation and currently utilized by multiple clients in various scenarios. Furthermore, the paper includes comprehensive benchmarks comparing the Bosco optimizer with other top-notch optimizers across a wide range of problem classes. Interestingly, the results show that the Bosco optimizer consistently outperforms other optimizers or achieves comparable performance for vertex-based optimizers across various problem classes. It's worth noting that the Bosco optimizer's facet-based approach occasionally exhibits slower timing compared to vertex-based algorithms, but its solutions generally exhibit better quality. Interestingly, the exceptional performance of the Bosco optimizer is particularly noticeable in problem scenarios characterized by sparse constraints and low rank. In particular, the algorithm's efficacy is evident in scenarios where the rank exceeds the number of variables or, more specifically, when the rank equals the number of variables. Moreover, the results suggest that the exceptional performance of the Bosco optimizer is not entirely due to its parallel computing capabilities, as it continues to outperform other optimizers even in the sequential setting. Notably, the algorithm's exceptional performance is also observed in certain problem classes characterized by high dimensions and low ranks. Overall, the research indicates that the Facet Pivot algorithm is an effective enhancement that consistently outperforms the Vertex Pivot algorithm, delivering better results across a range of problem classes. Consequently, the results suggest that the Facet Pivot algorithm should be a valuable addition to optimization toolkits, particularly when tackling certain classes of sparse optimization problems. In light of these findings, the paper includes a simple demonstration of the algorithm's efficacy in the context of a widely-known machine learning-based problem. Specifically, the researchers demonstrate that the Bosco optimizer can consistently outperform other optimizers when solving maximum margin loss linear classification problems, often achieving up to 10 times faster timing

In our work, we explore an advanced generalization of Quillen-Suslin theory for graded rings, building upon the concept of graded projective modules. Unlike in non-graded algebraic theory, we encounter difficulties in identifying why graded projective modules freely generate their respective ideals, which stems from issues in proving the graded version of the fundamental lemma of Suslin. We overcome these challenges in the context of polynomial rings over group algebras, while examining the underlying reasons for why graded theory in these specific cases is more straightforward. We also derive new results in situations where enough projective modules in the graded plane are available, which in turn enables us to find new connections to generalized matrix languages, Wodzicki collages, and the study of determinants across various graded settings. To conclude, we delve into additional applications of our findings, which involve studying graded analogues of nilpotent layers and determinantal varieties. Throughout this journey, we find that graded theory not only presents novel, challenging problems but also offers a remarkable array of beautiful and intricate connections with other areas of mathematics. In particular, we discover that graded algebraic geometry, geometry, combinatorics, and numerical analysis are deeply intertwined in ways that are not immediately apparent from their respective classical frameworks. To facilitate further research in these interconnected domains, we will provide a comprehensive overview of the principal achievements in each field, followed by a detailed presentation of the principal tools and techniques utilized in our work, which leverages established results in graded algebra, geometry, and combinatorics, while also offering generalizations of the fundamental problem in generalized matrix languages that aligns with our findings in graded theory. In addition, we will provide a comprehensive exploration of the connections between graded theory and the study of determinants across various contexts, which yields notable outcomes in settings such as $R$-ordinary polynomial rings. Ultimately, we will outline several key challenges and questions that naturally arise from our work, which we hope will contribute to further advancements in these areas. In particular, we will provide a detailed overview of the difficulties in extending our findings to more general settings, such as rings with nilpotent ideals that do not satisfy the nilpotent degree condition, while highlighting the central role of localization in graded algebraic geometry, geometry, and combinatorics. We will also provide a detailed exploration of the generalization of the growth rate of the homologies of generalized collages and the study of determinants across graded settings, which yields notable outcomes in settings such as group rings over local fields. When examining differential top quark distributions, utilizing the narrow width approximation may lead to inaccurate or misleading conclusions, especially when interpreting experimental results. The issue arises from the fact that frequently used quantities like lepton charge asymmetry and top quark kinematic distributions are sensitive to next-to-leading order contributions from top quark decays, which are overlooked in the narrow width approximation. To quantify this discrepancy, variations in renormalization and factorization scales and dominant electroweak corrections were analyzed for selected asymmetry and top quark distribution observables. It was found that in top quark studies, adopting the narrow width approximation may result in underestimation of standard model backgrounds by as much as 10% and inaccuracies in top quark measurement results by as much as 1-2% (summed over systematic and theoretical uncertainties). Furthermore, it was observed that electroweak top quark decays contribute significantly to differential distributions, especially in instances where quantum chromodynamics processes dominate, emphasizing the necessity of incorporating these effects in the analysis. To facilitate accurate enough predictions, we suggest using low scales in the renormalization and factorization scheme, although this approach is associated with large residual uncertainties. Given the prominent role of top quark information in extending the Higgs and standard model boundaries, we believe that accurately accounting for resummation effects is essential for precise top quark analysis outcomes. The resummed asymptotic formulas provided here can serve as rapid assessment tools. The research findings will be used in a forthcoming analysis to measure the top quark's mass with the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The methods developed here can also be applied to other top quark studies. The code used for the calculations is made available for public use. The reference for the code is provided at the end. The rescaled code, which takes into account resummation effects, is provided in a separate note, which can be accessed through the provided link. Our investigation reveals that deep neural networks trained on large collections of images can also leverage knowledge from related domains, like video, through transfer learning. Focusing on facial anti-spoofing and person re-identification, we evaluate various architectures and training protocols for their effectiveness. Notably, models pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset, specifically the Vision Transformer, exhibit superior domain adaptation when applied to person re-identification tasks, surpassing traditional architectures. Moreover, combining Vision Transformer models with domain adaptation techniques yields remarkable enhancements in accuracy, up to 80%, for person re-identification tasks, underscoring the significance of methodological transfer learning. These findings demonstrate the potential of large-scale vision datasets to empower innovative applications in related domains. All implementation details are made available on GitHub via the following link: https://github.com/RuntingLi/TfLViT.

A particular aspect of its complexity arises from its nature of partially
observable systems where the current state of the system is influenced by its
past states and unrelated external factors. Recurrent Neural Networks exhibit
excellent performance in this area due to their capability to incorporate past
information in their decision-making processes. A study examining the use of
Recurrent Neural Networks in autonomous vehicle applications revealed that the
networks demonstrated superior performance when the observation input data
contained visual information of the road and surroundings, as well as when the
networks had access to the observation history during training. However, the
networks struggled with inconsistent results when provided with mixed datasets. 
To address this issue, the research introduced a novel type of Recurrent
Neural Network called the soft-RNN, to a value estimation method, which allows
for the effective incorporation of inconsistent results. A major advantage of
the proposed algorithm is its capability to process a large volume of data with
the aid of a parameter reduction technique, as a result, the accuracy of value
estimation increased significantly when using the soft-RNN in the evaluation of
autonomous driving systems with mixed datasets. 
Ultimately, the accuracy of decisions made by the soft-RNN is dependent on
the accuracy of the value estimation and edge cases where the network may not
be accurate. A failure case study was conducted to examine the performance of
the soft-RNN in such scenarios and to explore the potential of improving
the-nets by providing it with additional information from sensors, such as
camera, lidar, radar, and GPS.

accurate, such as when failure cases are linked to imperfect sensor data, 
imperfect environmental conditions, and lastly, system failures such as
hardware failure, so the proposed algorithm may need to be reevaluated in the
light of these factors.

evaluation of different algorithms and networks for value estimation in the area
of autonomous driving.

To increase overall search progress in Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (PEAs), we introduce a novel parent choice strategy that takes into account the fitness improvements yielded by each subpopulation during a current generation. In contrast to traditional PEAs feeding the fittest individuals to the next generation, this method deviates by using a more informed decision. Subpopulations are merged into a new population, with individuals selected based on a combination of their fitness scores and the improvements yielded by their subpopulations. Empirical evidence is presented to confirm that our model accurately reflects this informed decision. Experiments across three real-world optimization problems reveal enhanced convergence in PEAs utilizing this novel technique. Notably, this approach can be seamlessly integrated with existing PEAs without necessitating changes to their algorithms. Moreover, we investigate the potential of incorporating a variance-based metric as an additional factor to aid in parent selection. Initial findings suggest that parent selection using variance can be a valuable decision support tool, though its influence on search progress appears to be problem-dependent. Further research is necessary to fully explore this technique's implications. Consequently, this parent selection strategy might be suitable for adapting existing PEAs to varying problem settings. Finally, we discuss theoretical possibilities for leveraging information about fitness improvements, including variants that operate within specific computational constraints. These variants can be seen as evolutionary algorithms with reduced memory requirements. In particular, we explore a variant that eliminates the memory requirement for storing population information, resulting in an EA that adapts its population over multiple runs. Search progress in this EA is informed by the last encountered subpopulation. Results indicate that this EA is capable of replicating the performance of the PEA algorithm. Given its simplicity and the absence of additional memory requirements, this EA is a reliable candidate algorithm. Research suggests that this EA is a suitable tool for setting up experiments, though its effectiveness is largely dependent on specific problem characteristics. Moreover, we identify a scenario in which this EA is capable of converging to optimal solutions across a range of problems. This research lays the groundwork for an interesting investigation into the computational complexity of the PEA algorithm when applied to artificial polynomial landscapes. It is essential to note that our parent selection strategy has the potential to widen the applicability of PEAs to previously intractable problem classes. In the final section, the implications of our research for future developments in evolutionary algorithms are considered. These future developments could encompass varied, increasingly complex domains such as artificial intelligence, computer vision, and machine learning. To future researchers, we suggest an emphasis on crafting innovative techniques to harness information from fitness landscape areas

The relationship between the microlensing phenomenon and the physical properties of the involved celestial bodies is highly relevant to the study of the distribution of dark matter in the galaxy. By making use of the distance and angular size measurements derived from microlensing events, it is possible to obtain an estimate for the mass of the central object. This approach has provided insights into the physical characteristics of the objects producing these events. Although it has been observed that the majority of microlensing events come from stars with masses around the solar range, the objects responsible for larger magnifications can have masses varying widely, ranging from less than the solar mass up to approximately twenty times it. Recent research has led to a better understanding of the characteristics of massive microlenses, however there is a need for further studies, incorporating a comprehensive analysis of larger samples that take into consideration the differential distribution of lensing stellar masses across varying directions. This research aims at filling this knowledge gap by developing a method that allows for the measurement of the masses of microlensing stars within the galaxy. This method makes use of the distances and angular sizes of the stars to derive an estimate for their mass. By applying this approach to a large dataset of stellar masses from different lines of sight, it is possible to obtain a more precise estimate for the contribution that microlensing stars make to the overall dark matter in the galaxy. Furthermore, it is predicted that for certain sight lines with high densities of ultra-low mass stars, these stars could potentially account for a significant fraction of the dark matter in these areas, although it is expected that for most other sight lines with fewer ultra-low mass stars, these stars would not significantly affect the overall dark matter in these areas. On the other hand, it has been found that for one particular line of sight with high density of ultra-low mass stars, the contribution to the dark matter is significant at a level of $2.6\cdot10^{-3}$. We found that this dynamical protection, known as cochleae enhancement, can be achieved by combining planar micromotion with constant thermal forcing. It is most effective when the system follows a specific harmonic path and when the thermal forcing overpasses a certain threshold, after which cooling may actually occur. Observing this method's potential will depend on various factors, including the size of the system, the shape of its potential barrier, and the duration of the system's lifetime. Experimentally, cochleae enhancement has been identified in an ion trap system, where ions following harmonic paths within a certain barrier experience enhanced coherence for a limited time period. This research indicates that robust dynamical protection can be implemented through simple micromotion and may open new avenues for the investigation of out-of-equilibrium dynamics and the management of quantum information. The potential to apply this method in different physical systems is also present and may contribute to the advancement of two quantum bit systems. It is also feasible to adapt this protection method to larger and more complex many-body systems. There are existing technologies that can implement this method in different physical systems, such as superconducting qubits, optical cavities, and hybrid systems. It is also possible to implement this protection method in different phases of systems, such as topological insulators, non-Hermitian systems, and many-body systems with local interaction. It is also feasible to extend the concept of planar enhancement to other types of symmetries in different physical systems. It is also possible to apply the idea of amplifying coherence in time-based systems, such as electronic components. However, the current research only confirms the existence of planar enhancement in ion traps and requires confirmation in other types of physical systems. It is also possible to apply the idea of amplifying coherence in systems with multiple layers and apply this idea to different types of physical systems, such as nanowires and graphene. However, the current research does not confirm the existence of amplifying coherence in systems with multiple layers and confirms the existence of amplifying coherence in electronic components based on semiconductors. It is also possible to extend the concept of amplifying coherence to different metrics, such as entanglement and work. Consequently, the concept of amplifying coherence may contribute to the management of quantum information in different physical systems.

We undertook a comprehensive examination of the HINSA (Highly Variable Species) web, including N$_2$IO, to accurately map its emission and to determine varying fractional abundances based on different latitudes. This research explores the feasibility of incorporating voice-based specifications via natural language assertions to facilitate the formal verification of imperative programs, particularly those that cannot be modeled using mathematical formulas. Our proposed method involves translating voice-based specifications and program code into formal mathematical expressions, using a particular logical framework that is suitable for mechanical verification. Although the idea has existing solutions for program code written in a mathematical notation, the problem becomes more complex when dealing with voice-based specifications, due to the inherent translation errors. To overcome this, we developed two novel formal methods, one of which deals with the direct translation of voice-based specifications and the other with the subsequent processing of these translations. Our results demonstrate that voice-based specifications can be utilized in program verification, and we discuss the limitations of our method while identifying potential areas for further improvement. Additionally, we examine the practicality of voice-based specification use through user surveys. Our survey reveals that, although some program verification cases may not require voice-based specifications, it is still a viable and practical method for other types of verification, such as verifying closed-box constraints for program inputs. Moreover, we discovered that voice-based specifications have better performance on complex cases, but may be slower on simple cases. Ultimately, we discuss the potential applications and boundaries of voice-based specification use. Our formal method and verification process, along with the necessary translation tools, as well as the specifications and program verifications discussed in this research, are available online for public access.  A associated video explanation of this research can be found here. Our work uncovers numerous voice-based logical metaphors, such as the use of voice for negation, quantification over hypothetical situations, and quantification over past or future scenarios, which are not exploitable via text-based translation. Moreover, we show that voice-based specifications can be used to simplify the translation process from formal mathematical expressions to natural language, particularly when program hypotheses are involved. Ultimately, we believe that voice-based specification has the potential to become an attractive and prevalent method in program verification. Our research highlights several unresolved problems that need to be addressed in the future. Firstly, we need to streamline the formal translation process, particularly when dealing with intricate program structures or logic. Secondly, we need to leverage voice-based logical metaphors to enhance the expression capacity of natural language. Canopus is a distributed optimization protocol that ensures the resilience of distributed systems against single point failures by designing robust solution techniques in the basis of Black-box optimization methods. The existing Canopus protocol, however, is vulnerable to unique failures that do not affect its properties. We have developed RCanopus, a modified version of Canopus, to counteract this vulnerability, leveraging the concept of quorum covers to increase its resistance to failures. RCanopus enhances the existing solution schemes with fault-tolerant modifications, enhancing the existing properties while maintaining compatibility with a wide range of baselines, including stochastic gradient descent. We have explored RCanopus in the context of stochastic convex optimization for numercal testing purposes. Our analysis demonstrates that RCanopus can robustly handle failures previously able to compromise the Canopus protocol. The code for RCanopus is openly available on the GitHub repository located at https://github.com/complex-systems/RCanopus. Within the context of object detection, current approaches have focused on
enhancing data-driven uncertainty estimations for task inference and
object localization. Although uncertainties have crucial implications in
multiple fields, the underlying models are generally viewed as standalone
quantities. In contrast, we introduce the BayesOD framework, where uncertainty
is represented as a probability distribution governing the object detector's
parameters. Utilizing Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, BayesOD generates
multiple model configurations, thereby simulating an object detection process
to derive not only uncertainty estimations but also informative outcomes,
such as the distribution of object categories, poses, and confidences. When
evaluated on ImageNet and PASCAL datasets utilizing variations of a VOC model,
the BayesOD framework exhibited a substantial reduction in prediction errors
comparable to state-of-the-art uncertainty estimation techniques for object
detection. Notably, BayesOD's predictive distributions comprised notably lower
variances for misidentified objects and substantially higher variances for correct
objects, signifying the framework's capacity to both recognize objects and
express uncertainty around their identification. The implications of this work
extend beyond uncertainty estimation, enabling applications in object
tracking, multi-object interpolation, and uncertainty-based object
localization. Full details, model implementations, and data can be accessed at
https://bayesod.github.io. Lastingly, the BayesOD framework provides an
approach for incorporating implicit uncertainties within object detectors and
emphasizes the necessity of incorporating uncertainty in deep learning models
for accurate decision-making in critical applications. All framework sources are
available on https://github.com/bayesOD/GaussianObjectDetector. Lastingly, the
BayesOD framework provides an approach for incorporating implicit uncertainties
within object detectors and stresses the necessity of incorporating uncertainty
in deep learning models for precise decision-making in critical applications. 
All framework sources are available on https://github.com/bayesOD/GaussianObjectDetector.

This paper explores Unet++ as a template for developing efficient deep learning models suitable for real-time traffic forecasting applications. To validate the potential of Unet++, we conduct a thorough examination of its internal mechanisms and comparable state-of-the-art convolutional models. This analysis delves into three primary aspects: feature learning capabilities, internal data representation in intermediate feature maps, and the effectiveness of bi-directional data alignment. Following the evaluation, we propose enhancements to Unet++ that further enhance its performance within the traffic forecasting domain. Specifically, we recommend the gradual downsampling strategy at the encoder end and retaining residual connections to improve internal data representation. This paper further compares the computational complexity of the improved Unet++ model against other state-of-the-art models. The results demonstrate that Unet++ surpasses competing models in terms of predictive accuracy and computational efficiency, making it an ideal choice for real-time traffic forecasting applications. This study further highlights the exposure's significance in deep learning, suggesting that active learning-based exposure generation can effectively bridge the gap between real-world and simulated data. We then introduce the concept of a fully coherent precategory of rewriting models, where the strategy used to fire rewriting rules is also defined as a precategory. Building on these definitions, we adapt them to the case of a category with partial equality, yielding a new class of categories with partial equality that are of particular interest in the study of algebraic theories. Finally, we establish the possibility of representing any algebraic theory as a category with partial equality, where the corresponding rewriting system is derived from the theory's defining equations. This rewriting system is shown to be coherent and quasi-confluent, and its partial equality relation, when considered within the corresponding precategory, becomes a genuine equality relation. This result provides a new insight into the connection between algebraic theories, their corresponding precategories of rewriting models, and the various notions of equality associated with these precategories. Automated hippocampus segmentation is crucial for assessing atypical development and
predicting outcomes in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy, especially those with
hippocampus resections.  We conducted a study to find out if hippocampus
configuration affects segmentation accuracy and whether training models on
limited data from patients with intact hippocampi is sufficient for accurate
results in those with hippocampus resections. We analyzed two, publicly available:
(1) a dataset with medical images from patients who had undergone
epilepsy surgery (500 resected, 500 non-resected); and (2) a large dataset with
normal brain images (1100, 510 male; 1090, 510 female).  Hippocampus segmentations
were done using two different methods -  models that utilize the shape of the
hippocampus and those that use the signal intensity, then by mixing these two methods.
  Our study found out that current methods of hippocampus segmentation have lower
accuracy in cases where the shape of the hippocampus is altered.  We also noticed
that when developing automated analysis tools, collecting data from both normal cases
and cases where the hippocampus has been altered is very important for accurate
results in both groups. We recommend the use of special data processing techniques
(supervised adaption of segmentation models) that help bridge the gap between
normal and abnormal hippocampus configurations, ultimately increasing the
accuracy of hippocampus segmentation results.  By addressing these issues, we believe
we can make sure that hippocampus segmentation results are reliable and
representative. 
  Our study has been accepted as a poster at 2022 Conference of the International
Society for Magnetic Resonance in Biology, and will be presented in person. 

Keywords: hippocampus segmentation, epilepsy surgery, deep learning, MR imaging.

To guarantee the following mechanism's differential privacy, we develop a mechanism based on the Huber loss function and compare its performance to mechanisms based on Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms. The mechanism we create applies quantization to data before releasing it, using a optimization of the Laplace mechanism's deviation via variational approximation, which yields both a publicly available and a computationally private version. By testing on real datasets, we show that this mechanism achieves superior accuracy relative to the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms for both regression and classification tasks. Furthermore, we obtain significant improvements in classification precision, specifically up to $5.85\%$, and regression mean squared error, up to $0.46\%$. The Most Clicks Problem has been thoroughly researched in the context of recommendation systems, particularly with respect to the effectiveness of click prediction models.
