We revisit some fundamental aspects of the MCP, presenting new insights and highlights from the existing literature. The paper concentrates on the "global" aspect of the MCP, examining aspects that apply universally, such as the optimal grid size for testing, where we draw a parallel between the MCP and full rank and nullity concepts. Additionally, the paper revisits the first MCP model to pinpoint key innovations, offering an alternative interpretation of its success through the application of the Lorentzian K-means algorithm, and noting how its incorporation of angle-based similarity further bridges the gap between sparse and dense item lists. We end the section by discussing the Most Clicks problem from the standpoint of finding a balance between accurate recommendations and computational efficiency. As computational resources continue to scale, the demand for computationally efficient methods will only increase. We argue that the proposed MCP experiments serve as a suitable benchmark for evaluating algorithms, particularly those designed to handle large sparse matrices, where both quality and speed are essential. The paper does not focus on comparing the proposed MCP models to other methods but rather highlights their merits as promising candidates for large-scale recommendation tasks. The final consideration revolves around the role of communication costs, a critical concern in distributed MPC contexts, where we identify some interesting patterns and observe a parallel between the optimal number of rounds and the well-trodden doubling process known from the K-means algorithm. Finally, the paper ends by introducing possible integration points between the MCP and other prominent research areas, such as the SimRank and Networdek algorithms, to enhance our understanding of connected components and community discovery in complex networks. Real-world data in various domains, such as social networks, frequently contains data points that do not adhere to a given pattern or were inaccurately entered. It's essential to identify and isolate these data points to ensure subsequent analysis is accurate. A technique called Proximity Graph-based Outlier Detection has emerged that uses proximity graphs to identify outliers by analyzing a graph's local sub-connected components. Since the time complexity of this approach is affected by the types of connections in the original data, it can be inefficient and impractical in some scenarios. To improve this, a new type of proximity graph called the Modified Radius-based Graph has been developed. This MRPG exhibits better performance than existing proximity graphs, and when used for outlier detection, it outperforms the existing methods while having a significantly lower time complexity and requiring less memory usage. Experimental results using real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. Furthermore, the source code is freely accessible online. This research presents an in-depth analysis of the proposed algorithm by comparing it with traditional methods, such as Radius-based Graph and Modified Radius-based Degree Graph. It also explores how different parameters impact the accuracy and efficiency of the outlier detection process. As an extension of this research, a modification of the MRPG has been developed to accommodate weighted proximity graphs. This variant, called WMRPG, is capable of handling proximity graphs with varied edge weights, making it more applicable to real-world applications. It is worth noting that in such cases, data points are considered related only if they are connected directly or indirectly to a neighbor within a specific radius. Simulations using real-world datasets showed that WMPRG outperformed other weighted proximity graph methods in outlier detection, achieving a notable increase of up to 10% in the datasets from the IOannon dataset family. Similarly, it outperformed in the datasets from the Twitter Feeds dataset when focusing on a different metric of interest - recall. Furthermore, it was proven through analysis and experimentation that WMPRG is more resilient to hyperparameters than existing graph types. This variant, WMPRG, is more suitable for applications with distinct edge weights, and it is less affected by parameter sensitivity. Results from the evaluation process show that by using a specific approach to determine the radius - radio distance - WMPRG outperforms other graph types across various metrics. This variant also demonstrates better performance than other methods of selecting the radius - Iterative Lucas-Kanade and Van Neumann Gap clustering. When considering time complexity, WMPRG was proven to have a better performance than other methods.

In this research, a new approach referred to as the Review-Based Interactive Trust (RIT) model is presented. RIT aims to address this gap by developing a unified framework that integrates review reviews and interactive features to predict user preferences. Experimental results on real-world data sets demonstrate that RIT outperforms existing trust models, ultimately leading to improved accuracy in item recommendation. Furthermore, a deeper analysis of the model highlights the significant impact of review-based trust, indicating that interactive features can contradict review trust in predicting user preferences in certain situations. In practical applications, RIT is integrated with an online ranking algorithm called Online RIT (ORIT), which utilizes past interaction data and updates the trust model in real-time to recommend items. Experimental results show that ORIT effectively addresses uncertainty in user preferences and improves the diversity of top-recommended items. Consequently, the RIT model and its online variant, ORIT, offer item recommenders the ability to better understand and accommodate the complex aspects of human user preferences. Moreover, the models can benefit online retailers by increasing customer satisfaction, average purchase amounts, and ultimately, online revenue. Importantly, both models can utilize existing interaction history data without requiring additional user input. In practical terms, the RIT model and its online variant, ORIT, can be incorporated into e-commerce platforms, including Amazon, Google Shopping, and Facebook, to enhance item recommenders and increase user engagement. In doing so, the models can ultimately increase online revenue for retailers. Importantly, the models can utilize existing interaction history data without requiring additional user input. Ultimately, the RIT model and its online variant, ORIT, can be viewed as offering a superior solution to currently available trust models in recommenders, as they integrate a more comprehensive understanding of human user preferences and uncertainty. In terms of future research directions, one notable area is the exploration of the ethical implications and challenges associated with large-scale recommendation systems like RIT. In particular, the models can raise concerns regarding information overload, the propagation of biases, and unfair treatment of users, all of which are notable challenges in recommending items to users interactively. This study innovates by using translation probability as a guiding principle to create code-switched text by replacing consecutive English words with their corresponding non-English translations in bilingual text. Various translation models were tested, including character-level models trained on data from Google Translate, word-level models from the M-WMT14 dataset, and byte-level models from the Google Translate API. Results from evaluations and analyses on three datasets reveal that replacing English word segments produces higher FLEXT scores and greater improvements in BLEU scores than the original baseline, whereas concurrent Monte-Carlo sampling leads to more varied output and higher external validity scores. Interestingly, our findings on the ATIS dataset show that generated code-switching data can be used to misguide a English-based slot-filling model, creating a potential security vulnerability. This study contributes an automatic code-switching data generation method, providing a useful tool especially for languages with limited data. Moreover, our research outlines distinct types of synthetic code-switching data, expanding our understanding of this previously understudied area. The code for our approach can be accessed at https://github.com/18-Version/code-switching-synthesis. This study also includes synthesized data from two more languages, Dutch and Romanian, which can be found at https://github.com/18-Version/Dutch-RL-code-switching-RLP/tree/master/data. Our findings and code can inform the development of other code-switching data augmentation techniques. Ultimately, our research offers insights into the utilization of synthetic data in code-switching, serving as a foundation for future research in this area. Code for this study can be found at https://github.com/18-Version/Dutch-RL-code-switching-RLP. Our dataset can be used as a resource for various machine learning tasks and our research outcomes will guide future research in this area. The Google Translate API was used for data collection. Let $\Sigma$ be a compact surface with a non-empty boundary and let G be a subgroup of the diffeomorphisms of its interior, denoted as $\Sigma^0$. We examine the properties that G inherits from its action within $\Sigma^0$, including hyperbolicity, forward and reverse transitivity, and precompactness properties. We also investigate how these characteristics intersect to form a hierarchy among possible behaviors in this setting. Moreover, we broaden this framework by considering distinct geometric contexts: surfaces with a full boundary, surfaces featuring isolated points within their interior, and surfaces characterized as simply connected. Throughout our discussion, we provide detailed descriptions of specific subgroup actions that facilitate an understanding of these various scenarios. Ultimately, our review culminates in an exploration of open questions that challenge researchers to combat uncertainty in a wide range of circumstances. This work originates from a summer school program that introduced discrete subgroups, called torus knots, and their associated action within $\Sigma^0$. The document is available in full on arXiv. By capturing the essence of a particular moment in time, it aims to reflect the spirit of a gathering where both novice and experienced researchers convened to share their understanding of a complex topic. The document's initial presentation has been made available on YouTube. The core of the summer school's program was developed under the guidance of certain timing preferences. The document's content has been carefully structured to unfold at a precise moment in time. The core of the program has been divided into seven sections, with each corresponding to a distinct characteristic. The first section delves into hyperbolicity properties, presented by David Martel. The second section focuses on forward transitivity properties by Yvonne Buttle. The third section explores the precompactness properties by Svetlana Aguiar. The final three sections delve into various geometric contexts: isolated points by Sungjong Lee, simply connected surfaces by Rachel Roberts, and full boundaries by Jenifer Behlfar. The document also includes three appendices, featuring additional information by David Martel, Yvonne Buttle, and Svetlana Aguiar, as well as a list of problems identified by Rachel Roberts, Sungjong Lee, and Jenifer Behlfar. The program's content was overseen by Martel and Roberts. The document was organized by Roberts. The core of the program was developed under grant AGS-1602253. The summer school was hosted at Rutgers University. The program's content was made available online through Leaf Lahr's Collection

A mesh's accuracy depends not only on its meshes but also on the quality of each individual element. While many existing mesh quality metrics focus on coarseness or distortion, a new metric called elemental quality (EQ) has been developed to specifically measure the effect of elements on results and to prioritize elements that need improvement the most. EQ is formulated using data from isoparametric transformations to analyze elements and is specifically optimized for use with finite element methods. This approach has been tested on a variety of meshes from different domains and types and has been shown to effectively identify problematic elements that cause inaccurate results. In addition to its formula-based calculation, EQ can also be visualized using an EQ-based renderer that displays the mesh according to the estimated quality of each element, indicating which elements need to be improved to yield accurate computational results. This renderer is available for public use at https://graphie.github.io/equ/Equation-of-State-Renderer.html. Equ has also been applied to the remeshing process, producing improved meshes that yield precise results even when coarse meshes are initially used. This is because the EQ-based renderer suggests the most suitable element sizes for the mesh refinement process. By leveraging the power of the finite element method, Equ provides users with effective tools for both improving mesh quality and refining meshes to achieve accurate computational results. Knowledge graphs like Wikidata, DBpedia, and YAGO are enhanced with new links through a process called link prediction, which uses information from relation extraction to identify likely connections between entities. This research focuses on link prediction for attribute-attribute relations, where it analyzes two types of attributes, entities that can be found online, and values associated with those entities. To tackle this challenge, the authors developed a technique to discover missing attributes for an existing entity by examining, collecting, and combining data from content platforms like Wikipedia and web APIs. This technique was then applied to enhance Wikidata, yielding over 14 million new attribute-attribute relationships that were found in just 48 minutes without requiring manual input. A thorough evaluation confirmed the accuracy and usability of the acquired data, demonstrating potential to significantly expand knowledge graphs like Wikidata. The mathematical framework used for this model analysis is comprised of a piecewise linear function based on critical path technology mapping. The efficacy of the proposed model was evaluated in terms of absolute error, where it was found to be in alignment with SPICE simulations across various process nodes with minimal discrepancies. The new model also demonstrates its ability to achieve absolute errors less than 10% with respect to 30% static delay error in SPICE simulations. Consequently, this delay model can be utilized effectively to enable rapid design space exploration and optimization within electronic systems. The proposed model is currently available for evaluation and future research purposes. Furthermore, it is also intended that this model can be integrated into electronic design automation toolflows in the future. Although the proposed model is developed specifically for analyzing MOSFET delays, it is also capable of being extended to encompass the delays experienced by other types of transistors. The potential mechanisms that could enable this extension are discussed in further detail within this thesis. Offline reinforcement learning for continuous state-action spaces is challenging, largely due to current methods' inadequate theories of learning without experiences. The widely-used optimality gap in offline ORL is not a suitable measure of learning without experiences. We introduce a novel criterion based on the smoothness of optimal value functions to resolve this issue. To facilitate the implementation of our proposed criterion, we coarse-grain the state-action space based on local optimality such that optimal value functions exhibit smoothness across these coarse states. We leverage coarse scheduling to combine our criterion with coverage of the state-action space, achieving a more effective learning outcome. We validate the efficacy of our method through theoretical analysis and experiments on an Offline Pendulum benchmark. We demonstrate that our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art offline ORL techniques and delivers better coverage of the state-action space. Additionally, we observed that our method yields more interpretable optimal actions with our coarse-graining approach. We further showcase the applicability of our scheduling method in online reinforcement learning settings involving continuous state-action spaces. We found that our method offers significant speedup over existing techniques, accelerating learning by as much as 60%. We propose a novel dataset called IP6 to facilitate research in offline ORL, available at https://github.com/danielwang22/Offline-Pendulum-6D. Our code for learning in continuous state-action spaces is also published at https://github.com/danielwang22/LinQo. We offer additional empirical results at https://github.com/danielwang22/Offline-Pendulum-6D. We advocate for the promotion of offline ORL datasets with higher dimensions to address existing biases. We highlight that our scheduling method can benefit from approximating local optimality, enabling optimal value functions to exhibit smoothness across coarse states. Consequently, our method has less dependency on the level of coarse scheduling and achieves better results when the state-action space is more dimensional. We encourage researchers to address the issue of optimal value function smoothness in offline ORL and pursue deeper analysis of our proposed criterion. We encourage readers to watch our video at https://youtu.be/0Y8mHamT0L4 for better comprehension of our work. This study examines the interplay between visual categorization systems and agency in the perception of animacy. While previous research has focused on distinct aspects of animacy, such as agency and visual categorization, our research explores how these both contribute to our understanding of the animacy spectrum. We utilize a visual representation manipulation technique to probe the visual system for categorization and agency, as well as animacy. Our categorization tasks, agency tasks, and animacy tasks tap into various levels of visual detail, from coarse to fine, to understand how categorization and agency influence our visual perception of animacy. Notably, our results show that both categorization and agency independently contribute to our understanding of the animacy spectrum, and that visual agency is more sensitive to fine detail. Additionally, our data suggest that agency is a key factor that differentiates humans and animals, and that categorization tasks cannot distinguish between the two. This distinction between agency and categorization explains the known outliers in human visual perceptions, and illuminates the distinct mechanisms that drive our visual understanding of the animacy spectrum. This study also sheds light on the complexity of the animacy spectrum by highlighting cases like birds, which do not fit easily into our visual categorization systems yet are universally considered animate. Overall, our research paints a more intricate picture of how we visually perceive the animacy spectrum, and highlights the distinct roles that agency and categorization play in this perception. Our results suggest that future research should focus on the interplay between agency and categorization, and how these influence our visual perceptions of the animacy spectrum, and inform our understanding of the complexities of the animacy spectrum. Such research may ultimately lead to a more nuanced comprehension of the subtleties of visual animacy perception in human perception. X-ray analyses of the G22.9+0.2 by Swift and the MAXI telescope revealed that G22.9+0.2, a possible supernova remnant, has been associated with a black hole candidate, EXTRASwift J1820.0+1441, at its quiescence state, except for a 2-day X-ray outburst in November 2017.  This outburst was analyzed based on Swift and MAXI data which showed that the source transitioned through various stages during that interval.  Data from the Swift observations indicated that EXTRASwift J1820.0+1441 had exhibited characteristics of accretion powered X-ray pulsars with a fixed frequency during the middle stage of that outbreak but a distinct change occurred with a rising frequency when the source transitioned to an intermediate state and a 2.5 times frequency drop when it entered into the hard-intermediate state.  It also showed that the source exhibited an additional type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) that faded as the source entered into a hard state in that outbreak.  Data from the MAXI observations also showed that the source exhibited an additional type-C QPOs that faded when the source entered into a hard state in that outbreak.  Additional analyses indicate that the QPOs fading as the source entered into a hard state in that outbreak could be explained as a consequence of a cooling of the outer part of the accretion disk due to a decrease in the corona's efficiency in generating synchrotron cooling in the outer part of that disk. To facilitate scalable multi-agent reinforcement learning, the concept of transfer empowerment can enhance the performance of an agent transitioning between varying collaboration scenarios and uncoordinated environments. Empowerment measures the maximum achievable influence an agent can have on the environment, serving as a maximization objective that underlies many multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms. However, the original empowerment objective is often impossible to optimize directly in complex situations, which led to the development of the cross entropy method for estimation. Unfortunately, this method may not be suitable for all situations. In an effort to improve this, researchers have constructed a sequence of approximations that allow for the optimization of more complex, abstract objectives. These approximations, derived from variational versions of generalized Kullback-Leibler divergence, are used to facilitate empowerment estimation in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Estimating empowerment allows for the definition of a benchmark objective that boosts the performance of reinforcement learning agents, which was demonstrated through applications in various dynamic settings including independent identically distributed tasks and interconnected systems. These results show that the use of variational approximations has significant practical implications for improving the performance of existing multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms in these challenging scenarios. Moreover, the proposed approximations provide empirical guarantees on the quality of the estimation, which varies depending on the intrinsic complexity of the objective function. Results indicate that the use of approximations can significantly improve the performance of existing multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms in different settings. Moreover, the empirical guarantees provided align well with observed experimental outcomes, which highlights their practical value in guiding algorithm design and improving reinforcement learning tasks. By leveraging these approximations, researchers can design tailored variational objectives that maximize the cumulative reward in targeted scenarios, which offers a new paradigm for multi-agent reinforcement learning. As such, the proposed approximations have broad applications and can be utilized in other fields where maximizing intrinsic motivation or empowerment is relevant. Moreover, the approximations' generalization properties make them suitable for targeted but unknown distribution settings, which further increases their practical utility. Lastly, the use of approximations in online learning settings allows for the development of near optimal policies that can adapt to changing situations, which aligns with current research trends in this area. Discovering novel substances is a crucial aspect of various scientific endeavors, as it involves identifying objects seen for the first time. Present techniques for this are unsatisfactory, particularly when substances are misidentified or when objects are seen in unusual contexts. Training models to adapt to unfamiliar substances is an expensive and time-consuming process, as it often relies on extensive datasets. We propose a novel machine learning approach called one-shot learning, which allows models to accurately identify an object seen only once. We collected a vast dataset of 80,000 images of 228 substances, which we used to train a deep learning model capable of classifying substances. This model was then compared to existing models, including a ResNet-50, in terms of performance on substances seen for the first time. Results indicated that combining our one-shot learning method with transfer learning using a pre-trained models produced 74% accuracy for substances seen for the first time, while a pre-trained ResNet-50 achieved a mere 22% accuracy for substances seen for the first time. This new approach is crucial for identifying unfamiliar substances under diverse conditions. The complete dataset is available for research purposes at https://github.com/joeljfb/dataset_anomaly_chemistry. This work has been accepted for presentation at the 2022 ICASSP conference. A pre-trained model capable of classifying substances is available at https://github.com/joeljfb/one-shot-learning. A video illustrating our one-shot learning approach is available at https://youtu.be/OPKQ6d4lamA. A demo of our project is available at https://joeljfb.github.io/one-shot-learning/. 

Machine learning has been successfully applied to various chemical identification tasks in recent years. However, when analyzing diverse substances under unusual conditions, even the advanced models available today are often unreliable. We propose a novel deep learning approach that enables the identification of substances seen only once and under unprecedented circumstances by combining the knowledge within large datasets. This is analogous to how humans learn new words by relating them to existing words in their vocabulary. We training our model to specific areas of interest within a vast dataset of 80,000 images of 228 substances, which allows it to adapt to unfamiliar substances. As an example of its potential, when presented with images of only one example from each of three classes (e.g., aluminum, copper, and steel), our model is able to accurately classify a test image from an entirely new category. This cohomology framework extends Lie and Bundles cohomologies, capturing the intricate 2-group-like actions and transformations. By analyzing the lower-degree cohomologies, we obtain insights into their intrinsic properties. Specifically, the first cohomology class reflects automorphisms, the second cohomology class reflects deformations, and the third cohomology class relates to coboundaries of crossings, providing a comprehensive understanding of these structures. Opaque structures within these maps render incomplete measurements that distort the actual magnetic field. Consequently, the magnetic packing factor must be accounted for in order to extract the intergranular magnetic field environment accurately. However, the application of inversion codes that do not consider magnetic packing factor can lead to distorted results. Researchers have suggested, for instance, that the depth of penetration is directly related to the magnetic field strength. In this study, we investigate how taking into account magnetic packing factor in deep penetration imaging improves the accuracy of depth measurements. We found that applying the magnetic packing factor correction yields improved depth measurements regardless of the inversion code used. In fact, the magnitude of the correction factor depends on the type of inversion code employed. When the upper atmospheric field strength is 1000 G, we found that applying the magnetic packing factor correction results in a 20% to 70% improvement in depth measurements. In contrast, for fields stronger than 800 G, we found that applying the magnetic packing factor correction reduces errors associated with depth measurements. We used TERRA MODIS satellite imagery to track active fires from 2000 to 2016 across Peru's Amazonas, Loreto, and Ucayali regions, and analyzed the data as a mean field model with diffusion. The analysis focused on annual fire seasons, and we incorporated findings into multi-scale interpretations. Despite initial skepticism due to to the 'ignition and propagation' model of fire onset, which suggests fires are primarily initialized in low elevation regions, and then spread, our results showed regions at higher elevations exhibited greater trend stability. Furthermore, mean field models can be used to simulate fire growth. Total fire sizes in the analyzed regions were small, averaging less than 10% of their respective areas, and fires were most prevalent at the region's borders. Region-specific trends in fire activity varied. Total fire sizes differed significantly, with the Amazonas region having the smallest average, and the Ucayali region the largest. Fire counts in the analyzed regions demonstrated mixed trends. Fire seasons in the Amazonas, Loreto, and Ucayali regions showed decreasing, mixed, and increasing activity respectively. Region-specific factors likely influenced the outcomes. Notably, mean fire sizes in the analyzed regions were uniform, ranging between 37 and 42 square kilometers. Fire counts in the analyzed regions showed significant correlation with total fire sizes in subsequent seasons, indicating the potential to use this data for predictions. However, modeling the spread of fires as a mean field process may not accurately capture individual fire characteristics when they are small in comparison to the region as a whole. Nonetheless, this approach can leverage simple models to utilize this data for predictions. Moreover, utilizing geostatistical methods may help to tailor models to specific scales, and thereby enhance predictive accuracy.

In practical quantum key distribution, generating a key solely based on a source's randomness would be ideal, requiring only a single estimate of its average min-entropy. We examine what happens when this estimate is uncertain, potentially influenced by multiple post-source measurements. Our analysis shows that when these measurements are taken after the source's randomness has been utilized, they don't impact the secure data transfer rate. Conversely, if the source's randomness is assessed prior to utilizing its randomness, the secure data transfer rate is diminished. To illustrate the implications of these findings, we take the specific example of generating a key using the blockwise von Neumann entropy and its relation to the shrinker in quantum key distribution, showing that when the source's entropy is unknown, it's as though the source's efficiency is reduced. We also verify our results through a practical test: conducting a key distribution experiment without making adjustments for the source's uncertainty, and comparing this to the secure key rate estimated by the THREESHADE algorithm, which also doesn't account for post-source measurements. Ultimately, we suggest that if the secure key rate is substantially reduced due to an uncertain source, a further post-source measurement that estimates and utilizes the source's randomness can recover much of this reduction. Once again, we verify this by comparing this strategy to the secure key rate estimated by the THREESHADE algorithm, showing that if the source's entropy is known, it's as though the source's efficiency is recovered. The research paper in question investigates the stochastic differential equation (SDE) that underlies the success of invasive species in the context of spatially and temporally adaptive invasion dynamics. Specifically, the SDE incorporates mutational steps that can be likened to a birth-death process characterized by a dimension $N$ in $R_N$, where $N$ represents the number of population groups. Given the equation's structure, we demonstrate that it exhibits analytical solvability and analyze its key parameters, in particular the invasion speed, when mutations become rare. As a consequence, we distinguish between two primary scenarios: subcritical ($N=1$) and supercritical ($N>1$) diffusion modes, where the latter accommodates multiple population types undergoing mutations. Furthermore, we outline two specific methods for solving the equation: a functional approach applicable to both sub- and supercritical cases with limited diffusion, and a stochastic phase-field approach specifically tailored to supercritical scenarios with extensive diffusion. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the supercritical equation can be reduced to a deterministic diffusion equation governed by the minimizer of an associated variational free energy subject to constraints. In addition, the stochastic phase-field equation provides a probabilistic interpretation of the deterministic equation's initiation of invasions near equilibrium points. The methods discussed here can be readily extended to analyze invasion dynamics involving multiple competing species, a scenario explored in a companion paper. The authors recognize the inspiration and foundational contributions of J. Simons and M. Escobés-Ruiz in the initial phases of this research. The work is further supplemented by an appendix that sheds light on the equation's structure and its analytical solutions, as well as a more in-depth exploration of the method used in the study, in particular the central role played by the equation's drift coefficient, a quantity known as the conditional invasion spread rate, an object of interest in itself. The authors acknowledge and respond to certain mathematical objections raised regarding the method's applicability and its range of validity, in particular to challenges raised by J. Simons and M. Escobés-Ruiz regarding the method's applicability to supercritical scenarios with extensive diffusion. The work concludes by outlining a number of potential future research directions, in particular the application of the method in the context of multi-species competition dynamics, as explored in a companion paper, and the further development of the method to analyze spatial adaptation, an object of future research within the authors' future research agenda. The standard approach to these matrices, however, assumes coherent quantum feedback without considering any time-related delays. We have now expanded the N-photon scattering matrix concept to incorporate delayed coherent feedback and have developed a broad category of scattering matrices that encompass diverse quantum feedback models. We have derived an analytical solution for these general matrices, which can be expressed as a series of terms involving matrix products. We have also found that despite the complexity of delayed feedback, N-photon scattering matrices remain relatively easy to calculate for Qubit-Cavity-Microcavity systems. We have further demonstrated that our results are applicable to a range of quantum systems, including those with complex structures. We have specifically verified this approach for two specific systems: a three-level atom and a quantum box with electric dipole interaction. We have determined the N-photon scattering matrices for these systems in closed forms and verified their analytic expressions. The theory of boosted dark matter with low-energy spin properties has been largely unexplored, largely due to a lack of suitable effective operators that conserve Lorentz symmetry. In this research, we establish a generalized description of spin-dependent dark matter interactions that incorporate boosted components through modified wave functions. Then, we apply this framework to interpret the results of existing experiments and to assess the sensitivity of upcoming experiments to these interactions. Remarkably, our findings reveal that in many instances, the interactions yielding the anomalous boost factors result in significantly lower limits on the interaction strength compared to the standard contact interaction model, thus making these scenarios potentially more resilient. Nonetheless, our analysis also identifies a few scenarios where the anomalous boost factors remain undetectable by current experiments, thereby opening up new opportunities for constraint settings with better experimental reach. Finally, to facilitate a deeper understanding of these novel interactions, we provide a direct model example illustrating their origins. In particular, our example demonstrates how the anomalous boost factors can arise from scalar or vector mediators with mass below $\mathcal{O}(100\,{\mathrm{GeV}})$. Moreover, our analysis reveals that in the limit of very large interaction strength, the anomalous boost factors can result in a non-linear relationship between the interaction parameters and the limits set on the interaction strength. In general, our analysis discloses new avenues for investigating various aspects of sub-GeV dark matter with both spin-dependent and spin-independent properties. In order to aid in future research, our analysis provides a comprehensive code called MadDarkBoost, which computes the one-loop loop integrals required for low-energy dark matter interactions. Our analysis can be further extended by our additional research where we investigate the possibility that the anomalous boost factors can originate from a $10\%$-$40\%$ inelasticity in the dark matter component. A case in point is shown in the study of nonlinear lattice systems, such as the nonlinear lattice system characterized by nonlinear site-to-site coupling, which, despite its widespread occurrence, remains poorly understood. Crucially, the results confirm that the system's ordered states can arise not only despite frustration, but also as a result of it, and that the interplay of nonlinear dynamics and frustration can give rise to complex resonant patterns of chaos. In this study, we examine how the eigenvalues of random Hermitian matrices within a specific range change when its band width is varied. These matrices are derived from discrete versions of continuous distributions, such as the complex Gaussian and the Laplace. Regardless of the distribution, as the band widens, the eigenvalue distribution shifts from a localized, unique pattern to a standardized form that depends exclusively on the band's dimensions. Additionally, we investigate the effects of discrete sampling on the eigenvalue distribution, discovering that, although discrete effects persist in high dimensions, they diminish with increasing matrix size. Discrete effects are particularly noticeable in small matrices and sub-Gaussian-sized matrices but disappear in extremely large matrices. However, in intermediate scenarios, the eigenvalue distribution displays a mixture of two distinct limit theorems, blending in with increasing matrix size. This behavior is quantified through a dimensionless parameter that represents the ratio of the band's dimensions to the matrix's square root, with the parameter's use dependent on the distribution's nature. For the complex Gaussian distribution, this parameter is simply the band's width divided by the square root of its size. In contrast, the Laplace distribution requires an adjustment factor of 1/3 in place of 1/2 for more accurate comparisons, with these numbers corresponding to the respective systems' mean squared errors. Importantly, within certain bands and dimensions, the time evolution of the eigenvalues, driven by the non-Hermitian matrix's diagonal and off-diagonal dynamics, follows a unifying pattern that is influenced by these parameters and can be characterized as a unifying pattern of periodic motion embedded in an otherwise randomized trajectory. Notably, the period and distance covered during this periodic motion are directly accessible through a dimensionless parameters. This study's findings are further validated by discrete effects detected in low-dimensional matrices, where the ordering and proximity of their eigenvalues depend on discrete sampling, resulting in a pattern that is independent of the distribution, much like in the Hermitian case. Nonetheless, in extremely large matrices, the ordering and proximity of its eigenvalues converge to a standardized form that depends exclusively on the band's dimensions. Moreover, in intermediate scenarios, the ordering and proximity of its eigenvalues display a blended pattern of two distinct limit theorems, with the same dimensionless parameters used in the Hermitian case to quantify this blending. To enhance the efficiency of language models in grasping semantic relationships within dialogues, we developed a specialized knowledge filter that incorporates these relationships. This customized filter leverages external knowledge to improve the naturalness and coherence of generated text. We implemented a knowledge filter for the dialogue domain by adapting the Borges model, which draws knowledge from a semantic network during decoding. This allowed us to validate the importance of external knowledge in producing well-formulated text. Notably, the Borges model with the dialogue filter outperformed the existing TOP model in terms of beam search diversity using only 10 generated sentences, without sacrificing coherence or meaning. Furthermore, the Borges model with the dialogue filter surpassed the TOP model in METER and BLEU metrics, with even greater gains observed when it was compared to other models like GLaS and RUMOR. Additionally, when we used the LENGTH metric to assess text length variability, the results indicated that the Borges model with the dialogue filter exhibited greater variability in length compared to the TOP model. Lastly, to further establish the effectiveness of our model, we conducted a human evaluation to determine its superiority over other models in terms of human length variability, coherence, and overall quality ratings. Upon conducting the human evaluation, the outcomes confirmed our hypotheses, demonstrating that the Borges model with the dialogue filter outperforms other models in terms of coherence and quality. However, the human length variability results showed that this model was less concise than others, such as the TOP model, which may be attributed to its tendency to fill gaps in understanding by seeking external knowledge to complete unlearned relationships. In light of these findings, to reduce redundancy in output while preserving the length variability of the previous model, we developed a knowledge filter update that incorporates posterior length probabilities and guides the decoding process as an axial interaction layer. This updated layer exploits the knowledge of the model's length distribution to produce outputs with variability in length. Consequently, the updated model achieves a posterior length probability update that streamlines the decoding process while retaining the length variability of the previous model. Notably, the updated model with this layer yields shorter outputs with higher variability in length, according to both automatic and human evaluations. Moreover, the updated model produces outputs with coefficients closely aligned with human length variability in terms of magnitude and direction. Finally, when we compared the updated model at various stages of training with strong baselines like the TOP model and GLaS, the results showed that the updated model outperforms these baselines in terms of coherence and quality, both in automatic and human evaluations

The remaining limitations of AI system models are seen as limitations of the field of AI explanations as a whole. This paper introduces an efficient, standalone online anomaly detection method grounded in the Isolation Forest algorithm. This new approach assigns each data point an anomaly score that serves as a time-sensitive indicator of anomalous behavior. As with Isolation Forest, our algorithm generates multiple instances of anomalous data points via sample splitting, followed by a collaborative processing strategy between ensemble trees. Notably, our online method circumvents the need for explicit ensemble construction, calculating intrinsically connected scores for all data points as they arise. Experimental evidence confirms that this approach effectively identifies recent anomalies and offers a superior balance of precision and recall over competing online detection techniques. Additionally, we highlight the algorithm's versatility, noting that it works seamlessly with any data input, and highlight its natural integration with downstream processing tools such as the Threshold Tracer. This broader framework enables detailed analysis and visualization of detection accuracy and the practical utility of the online algorithm in real-world applications. All implementation sources are available on GitHub under the header "IFTOnline". This new method has significant implications for handling sequential data in context of IoT events, search logs, surgical workflow recognition, and other complex data types where real-time online anomaly detection is crucial. Comprehensive detailed descriptions and the accompanying source code are available at https://iftonline23.github.io/. All execution times reported in the results section were documented using Jupyter Notebook with the same version of the code used for training and testing purposes. This approach can be easily adapted in other programming languages such as Python, Java, and C++, and we suggest exploring the open source code for further improvements and optimizations. Ultimately, this online anomaly detection algorithm holds substantial practical value in diverse application domains where safety, security, and efficiency are paramount. Research into the algorithm's performance under specific data distributions is an area for potential exploration in the future. The open source code at https://github.com/IFTOnline23/IFTOnline awaits contributions and collaborations to identify additional areas of improvement and applicability. The GARCH model's ability to model volatility is highly influential but has significant drawbacks, primarily due to its parameter parameter space's full dimensionality. Theoretical and computational limitations prompt the adoption of various dimension reduction techniques. A Bayesian model employing a stick-breaking process allows for automatic, data-driven dimension reduction by selecting relevant GARCH parameters but faces its own set of issues including theoretical and computational difficulties in determining the optimal number of retained parameters. To mitigate this, we introduce an informative priors approach by treating the GARCH model as a special case of the more comprehensive Bayesian Network Archimedean Regression model and imposing priors on the parameters' distributions. However, the efficient estimation of these parameters' distributions is unfeasible due to the model's complexity and high computational requirements, prompting the adoption of a flexible and efficient estimation method: the Mini-BP algorithm. This algorithm makes theoretical and computational contributions by demonstrating its convergence and justifying its efficient computation by reducing the estimation problem in a specific Bayesian model through singular spectrum decomposition and proving the convergence of the estimated means towards Gaussian mixtures under Sufficient Statistic Conditions. A simulation study and an analysis of real data from 117 U.S. stock-returns from July 2020 to July 2021 demonstrate the effectiveness of the informative priors approach by highlighting the importance of the choice of the number of retained parameters (m) and the corresponding number of retained observations, and their implications for the accuracy of the estimated volatility. A companion R package (iBNAR) facilitates the implementation of the informative priors approach in conjunction with other models such as the Multivariate BARS and the Multivariate ARCH model. In this research, we focus on understanding the special properties of stationary objects in 2D and 3D space. Given a unit volume, we investigate how various shapes achieve stationary mass functionals under different types of transformations, including translations, rotations, and reflections. Although certain shapes exhibit unique properties in 2D space, we find that these characteristics disappear when examining the same properties in 3D space due to the loss of symmetry. Conversely, when exploring how these shapes change when viewed from different perspectives, we discover that 2D and 3D share certain similarities. Additionally, we identify specific shapes with unusual features: a triangle, a square with a circular hole, and a piecewise constant function, which are seen to be optimal in both 2D and 3D space. In contrast, while a disk and a sphere exhibit optimal characteristics in 2D space, their 3D counterparts lose these unique features. However, we find that a sphere shares similar characteristics with its 2D counterpart, the triangle, and the square with a circular hole, which are seen to be stable in all dimensions. Lastly, we outline various future research directions in this area. The methods presented in this study rely heavily on specific mathematical theorems and lemmas, which are discussed in further detail in accompanying research papers. These theorems and lemmas validate that the shapes examined in this study indeed possess the characteristics suggested by their analysis. We outline our data processing and analysis techniques for the Hi-GAL survey. This involves a comprehensive data reduction pipeline for the GASS Legacy compact source catalog, based on the 70$\mu$m. These techniques include: initial data screening, development of an efficient source catalog using the Rapid Association Detection algorithm, statistical analysis for source identification, validation, and catalog refinement. These methods include: (1) selecting high-quality data points from the survey, (2) applying the ROMA algorithm for source detection and catalog construction, (3) verification and refinement of the catalog through analysis of associated data points, and (4) finally generating the final source catalog. Additionally, we employed the Sub-Grid Galactic Plane Evolution model to derive a pure background noise map, facilitating source detection and catalog construction. Following this, we employed a corruption map to account for data corruption and establish a comprehensive quality control process. Consequently, our data reduction pipeline achieves a catalog with an reliability of 95%, 85%, and 80% for single, double, and triple associations, respectively. Moreover, our technique allows for the identification of about 2.6 million sources in the Hi-GAL survey, with a significant reduction in data size from 2.3 Petabyte to 270 Terabyte following noise removal and catalog construction. These outcomes form the basis for an comprehensive data release, comprising: (i) a pure data cube with removed instrumental and calibration artifacts, (ii) Hi-GAL survey maps, (iii) a pure background noise map, and (iv) a catalog of compact sources. These, and all associated Hi-GAL survey, products, are available at: https://irsa.hebrei.nl, and https://archive.eso.org, respectively. Since both models rely on Bayes' original formulation, which applies to independent conditional probabilities, they highlight a limitation in applying this formulation to quantum mechanics. A quantum version of Bayes' formula can be derived without assuming anything beyond what is known about quantum mechanics. This formula maintains consistency in both models and thus resolves their apparent contradictions. As a result, it provides a foundation for interpreting the results of both experiments in the quantum framework. By applying the quantum version of Bayes' formula to both scenarios, we show that both experiments produce expected outcomes that match their inputs, which demonstrates that they do not after all contradict each other. Furthermore, the quantum version of Bayes' formula allows for its application to other situations, like local measurements, where Bayes' original form would lead to apparent paradoxes. As a result, it provides a consistent way to tackle various challenges in relating quantum mechanics to reasoning processes.

We investigated Lyman-$\alpha$ photon filtering using molecular hydrogen in an absorption cell, taking into consideration molecular orientation as a factor. Molecular hydrogen in its ground state exists in two distinct orientations, resulting from different spin orientations of the proton and hydrogen atom. This phenomenon allows for orientation-dependent filtering of Lyman-$\alpha$ photons. To determine which orientation is responsible for filtering these photons, we analyzed data from the Simulating Systematic Optics Spectrograph (SIMOS) during the Experiment for Planetary Transits and Atmospheres (EPTA) campaign, using a one-dimensional radiative transfer code to simulate the observed data. The results of this analysis further clarified the properties of Lyman-$\alpha$ transient bands, as they are not solely attributed to the $X^3O$ (1)$\rightarrow X^3O$(2) transition. Additionally, we identified potential sources of noise that could affect measurement results. Further experiments are being conducted to resolve uncertainties surrounding the pressure of molecular hydrogen in the absorption cell, which needs to be minimized to optimize Lyman-$\alpha$ filtering efficiency. The study also highlighted limitations in measuring Lyman-$\alpha$ transmission losses, primarily stemming from sinusoidal noise at high pressures and from a linear component at lower pressures. We proposed two methods to mitigate these respective issues. The first method involves reducing the pressure of molecular hydrogen in the absorption cell to lower levels, which in turn demands equivalent increases in the temperature of the absorption cell to maintain a constant total pressure. We observed that this approach is feasible from a technological standpoint. The second method involves data analysis techniques to mitigate linear noise, which we demonstrated to be effective according to our simulations. Ultimately, we concluded that molecular hydrogen is a viable tool for efficiently filtering Lyman-$\alpha$ photons, which could be utilized in future Ly$\alpha$ sources for various scientific applications. The development of a self-filtering Lyman-$\alpha$ source, paired with advancements in simulating complex radiative transfer processes, could significantly enhance research efficiency in this field. Furthermore, the molecular hydrogen filtering method could also be adapted for multiple-element filter designs, which would provide greater control over beam selection during source mode selection experiments. We outlined the necessary steps to implement this technology and discussed the significant benefits it could accord to researchers, particularly those studying interstellar medium using the SIMOS instrument. The project notably contributed to the public access, to a qualified research audience, of unpublished SIMOS instrument findings spanning a period of over five years. A notable figure, Richard Bellman, played a crucial role in influencing the integration of AI and control engineering through his interdisciplinary approaches. This paper aims to revisit Bellman's legacy by focusing on his unpublished manuscripts and engaging discussions with him, which reveal his vision for the intersection of AI and control engineering. A core aspect of his vision is demonstrated by a specific problem that he had hoped to explore, namely the balance between communication costs and performance efficiency in distributed control systems. Consequently, this paper serves as a personal tribute to Bellman's legacy, emphasizing the need for AI and control engineering to continue exploring common themes and interfaces that have historically driven innovation in the science. Understanding the specific type of entity is vital in organizing knowledge and achieving certain tasks such as information retrieval and summarization. Existing entity typing systems perform entity classification based on their surface form or text context, but these methods have not led to substantial improvements in performance. To address this limitation, this research introduces the ConceptNet-Referenced Hybrid framework (FGNET-RH), which refines conceptual mentions by integrating external knowledge from ConceptNet and reference mentions within a mention-enhanced decoding scheme. The concept of mentions is considered valuable and worthy of further improvement. As such, instead of directly predicting entity typing based on surface form or text context alone, the FGNET-RH framework is designed to make incremental updates to the initial mention encoding, then conduct mention-enhanced decoding to generate typing information. The FGNET-RH framework is capable of merging different typing models and mentions to achieve stronger performance. In experiments, the FGNET-RH framework delivered outstanding results, outperforming other existing approaches notably on the TAC 2016 and 2017 datasets and matching or surpassing state-of-the-art performance on more recent datasets like TAC 2020 and 2021. This research advances the Prepartition virtual machine scheduling technique within cloud computing environments. Prior to scheduling, resource allocation is determined based on application demands and constraints. Scheduling then takes place according to the established prepartition plan without needing further resource allocation adjustments. We develop an optimal search algorithm for generating comprehensive prepartition plans based on the MRT (Most Resource-hungry Task) policy and a fitness function that prioritizes resource utilization efficiency in cloud computing environments. In contrast to traditional scheduling methods that adjust resource allocation during scheduling, our proposed approach permits flexible co-location of applications and enhances resource utilization efficiency. We validate our algorithm's effectiveness through simulations, demonstrating that it outperforms existing methods based on prepartitioning. Specifically, our results indicate that it can increase average resource utilization by 30% compared to optimal search and 25% compared to the heuristic search algorithm. Moreover, the underlying search algorithm's source code and simulation models have been made available for further development and improvement. As a result, our proposed approach can contribute to cloud providers' efforts to optimize energy efficiency and resource utilization. This study investigates how employing dimension reduction methods impacts the intersection of causal and statistical modeling techniques, revealing that this intersection may come at the cost of compromising both precision and accuracy. Although previous research has highlighted the effects of reduction methods on estimation power (Varadhan and Wang, 2014), we demonstrate that this is not the primary concern in the context of causal analysis. Instead, we focus on the trade-off between bias and estimation power, showing that this equilibrium is optimized by an algorithm which, under certain conditions, utilizes correlations to select variables. This algorithm, designed for categorical data, is part of the ICE package (Lutz, 2016) and the DGX method (Tzavelas, 2017) for continuous data. Additionally, we compare the performance of our proposed approach with that of existing techniques, notably Correlation-based Dimension reduction (Cordier), in the context of the Prostate Cancer data set and find that it outperforms Cordier under Causal inference criteria. This trade-off between bias and estimation power is then illustrated with respect to Causal Bandits a state-of-the-art method for causal learning (Jamieson et al., 2011; Tidvad and Andersson, 2011; Tidvad et al., 2012), and we demonstrate the impact of dimension reduction on its root mean square regret in both the context of continuous and contextual bandit problems for the prostate cancer data. Ultimately, we conclude that though dimension reduction may facilitate the identification of causal variables, this is not always beneficial as it can lead to decreased accuracy and, by extension, the root mean square regret in the context of Causal Bandits. Training a Variational Autoencoder effectively involves striking a balance between minimizing the reconstruction error and capturing the data's underlying uncertainty. A key challenge in this process is determining the optimal level of complexity in the encoder and decoder models. Our research introduces a new approach that utilizes the uncertainty estimate from the Variational Autoencoder to construct an optimal model, representing the data's inherent structure. Our method estimates the uncertainty by sampling multiple latent variables and calculating the density matrix for each sample, using the calculated entropy as an approximate measure of the data set's underlying structure. With this uncertainty estimate in hand, we apply a cross-validation technique to select the model that best fits the data. Our approach can be used with a range of established VAencoder loss functions, including the ELBO optimization method. Our results demonstrate that these unsupervised techniques can outperform their supervised counterparts in estimating the data set's underlying structure. Our research also explores the theoretical limitations of these methods, demonstrating that they are susceptible to overfitting when dealing with complex data sets, requiring careful tuning of model parameters. Our approach has significant implications for the use of Variational Autoencoders in medical imaging, where it has the potential to improve analysis and detection tasks by providing a comprehensive understanding of images, rather than relying solely on specific regions or features. A general covering array was first introduced by Godlinger et al. in 2014 as a variation of the uniform covering array theory, but despite its shorter row lengths, this variant doesn't offer a simplified uniform covering array construction. In fact, every general covering array turns out to be a uniform covering array. This paper presents the inaugural instance of a uniform covering array that cannot be reclassified as a general covering array. Additionally, this rare example arises from a multiplicative combinatorial design that is not additive. As a result, it poses the question: can a general uniform covering array always be reduced to a uniform covering array? If the answer is yes, it would mean that our proposed design is not an isolated occurrence. Conversely, if the answer is no, it would demonstrate the usefulness of our presented design in distinguishing between these two related concepts. Lastly, this paper discusses several open questions related to both uniform and general covering arrays. Specifically, can a general uniform covering array always be converted into a uniform covering array? Additionally, is it true that every general uniform covering array must have at least one uniform covering array equivalent? In other words, can any general uniform covering array be considered equivalent to a general uniform covering array? If the first question is answered positively, it would establish that our previously constructed design is one out of a finite set of isolated instances. Despite the significance of method mutation in testing, there is a lack of comprehensive study specifically on evaluating method mutation in crash testing. To fill this knowledge gap, we conducted an investigation 'backwards' by first focusing on re-producing software crashes using method mutation as the guiding principle. Our investigation involved (1) examining how prior research applied method mutation in crash testing, (2) identifying potential reasons why method-based crash testing may fall short in replicating real-world crashes, (3) carrying out crash testing using four popular method mutation tools on 200 evolved versions of industry-grade, publicly available Java methods that were prone to crashing. Our testing included three types of crashes (out-of-bounds, null, and logic) and we found that tool performance varied significantly. Notably, we discovered that crash data provided by one of the tools was inconsistent with its own testing results, suggesting that the tool may have introduced errors artificially. Our investigation implies that further research is needed to validate the effectiveness of method mutation in crash testing. Based on our findings, we propose new directions for future research 'forwards', including topics, comments, and approaches. Our complete set-up for re-producing software crashes is made available for public use. Furthermore, we conducted a similar investigation on industry-grade, C/C crash-prone testing methods to validate the effectiveness of real-world, logic crashes, and we found that tool performance varied depending on how tests were carried out, suggesting that mutation-based crash testing could be improved in this area. Our results may have implications for industry practitioners working in crash testing. Furthermore, we found that crash-prone evolutionary testing methods have successfully identified hard-to-reach, logic crashes in industry practices, yet these successes are not well-represented in recent crash testing research studies. Our study bridges this gap by combining research insights from both practical experiences and novel empirical studies. Our findings may have consequences for future crash testing research studies. For publicly available testing tools, we found evidence of inadequate tool documentation that may contribute to introducing artificial errors, and we discovered that tool developers and users have different perspectives on this issue. Our investigation implies that further research is needed to address these concerns. Our analysis suggests that based on our investigation outcomes, EvoCrash may have failed in reproducing some crashes due to how it was tested, and we discovered similar safety concerns with crash testing. Our study highlights that crash testing research studies and practices face common challenges, and we found correlations between concerns from research studies and practical experiences in all three areas of crash testing (mu, PR, and LP).

During large-scale software development, developers face the challenge of locating specific concepts based on the code reads they perform. Concept location involves pinpointing the parts of the code that relate to a given query, but this task is complicated by the vastness of software projects. Researchers have suggested crowdsourcing as an effective approach to enhance concept location by tapping into the collective knowledge of software communities. In this study, we explore the potential of crowdsourcing and develop a framework that utilizes it to facilitate the discovery of software code concepts. Our framework can be seen as an abductive reasoning model that draws on user queries, code snippets, and community-provided knowledge to guide users toward relevant code segments. We validate our framework's efficacy through an empirical study, finding that it successfully guides users toward accurate answers based on their queries. Furthermore, our results reveal that the crowd-sourced knowledge gathered in this context exhibits meaningful properties, including organization, coherence, and relevance. Moreover, our study shows that the crowd-sourced knowledge accumulated over time leads to significant improvements in accuracy, reaching up to 77%. Ultimately, our findings have important implications for future research on concept location: the integration of community knowledge can enrich query terms, enhance snippet quality, and increase accuracy, suggesting avenues for further investigation. Generally, our approach allows developers to locate relevant code segments more effectively using their queries, code insights, and community knowledge. The framework and query examples demonstrated in this study are available for public access at http://gitub.com/yangxie33/CL4CL. Our research highlights distinct roles for users, crowd-sourced repositories, and concept location tools in facilitating developers' work, suggesting opportunities for integrating these components to boost productivity. As developers increasingly rely on concepts and principles in guiding their code reads, the necessity for efficient concept location will only grow in the future. Consequently, our study's findings will have far-reaching implications for researchers in this area going forward. The CL4CL framework is compatible with existing concept location tools and can be easily incorporated into future systems; moreover, all our data, including accumulated query terms and code snippets, is available for inspection. Generally, our work in this study lies at the intersection of two distinct research traditions, abductive reasoning and software concept location, and sheds light on novel applications and characteristics of crowd-sourced knowledge from the software development perspective. Ultimately, our study has significant implications for researchers, developers, and practitioners in this area, highlighting intriguing connections, differences, and relationships between crowd-sourced knowledge and concept location. Conversational models have made significant progress in recent years. A key aspect of natural conversation involves an element of give-and-take, also known as turn-taking. In our research, we focus on creating a method to assess the presence of turn-taking in spoken interactions. Building on existing work in Neural Entrainment Distance, which uses neural models to evaluate the presence of social cues in spoken language, we develop and train a customized turn-taking model leveraging the MOCHA spoken corpus. Unlike previous approaches that relied solely on pre-existing language models, we employ a data augmentation technique to fine-tune a bidirectional Transformer model for turn-taking analysis, also providing a word embedding that accurately captures turn-taking information. Furthermore, we establish a connection between our model's embeddings and fake conversation detection, facilitating the development of turn-taking detection without human annotation. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art in turn-taking detection and accurately identifies real conversations based on existing datasets. A subsequent case study also sheds light on the potential applications of turn-taking detection in verifying the authenticity of spoken interactions. As an additional contribution, we introduce the first turn-taking model based on end-to-end neural architecture designed for audio analysis, specifically designed for use with spoken language. Audio samples and model code are available for evaluation and further research on GitHub. Lastly, we explore theoretical aspects of our model and examine how our embeddings correlate with actual social cues from unannotated audio data, also addressing potential biases in our model's design. It is our hope that this novel method will contribute to the development of more realistic conversational ai that ultimately leads to the creation of more natural interactions. A public call has been made to gather a diverse range of datasets to further refine the accuracy of turn-taking analysis in spoken language. A related research paper detailing our findings has been published at Interspeech 2021 and was selected as one of the conference's top papers. A shorter summary of our research has also been presented at FLORETDA 2021. A more in-depth review of our work, including an overview of related research, is available as a chapter in the book "Annotated Corpora for Spoken Language Processing: Selected Subdomains", published by IST-Ed research. A short movie illustrating our research has been submitted to the 2021 ACM Richard A. Goldstein Award and was selected for presentation at HRI 2022. A more recent research paper detailing the potential applications of turn-taking analysis in audio technology has been accepted for presentation at ACIVIZ 202

We introduce a widely applicable method for deriving physical characteristics from a galaxy's emission lines, which can identify abnormalities in both gas and star formation. This method produces a galaxy's gas velocity maps, determines its ionization levels, and categorizes its star formation activity using BPT diagrams. These results are represented in an interactive 3D visualization that quickly responds to user queries. To facilitate future research, we provide a comprehensive classification framework that outlines the technical requirements for automating a galaxy's emission line analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a dataset of 740 galaxies spanning $z=2.7-3.0$. These data, comprising 34 bands across three spectrographs, were analyzed under the CoDaGAL project. To validate our emission line measurements, we conduct various internal consistency checks and compare them to alternative redshift sampling methods. These comparisons confirm that our measurements are accurate and reliable. In addition to our emission line measurements, we provide full-resolution continuum surface photometry and Catalogue of Massively Red Objects (CMOR) data. These data, which were also computed as part of the CoDaGAL project, are made available through the Data Release 2 (DR2). Furthermore, we provide a unique statistical comparison of our BPT diagram catalog to three other emission line catalogs derived from various surveys. These findings reveal that our BPT diagrams align with existing data but also reveal some inconsistencies in the data. In particular, we observe a significant overabundance of "composites" relative to the stacked mass distribution. These "composites" comigrate with galaxies with high stellar masses (M$_\star>10^{10}$M$_\odot$), posing a challenge to current understanding of massive galaxy formation. Therefore, we suggest that these "composites" may represent an early stage in the formation of "red-sequence" galaxies. These findings highlight the significance of emission line data in understanding galaxy evolution across 13.5 billion years of cosmic history. This paper explores the challenges of adapting supervised learning models across different domains, specifically when the source domain is unavailable for transfer. Unlike traditional domain adaptation techniques that fail without source data, we propose the Generative Adversarial Artifacts for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (GAUDA) approach, which relies solely on target domain samples for adaptation. GAUDA employs an unsupervised pre-training method using generative adversarial networks to create target domain artifacts, along with a domain-invariant feature extraction module that eliminates domain-specific characteristics. Through cross-validation, our method demonstrates domain invariance and domain shift removal. Experimental evaluations on the CIFAR DS, CIFAR RS, and MSTAD datasets reveal that GAUDA outperforms existing domain adaptation methods, achieving improved performance even with limited target domain samples. The proposed GAUDA method is shown to be robust against varying target domain sizes and the quality of the target proxy labels significantly improves the performance of existing algorithms based on proxy labels. The efficacy of our approach is further validated by visual ablation studies, which illustrate the importance of learning target domain distributions for domain adaptation. Due to its density, the plasma generated by the reactor has a significant impact on the particle accelerator's performance and efficiency. To optimize the reactor's effectiveness, researchers are currently working on modifying its design. In this study, we used Monte Carlo simulations to study how varying the pressure inside the reactor's central column affects the plasma's global behavior. By changing the pressure, we observed distinct changes in the plasma's behavior, including the initial disappearance of sparks, subsequent production of many sparks, and eventually, extreme plasma formation that fills the entire system. Our research demonstrated that the plasma's behavior is highly sensitive to pressure changes and that controlling the pressure can help researchers achieve better plasma control and efficiency. Furthermore, our study could lead to the development of better, more efficient gas core reactors in the future. Finally, we note that our model can successfully simulate plasma processes at very low pressures and is therefore applicable to other low-pressure plasma-based technology systems. output. These projections are used as inputs to a fully connected neural network
that predicts the particle identity. By utilising Bayes' theorem, we incorporate
prior knowledge of the detector, making the network's training faster and more
resistant to noise. This is particularly beneficial when there is a low number

quarks. We compared the network's performance with that of the Bayes' filter
used in the TWiki analysis and other neural networks with fully connected input.

similar accuracy with a smaller number of parameters. Furthermore, it can be
used with a larger range of detector geometries with minimal modifications. This

We have developed a computer program that generates a function, based on a predetermined line list, to calculate the total opacity of a gas for 40 distinct atomic species relevant to ultra-hot Jupiter atmospheres and M-dwarfs, valid for various temperatures and pressures, and expandable to accommodate additional line lists. By utilizing this program, we derived and analyzed the impact of line-list variations on the atmospheric structure and spectra of UHJs and M-dwarfs, and found that different assumptions about the pre-equilibrium chemical composition can result in notable discrepancies in the model's properties and spectral predictions. All of the line lists and model code were made publicly available to facilitate further research.
