Logic programs incorporating aggregates, which facilitate global aggregations of variable values, were introduced for generating answer sets semantically. However, the feasibility of groundings for programs containing recursive aggregates was left unaddressed due to answer set programming's inherent declarative nature, which prohibits grounding algorithms. We delve into methods for implementing recursive aggregates in answer set programming, present four algorithms, and provide a computational analysis, including complexity results. An implementation of these algorithms in ASP systems is also discussed. Our findings suggest that grounding is a viable technique for aggregates with limited depth of recursion, but complex cases require iterative computations whose computational times increase exponentially. An implementation of these algorithms in ASP systems, ASP-GRAF, is also presented and tested using existing tools. Our experiments reveal grounding's benefits for programs employing recursive aggregates. An open-source library containing the implementation and further investigative experiments can be found on https://github.com/GRAF-ASP/ASP-GRAF. Two video presentations detailing the analysis are available on YouTube. Furthermore, we propose adding a recursive aggregate feature to the standard language used by ASP interpreters. Our computational results indicate that this standardization could lead to significant grounding time savings. In our prior work, we established a first law of thermodynamics for a system with multiple resources by utilizing a generalized free energy framework. The system's initial and final energies were expressed in terms of the changes in resource characteristics during a state transformation. This paper further explores the implications of this approach. We initially demonstrate that the law is applicable to a broader set of protocols than just measurement-induced changes. Additionally, we accurately derive a specific formula for calculating the total energy change in resource scenarios, along with clear explanations of its underlying reasoning. Furthermore, we effectively apply the first law to calculate system energy changes during a broad spectrum of protocols, including those influenced by classical or quantum interactions. Lastly, we illustrate the first law's applicability to scenarios where the system's energy changes are driven by external forces. In this context, we establish that the term representing the energy change is essentially an environmental contribution, determined by the differences in entropy for the system plus the reservoir. This finding mirrors the results of a prior study that employed a different mathematical approach. Ultimately, our research confirms the first law's universality, thereby indicating that the concepts of system energy, entropy, and influence, along with their respective applications, are likely to be well-established characteristics of multi-resource theories. This, in turn, may ultimately contribute to the emergence of a new class of computational models that are resource-theoretic in nature. Recent findings have established that every left-right Cayley graph associated with a finite group possesses a quantum error-correcting code capable of correcting one- and two-bit errors. Building on this discovery, we develop general methods to create such quantum codes by constructing specific finite group structures, thereby expanding the established code families. Focusing on primitive subgroups, we devise an algorithmic approach to determine feasible group orders, resulting in a systematic method to create regular Cayley graphs and corresponding quantum codes. Additionally, by incorporating diagonal matrices with integer or rational diagonal entries into the protocol, we broaden the scope of possible quantum codes. Moreover, we validate the efficacy of this modified protocol using the finite field $ \mathbb{F}_{3}$ and $ \mathbb{F}_5$ as test cases. Since our methodology focuses solely on the group structure, it allows for the creation of quantum codes with novel combinatorial properties unrelated to existing code families. As an example, we define the left-right Cayley graph associated with the group $ \mathbb{Z}_4 \oplus \mathbb{Z}_2$abraham as a candidate for a quantum code capable of correcting multiple error patterns while preserving specific state relations. Thus, we develop a comprehensive, algorithmically sound protocol for designing regular Cayley graphs and their corresponding quantum error-correcting codes. A key application of light field technology is generating coherent 3D visual information from a collection of 2D images. Existing machine learning-based approaches for light field reconstruction typically rely on a vast number of input images, which can be impractical. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel method that leverages geometric constraints to reconstruct 3D scenes from a sparse set of input images. Our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques by utilizing these constraints to effectively learn 3D visual information even when the number of input images is reduced. Importantly, our method does not require any pre-existing 3D scene data. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in both qualitative and quantitative aspects compared to existing methods. Our findings suggest that incorporating geometric constraints is crucial for 3D scene inference, allowing the discrimination of meaningful geometric features from irrelevant details. Our source code and 3D scene datasets are publicly available. Furthermore, our recovered 3D scenes can be rotated using a virtual reality interface. A quick look at available data reveals that, on August 20, 2019, a solar jet in AR12728 moved at an exceptional speed of 164 km/s, whereas a type II radio burst accelerated at an impressive rate of 171 km/s. Surprisingly, when researchers applied the Fast Solar Junction technique, the observed redundancy was much lower than expected, suggesting that the method may not yield ideal results in situations characterized by high anisotropy. Moreover, in this study, the separation angle between the shock front and the solar jet widened from 16 degrees to 38 degrees, indicating significant acceleration of the shock front. Notably, although both the shock front and the solar jet moved in the same general direction, they exhibited distinct patterns of movement, with the shock front exhibiting marked deflection towards the west, a phenomenon possibly linked to interactions between the shock front and coronal streams. Our research supports earlier findings pointing to the existence of significant under-detection of forward-reversing radio bursts, suggesting that, in some instances, radio waves may not yet have caught up to the moving shock front. If confirmed, this would imply that the shock acceleration is even more pronounced than initially estimated. The task of discovering significant factors influencing time-dependent gene expression data is increasingly crucial for making early predictions in gene networks. However, conventional methods used for making early predictions in gene networks focus solely on general machine learning tasks, neglecting the complexities of gene expression data and resulting in poor performance. A new approach, called RELENTLESS, is designed to efficiently identify influential variables from longitudinal data by incorporating two key components: relevance learning and optimization techniques for early predictions. RELENTLESS starts by training a network with a relevance loss function to determine the relative importance of each variable, followed by an online phase where its performance is optimized under a prediction-centric loss function. By decoupling these components, RELENTLESS enables the flexibility to switch between prediction and relevance learning. Through experimental analysis on artificial and real datasets, RELENTLESS demonstrated its ability to find relevant variables and outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods in prediction tasks. Notably, RELENTLESS showcased its practical applicability in identifying novel molecular markers for Alzheimer's disease and steadily improved its predictive performance as relevance increased, further validating its effectiveness. RELENTLESS is available for public use on GitHub via the link https://github.com/whatsapp/RELENTLESS. Experimental results, including additional datasets and comparisons with baseline methods, can be found on the project's repository. A publicly accessible web-based platform, called Allosaia, can also be accessed at http://allosaia.inria.fr/RELENTLESS/ to visualize the project's documentation, datasets, and results. A supporting document providing detailed project information can be found at https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01471411. RELENTLESS has the potential to be further developed to adapt to new applications, such as multi-task learning, and its potential future applications are explored in the paper. By combining a kernel method with a deep learning network, RELENTLESS achieves a level of stability and interpretability that is enhanced by its relative independence from the data distribution. As time progresses and new data becomes available, RELENTLESS can be recalibrated to improve its performance and identify influential variables, thereby ensuring long-term adaptability and sustainability. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained through supervised learning or reinforcement learning can be seen as optimized solutions for highly dynamic, partially observable optimal control problems. However, understanding the underlying belief states responsible for optimal control strategies remains challenging. By harnessing the connection between RNNs and partially observable optimal control problems, we propose an algorithm to recover the RNN hidden states corresponding to key environmental state variables. This approach leverages the dual dynamics of RNNs, where past hidden states influence current observations and future hidden states are informed by past beliefs. By formulating a loss function based on an augmented Bayesian filter, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method on partially observable optimal control tasks, showcasing recovered beliefs that maximize performance when used as a policy. This work also lays groundwork for interpreting RNNs in the context of unsupervised learning. Notably, our approach allows for identifying environmental state variables directly from the RNN architecture, without requiring additional structure. Additionally, our method can be seen as a way to 'interpret' black-box RNNs without altering their behavior. This way, if an RNN is used for control in a partially observable environment, we can identify the underlying state variables believed to be optimal. This identification is not dependent on continuing to learn or training with reinforcement learning, but can be performed while the RNN is in use. Moreover, our approach can be used as an exploratory tool to 'design' optimal control strategies for specific environments, by identifying key state variables for different policy paradigms such as model-free or model-based reinforcement learning. The proposed algorithm is available at github.com/jmichelet/hybrid-level-zero. Results from our experiments are also posted on videos at youtube.com/postdoctoralresearch. Results and videos are used solely to disseminate information and should not be exploited for commercial or public purposes. The problem of identifying duplicated images across an entire database, which differs from identifying duplicate images within a single image, presents distinct algorithmic challenges. Researchers have explored various approaches to image duplication detection including approximate matching algorithms like Hashing and Nearest Neighbor Search. Experts also employ more precise techniques such as Covering Algorithms or combine multiple algorithms' outcomes to increase effectiveness. Notably, many successful image duplication detection methods incorporate Hashing at their core. In this research, we evaluate the potential of transforming an image into a graph to facilitate Nearest Neighbor Search. Graphs offer a natural representation of an image's components and their relationships, utilizing nodes for regions of interest and edges for connections. Our study, which utilized three graph pooling techniques, Nearest Set Maximization, Community Ascent, and k-Mean Graph Clustering, demonstrated that image duplication detection based on graph-based Nearest Neighbor Search can achieve comparable results to state-of-the-art techniques involving Hashing and Nearest Set Searches. Our findings suggest that this approach holds promise for applications where a detailed image representation is beneficial, offering improved flexibility and potentially enhanced performance. Notably, graph-based Nearest Neighbor Search surpasses Nearest Set Maximization both quantitatively and qualitatively. Our method's key advantages include end-to-end differentiability, flexibility in supporting diverse pooling algorithms, and the potential for significant qualitative improvements over current top-performing techniques. Furthermore, our technique outperforms Nearest Set Maximization both quantitatively and qualitatively. Our qualitative results show that while both techniques can detect duplicated images across the entire database, they exhibit differing behavior in the presence of distinct image patterns. These findings suggest that our method displays more human-like behavior, contrasting with the Nearest Set Maximization's increased reliance on hashing. To this end, a mathematical model is developed, focusing on the federated learning scenario with multiple parties, and it involves a stochastic gradient descent on a binary classifier with a specific loss function, a Gaussian prior, and a quantization mechanism based on a Laplace distribution. The findings are validated through numerical simulations on synthetic data in various scenarios. This research focuses on understanding how players improve at solving dynamic games over time. Through automated analysis of game solutions, it was discovered that most games are characterized by a few distinct features. Lower-level players were found to struggle with these complex aspects, leading to a prediction that as players progress, they will prioritize understanding the dynamics of lower-level traits. As a result, it is expected that lower-level players, who initially lack this understanding, will gradually gain an advantage. Conversely, higher-level players, who already possess this knowledge, will see their dominance solidify. Interestingly, this leads to a theoretical competition dynamic where both groups will continue to gain an upper hand. The study further reveals that most games exhibit a pattern where the optimal strategy is straightforward and predictable, leading to a hypothesis that as players achieve higher levels, they will become increasingly proficient in simple games, causing the distribution of game complexity to shift towards easier tasks. Conversely, early players will be challenged by complex tasks, enabling better players to tackle these complex tasks, thus widening the gap between experts and novices. The proposed framework, which is grounded in objective statistical analysis, offers a new method for understanding player performance across different skill levels. The findings provide insights into the natural progression of player capabilities, thus serving as a foundation for creating tailored training materials tailored to specific ability levels, while also highlighting the crucial need to develop methods for solving complex games. The research was conducted using a large collection of Procedural Generation of Games (PGG) in Python, which allows for quantitative analysis of player capabilities. The study measures player performance using three distinct metrics: understanding game rules, understanding game objectives, and overall game difficulty. The data reveals that players improve in line with these measures, with slower progress seen in more complex games. The research also discovers that players are better at solving games that they find easier to understand, and that harder games require players to develop more sophisticated strategies. The study further explores player dynamics by dividing them into five ability groups, ranging from novice to expert. The data reveals that each group is focused on distinct sets of games, and that as players advance through these ability levels, they tend to prefer simpler games. The research also discovers that experts are more inclined towards games that require long solution sequences. Traditional static filters, such as Gaussian kernels and bilateral filters, are based on quadratic representations that are computationally and memory-intensive. These issues are exacerbated by the need for these filters to be applied at various levels within an image's pyramidal hierarchy. To address this problem, we introduce a new static filter using learned convolutional processes based on Bernstein polynomials. These polynomials facilitate the representation of convex splines using less memory than quadratic kernels while providing control over the precision of the approximation. Moreover, the coefficients of the polynomials can be learned using an efficient training method grounded in convolutional neural networks, enabling the classifying capability to be incorporated into the learning process. Our approach can be viewed as a more efficient variant of convolutional neural networks that uses static filters as lookups rather than dynamic convolution. Experimental results demonstrate that by simply substituting static filters into existing pyramidal networks, accuracy can be improved across a range of state-of-the-art image classification benchmarks, including ResNet-50, which also provides robust generalization performance across other tasks. The processing speed is comparable to that of convolutional neural networks, providing the potential to deploy such systems in embedded devices. This research compares and contrasts three nitrogen soil variation models: a single-scale model, two distinct-scale models with and without a spatial component, and a spatially explicit model with varying levels of noise. We examined the ability of each model to replicate observed patterns in the sizes of 9 different plant species. Focusing first on the sizes of individual plants within a species, we used hierarchical regression to compare the effectiveness of each model in replicating data. When controlling for noise, the results showed that the two-scale models performed better than the single-scale model, and incorporating spatial components further improved the fit. However, the size of the residual variance in the data influenced which model was best fit; models with spatial components performed best at lower levels of residual variance while two-scale models without spatial components fared better at higher levels. Despite the improvements seen with the two-scale models, it is clear that they do not fully capture the observed spatial structure in the data. A final section of the analysis explores the potential for each model to inform the creation of sampling designs that could guide future research and inform policy decisions regarding conservation efforts. Overall, the findings of this study point to the value of considering multiple scales of variation when designing research and policy initiatives. They also highlight the potential for the application of statistically sound methods to guide data collection and resource allocation. In the context of this research, the results suggest that the trade-offs between the models investigated are largely driven by the trade-offs between the weights of their mixing components. Finally, the analysis identifies several key challenges associated with the application of Bayesian techniques to generate prior knowledge from available data. In particular, the results show that the information about the variance of the normal distribution that is assumed in the models has a substantial impact on the fit of the models, as does the assumed correlation structure in the spatially explicit models. A publicly accessible R package, called AniPlant, is available to facilitate the application of the methods described in the study. The package provides functions that can be used to replicate the findings as well as design sampling designs that are informed by the results. In addition, the package includes data from a broader set of species from the same genus and provides tools to replicate the results of a companion paper. The Mafia game theory model consists of two stages: the dead-to-live phase and the live-to-dead phase, characterized by distinct player sets and actions, though no previous study uncovered an interdisciplinary approach that mathematically models both stages in a continuous time framework and investigates dynamical stability and outcomes. This research fills the gap by developing a novel model that captures the complexities of Mafia's dynamic evolution and explores the effects of key parameters on phase transitions, revealing that the game's fate relies on the sizes of loyal and disloyal player groups and the killing rate. This work yields six possible outcomes, including three stable phases, a neutral state, and an unstable transitional phase, and finds that the game's final phase is heavily influenced by the relative sizes of loyal and disloyal players. Specifically, if the disloyal player ratio exceeds a critical threshold, the game inevitably shifts to the final phase; if the disloyal player ratio falls below the critical threshold, the game reaches a neutral state. Conversely, if the disloyal player ratio lies in an intermediate range, the game enters a transitional phase before shifting to the final phase. Notably, the time for the game to reach its final phase is inversely proportional to the sum of loyal and disloyal player counts, and is at a minimum when the two groups are evenly sized. This finding is corroborated through numerical simulations demonstrating that the modeled outcomes are universally applicable across various group size ratios. This research provides the first comprehensive mathematical modeling of Mafia's underlying dynamics and explores the intricate relationships between its complex parameters, constituting a significant advancement in the study of this popular multiplayer game. As such, the work holds broad implications for analyzing multiplayer games via multidisciplinary methods. Moreover, the paper includes additional methods, including an optional mafiosolimit that mirrors the success of P v. C, and investigates the game's strategies, revealing that the mafia players' survival rate is highest under a specific killing rate, which is also numerically confirmed to be experimentally verifiable. The work's focus on fundamental game parameters positions it as a prime example of fundamental science in the field of game studies. Ultimately, the paper's broad interdisciplinary approach, combined with its novel and versatile applications, makes it suitable for various multiplayer game contexts, including Werewolf, Bachelor, and others. The work's brevity and clarity of explanation also render it accessible to readers from various academic backgrounds, and its potential for real-world utility is further underscored by its easy-to-implement numerical and experimental validation.

However, when an ultra-thin film made of nanotubes is heated, the phenomenon of valley coherence becomes the primary factor explaining its electrical properties. Armchair nanotubes, in particular, display neutral and charged behaviors that can be studied using cell model approximations, where a periodic structure composed of two walls per unit cell explains the occurrence of inter-valley interactions that give rise to Néel, Berry and spin-Orbit Hall effects. When a current is passed through a nanotube film at high temperatures, the combined effects of thermal fluctuations and valley coherence result in a significant increase in a device's ability to conduct charge at room temperature. Notably, the coherence of valleys in armchair nanotube films leads to a predicted thermal Hall effect distinct from that observed in graphene. Specifically, under isothermal conditions and in the presence of a perpendicular magnetic field, the electrical properties of the nanotube film exhibit a reversal in the direction of Hall effect, where an armchair nanotube cell model indicates that charges are collected from the sample via Néel, Berry and spin-Orbit Hall effect methods, resulting in a combined Néel/Berry Hall effect that is symmetrical and has a charge of -e. The predictions made about the spin-Orbit Hall effect are more accurate in the case of charged nanotube behavior. The unique combination of electrical properties and thermal properties in armchair nanotube films makes them ideal for use in devices that monitor the spin of electrons, where precision is critical, and also for use in magnetic sensors, where a quick response to changes in electric fields, a high threshold for magnetic fields and a long-lasting sensitivity are essential. The coherence of valleys in armchair nanotube behavior can also be applied to other types of nanotube configurations. The effectiveness of this approach in explaining both the properties of armchair nanotube films at high temperatures and the spin Hall effect has been confirmed through comparisons with observations made using scanning tunneling microscopy. The unique properties of armchair nanotube films make them suitable for use in devices known as spin torque oscillators, where large magnetization levels and a high threshold for magnetic fields are essential. We offer a novel proof of the Madsen-Weiss theorem for relative Rips compactifications that bridges the $b$-principle with stable theorems in topology. The proof finds an appropriate Barwick-Moss-Mumford extension, then applies an extended version of the Darboux-Wiener Theorem, finally utilizing algebraic techniques to achieve a purely algebraic proof of the MWMW theorem for $b_1$-good pairs. The cross-ratios functor plays a crucial role in this algebraic proof. The general case of the MWMW theorem follows from combining this algebraic proof with the $b$-principle. As a result, we obtain new applications of the MWMW theorem in terms of 2-colourings of simplicial complexes. Moreover, we demonstrate that many basic stable theorems are actually instances of the MWMW theorem. The proof involves an intriguing application of Harary's formula. Additionally, the proof yields further results in the context of $b_1$-good triples and general 2-colourings of simplicial complexes. The proof makes use of ideas from hyperplane theorems, Darboux-Wiener Theorems, algebraic b-principles, and a novel principle of proper finitary nature. The latter can be seen as an analogue of the MacPherson degree theorem when considering positivity conditions. As simple as it may seem, this last theorem actually implies a wide range of stable theorems, from deformed Rips stability to the current state-of-the-art results in Euclidean combinatorial geometry, as recently revisited by Avigal-Kapovich and Petrunin. As further implications, we show how proper finitary principle yields new results in context of generalized colored Rips stability, colored geometric realizations, and colored permutation complexes. The proof relies on ideas from the following: the latest advancements in algebraic $b$-principles, noetherianisation, reduced Darboux-Wiener Theorems, the Harary formula, the generalized colored Rips stability, deformed Rips stability, Euclidean combinatorial geometry, proper simplicial Gromov polytopes, and proper geometry. Despite deep neural networks' unimpeded success, the inner workings of their ability to share knowledge across tasks remain poorly underestimed. In pursuit of this understanding, the concept of transferability in deep neural networks was further refined (building on prior studies like Rose et al., 2019) by examining how different linear classifiers and dimensions within the network contribute to task generalization. It was observed that early learning stages, especially in lower levels of the network, exhibit limited transferability despite having basic image features, while the final stages, although accounting for a larger contribution, might be too complex and overly specialized. Conversely, mid-level stages were found to be the optimal choice for building general and efficient models capable of tackling a wide range of tasks effectively. By applying this insight, a two-stage fine-tuning strategy was developed: first-timing high-quality mid-level stages and then adjusting parameters of the entire network with the aim of maximizing the linear separation between classes, resulting in notable performance improvements in both standard and semi-supervised learning scenarios. The proposed approach was further validated through comprehensive experiments and detailed visualization of the output activation spaces. The source code for this method has been made available. Moreover, the concept of transferability was extended to detect subtle differences in complex semantic features, such as various forms of visual biases, including face gender, age, racial, luminance, and viewpoint preferences. The findings indicated that mid-level stages, although contributing minimally to task generalization, might be more effective in capturing complex multi-faceted characteristics. The method's potential in detecting visually salient biases was demonstrated while addressing the issue of detecting racial biases in vision-based biometric security systems, particularly when using systems trained on imbalanced datasets, such as the NIST Top 1 Face Recognition Scoreleaderboard, resulting in noticeable race biases in tasks related to face recognition. The approach thus provides an efficient task-specific solution by re-designing the network's structure to significantly reduce racial biases in vision-based biometric security systems. Network structure affects information spreading processes, which impact communication, task performance, and vaccine distribution efficiency. We studied seed cascade size relationships in complex networks by varying network aspects, focusing on networks with two clusters and multiple communities, revealing biases due to their structural asymmetry. Equilibrium findings are often represented by a mean-field approximation, which we tested in this study. We found that, in general networks, optimal information spreading efficiency is independent of seed size or target cascade size. However, this holds true for networks split into two clusters; in networks with many communities, optimal efficiency is determined by the target cascade size. For networks with two clusters, we developed a mean-field approximation model that can accurately predict optimal efficiency. For complex networks with many communities, our model still provides a reasonable estimate; still, it is not as precise as in the two-cluster scenario. We also studied how dividing networks into smaller parts affects information spreading. Interestingly, even if the network structure doesn't change, partitioning can significantly impact information spreading efficiency up to 50%. This effect is especially apparent when the target is located in a smaller sub-network. The insights from this study can be applied to communicate effectively, understand information spread, or implement targeted vaccine distribution strategies. Moreover, our study lays the groundwork for investigating the impact of network structure on information spreading in networks with many communities. The developed mean-field approximation can be used to predict this effect in general networks. We hope that further research will utilize statistical mechanics in this context. All study's code and network generators are available for use at https://github.com/ttuerdo/seed-cascade-size. The network visualizations are presented using the Visual Network Toolkit. All study's results can be reproduced using the same tools and software with the provided code. The network structure and size parameters can be adjusted using the provided code to reproduce different network configurations. The paper's metrics and parameters are listed in separate files, referenced as S1, S2, S3, and S4, with S4 containing the additional figures as per eq. 2 in the study. The study refers to [DoO19] as a source for the modularity-based measure, to [KSZC20] for the overlap among community members, and to [KRTV20] for the mean-field approximation in the two-cluster networks. The authors declare no conflict of interest regarding this study. The daily COVID-19 report from the Portuguese National Health Authority inspired the study's scenario. The study aims to provide insights to help with targeted vaccine distribution strategies

These results are supported by evidence from simple models as well as by an existing operator theory for Lagrangian graphs. In particular, it is shown that the ergodicity of volumes implies the repulsion of their levels under varying Lagrangian angles, with implications for the dynamics of Lagrangian manifolds. These results have implications for the area conjecture of Lagrangian mean curvature flow, as well as the behavior of volumes in complex hyperbolic spaces. Finally, it is shown that the geometry of hyperbolic manifolds can be explained using an operator theory for Lagrangian graphs, with implications for the area conjecture of Lagrangian mean curvature flow. Many current methods of orchestrating services within containers have been based on bare containers, which provide mechanisms primarily for running individual container images.  The lack of generalized tools for managing services within containers has resulted in the popularity of frameworks such as Docker Compose for bare containers.  To address this gap, we are introducing a new concept called encapsulation patterns (ENPs) to facilitate the management of services within containers.  The Ozy container, which is based on our ENP approach, enables the detection of dependencies between services and provides normalized service configurations, leading to more effective resource allocation and fault diagnosis.  To validate our ENCs, we performed detailed analyses of four different use cases--NGINX-ALB, MEAN stack, MeDICus, and Northbound--demonstrating that our approach, implemented in the Ozy container, outperforms established best practices in service orchestration.  The Ozy container, which is open-source and written in Go, provides a new approach to managing services within containers.  The source code for the project is available at https://github.com/ozycontainer, with both GUI and CLI tools provided to facilitate the management of services within containers.  Additionally, our ENP approach enables developers to create encapsulation patterns providers (ENPPs), allowing for even more customized management of services within containers.  The Ozy container is also designed to facilitate real-time monitoring and fault diagnosis through features such as live node switching and service configuration management.  The organizational capabilities within containers using the Ozy container provide a new approach to managing services within contexts, enabling the creation of both horizontal and vertical service groups to facilitate failure recovery and the decoupling of services.  The Ozy container provides several benefits over established service orchestration techniques, including more normalized service configurations, improved fault diagnosis, and asset management.  To compare our approach with industry standards, we performed detailed analyses of four different use cases--NGINX-ALB, MEAN stack, MeDICus, and Northbound--demonstrating that our approach, implemented in the Ozy container, outperforms established service and container orchestration software such as Docker Compose, Weave, and Kubernetes.  Finally, our approach enables the management of services within containers based on real-time monitoring and fault diagnosis, enabling developers to create encapsulation patterns providers (ENPPs) allowing for even more customized management of services within containers. Robust learning methods use fewer model parameters, particularly in overparameterized scenarios. To highlight this advantage, we examine linear regression in both the noisy label regime and the distributional shift regime, finding that robust learning outperforms non-robust learning in the latter case with fewer model parameters involved. Notably, robust learning exhibits better generalization when the model size exceeds the number of observed examples. Our analysis explains these findings through the effect size of several common loss functions on the predicted weights under the theoretical Sharpening operator, ultimately resulting in improved predictions on unseen data. To support these findings, we used logistic regression as an example and defined a Sharpening operator based on the empirical marginal distribution. By analyzing how the Sharpening operator affects the predicted parameters, we demonstrated how robust learning can lead to better generalization when the model size exceeds the number of observed examples. Our conclusions highlight the significance of robust learning in producing predictable and interpretable models that excel in various applications. To facilitate the creation of robust learning methods, we provided an open-source implementation of our theoretical framework on GitHub (https://github.com/agarwalsakash/Robust_Learning). Our code effectively reproduces the theoretical outcomes and showcases its practical applications. Specifically, we demonstrated how robust learning can lead to better generalization on real datasets, such as the MNIST and CIFAR-10 image recognition systems, and the Boston House Prices housing market valuation system. To accurately evaluate the robustness of the learned models, we carefully defined datasets and evaluation protocols based on several assumptions, including the compatibility between the marginal distributions of the training and testing sets, the independence of the labels from the input data, and the compatibility between the label distributions of the training and testing sets. Our results showed that robust learning can lead to significantly better generalization when the model size exceeds the number of observed examples, as the theoretical predictions accurately aligned with the practical outcomes. The capacity for learning across multiple modalities, particularly text and vision, has rapidly advanced recent years. Despite significant breakthroughs in enhancing the capabilities of multi-modal models, the potential benefits of using knowledge graphs in model design have not been thoroughly investigated. We introduced the concept of knowledge modalities - pre-trained methods for querying knowledge graphs to incorporate prior knowledge into multi-modal models. This framework allows knowledge to be integrated at various levels of abstraction by combining multi-modal inputs with graph-based knowledge models. This innovation leads to improved model robustness and performance across multiple models and datasets, and our knowledge modulation strategy further boosts classification accuracy. This work demonstrates that incorporating knowledge modalities in model design can lead to better outcomes. Knowledge graphs, initially utilized for knowledge representation, are now also employed as training data for developing models capable of handling multiple modalities. This new application highlights the far-reaching possibilities of knowledge graphs in multi-modal learning. Furthermore, we reveal that the process of knowledge modulation can be utilized in conjunction with other techniques for handling modalities that are difficult to integrate, such as vision and sound. We propose a new framework for modulating knowledge based on attention and demonstrate its effectiveness. The modulated knowledge can be utilized in model design to improve the capabilities of vision-language models. We further investigate the role of knowledge in model design and demonstrate that the modulated knowledge can be employed as a pre-training task. We utilize knowledge-based pre-training for learning cross-modal representations, which leads to state-of-the-art performance in model robustness and overall performance across multiple models and datasets. Notably, the benefits of knowledge-based pre-training are most pronounced in models that utilize self-supervision during the training process. We also verify the effectiveness of knowledge-based pre-training for other applications, such as zero-shot learning and open-domain question answering. We conduct additional analyses of knowledge modalities to gain a deeper understanding of multi-modal learning and release our source code at https://github.com/sustcsil-mlmc/knowledge-modalities. In the final part of this research, we outline several future avenues for exploring knowledge modalities in multi-modal learning, focusing particularly on the integration of sound modalities. We believe that the integration of knowledge and sound presents numerous challenges that require in-depth examination. One promising area of study is the development of knowledge-based models for single image super resolution, another under-explored area of study. We anticipate that the study of knowledge modalities will significantly contribute to progress in multi-modal learning and signal processing in the years to come. A PDF version of this article

This work compares the effectiveness of the unsupervised model to a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN) that's been trained for diagnosing AD with Alzheimer's Attenuation Coefficient (AC) images. A metric to quantify AD progression was established from comprehensive clinical data and used to train the Memory-Based Map (MBM) network. A notable aspect of the MBM network is its ability to learn comprehensive AD diagnosis information from images while being resistant to variations in external datasets. This achievement highlights the effectiveness of the MBM network for use in automatic AD diagnosis by analyzing images to determine AD diagnosis information, including recent AD diagnosis and the extent of brain damage for individuals. Recent studies have found that gradients in certain directions can be negligible when learning features from data sets with long-term dependencies, which challenges the effectiveness of standard gradient descent algorithms. To overcome this issue, a new technique known as the Backward Dropping Algorithm has been proposed. This method utilizes information about the direction of gradients and can significantly improve the performance of standard backpropagation for multi-layer neural networks. We have successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of this algorithm on various data sets with different types of long-term dependencies, including problems of sequence identification and mixed cross- and long-term dependencies in problems of cooperative learning. Furthermore, we have found that specific characteristics of long-term dependencies can result in significant reductions of computational requirements with minimal impacts on accuracy. We have also observed that the effectiveness of this algorithm is not limited to neural networks with supervised learning, but it is effective for problems of non-spurious learning as well. We have tested its performance on data sets of vision that is learned in a semi-synthetic manner. We have discovered that there is a direct correlation between the presence of gradients in the direction and the occurrence of errors in classification for problems of long-term dependencies. We have also discovered that there is a substantial difference between the occurrence of errors in classification for standard backpropagation and the proposed algorithm. We have tested its performance on data sets of vision, including images of AlexNet, GoogLeNet, and ResNet, with no changes to the architecture or the learning code. We have found that there is a substantial reduction of errors in classification for problems of long-term dependencies through the use of the proposed algorithm. We have also demonstrated its effectiveness on a multi-task learning with data sets of vision, including images of PASCAL VOC and ImageNet. We have found that there is a substantial reduction of errors in classification for problems of long-term dependencies across multiple tasks. We have also discovered that there is an interesting occurrence related to the presence of gradients in the direction and the occurrence of errors in classification for problems of long-term dependencies, which we have termed "the return of the gradients." We have found that there is an inverse correlation between the occurrence of errors in classification and the presence of gradients in the direction for problems of long-term dependencies. We have discovered that there is an interesting time-dependent behavior of the occurrence of errors in classification and the presence of gradients in the direction, which we have found to be in accordance with the law of thermodynamics. In contrast to the well-researched doped mott transistors, research on carrier doping in Cd$_2$Ru$_2$O$_7$ is relatively un explored.  Using single-particle computational methods, we found that like electron and hole doping, carrier doping in Cd$_2$Ru$_2$O$_7$ causes a phase transition between an insulating and metallic state.  Moreover, just like electron and hole doping, the spin-orbit coupling gets weakened as the phase transition occurs, yet this behavior isn't an indication of a loss of intrinsic properties caused by the doping.  These findings contrast those from Sr$_3$Ru$_2$O$_7$, another doped ruthenate where the spin-orbit coupling doesn't seem to be affected by the doping.  Interestingly, the computational methods predict that the phase transition caused by carrier doping shares the same characteristics as electron and hole doping, making it plausible to experimentally study this transition and determine if it's of the same nature as the well-known mott transition.  Expanding research on the spin-orbit coupling in Cd$_2$Ru$_2$O$_7$ could also contribute to the growing understanding of the intricate relationships between carrier doping, spin-orbit coupling, and quantum properties, common in many doped ruthates.  Finally, the computational methods predict that the mott phase in Cd$_2$Ru$_2$O$_7$ wouldn't be affected by the presence of the spin-orbit coupling even if it's going through a strong regime, providing a unique opportunity to isolate this effect. The Resolution-Based Branch and Bound-Numerical Analysis (RBB-NA) algorithm offers an efficient approach to optimize the accuracy of deformed DNA and RNA structures predicted using the multigenerational ant colony optimization algorithm. By introducing a comprehensive evaluation function, RBB-NA ensures a detailed examination of DNA and RNA structures, thereby refining the search process and gaining insights into the deformed structures of nucleic acids. Through a test case involving double-stranded DNA, RBB-NA was shown to improve the accuracy of predicted structures when compared to the multigenerational ant colony optimization algorithm alone. As a result, RBB-NA provides an enhanced and improved method for optimizing deformed DNA and RNA structures. Furthermore, this approach has potential for exploring other optimization problems in related fields. Due to its versatility, RBB-NA can be applied to various research areas focused on nanotechnology and the engineering of carbon-based systems. In addition to fundamental research, RBB-NA can be used for practical applications, including the design of self-replicating systems. Consequently, this approach may help drive innovation in the molecular engineering of DNA and RNA. Here, we describe six predicted double-stranded DNA structures of varying length that were optimized using RBB-NA and the multigenerational ant colony optimization algorithm. The optimized structures demonstrated improved energy scores when compared to their counterparts, as measured using the multigenerational ant colony optimization algorithm alone. Using the triangle inequality, the structure of two double-stranded DNA models (20-mer) was validated, showing an average error of less than 2.5 percent. The RBB-NA implementation for DNA and RNA structure optimization is suitable for large-scale systems and can be scaled for use in related fields. In addition to DNA and RNA optimization, RBB-NA has potential applications in the design of ligand-based drug targets and the optimization of deformed DNA nanostructure designs. As molecular engineering advances, the RBB-NA approach is positioned to contribute significant insights and designs, thereby driving future innovation in this field. As such, RBB-NA provides an essential tool for researchers working in the molecular engineering of DNA and RNA. In the future, this approach could also be used in related fields to solve complex optimization problems. Furthermore, RBB-NA may help address challenges related to the design of self-replicating systems and DNA-based computing platforms for addressing complex problems. Here, we describe eight predicted double-stranded DNA structures of varying length that were optimized using RBB-NA

We introduce a modified range ANS encoding, rANS, to enhance the encoding speed by fixing a non-zero, pre-determined precision. This variant achieves better data division performance compared to traditional methods, while also facilitating higher encoding rates to expedite simulations based on the ANS coding and decoding algorithms from the GE library. Nonetheless, rANS does not significantly aid in the decimation process. In addition, we investigate the optimal precision settings for rANS to ensure optimal performance in both division and decoding operations. Furthermore, we outline strategies to expedite rANS decoding at high precision levels, particularly when the value 'zero' needs to be encoded, as this scenario presents an additional computational challenge. Ultimately, we demonstrate that rANS can significantly accelerate integer division operations by roughly one hundred times over traditional methods when applied to high-precision ANS encoded data, thereby increasing the overall system throughput and allowing for the utilization of the same hardware to handle higher data rates. This approach can be applied to diverse fields such as medical imaging, machine learning, and signal processing, ultimately resulting in faster performance. In support of the community, we have released an open-source rANS implementation that offers fixed precision integer division, thereby offering a competitive advantage over traditional methods. This rANS implementation can easily integrate with existing ANS coding and decoding libraries, thereby providing improved performance in diverse applications. The rANS source code is publicly available on GitHub at the following repository address: https://github.com/ultravixed/rANS/tree/master/rANS%20C%2B%2B%2B%2B%2B. In addition, we have also released an open-source ANS-based simulated radio-frequency signal decoder implemented with the GE library at: https://github.com/ultravixed/ans_simulated_radio_frequency_signal_decoder. This radio-frequency signal decoder also supports the rANS variant and showcases its efficiency in real radio-frequency signals. In a recent revision, we have expanded the rANS sampling strategy options to accommodate diverse use cases and further accelerate the ANS encoding process. This expanded strategy allows for accommodating 'zero' encodings in the division operations by adjusting the rANS sampling plan to achieve two or more bits per sample, thereby ensuring zero cross-correlation in the division operations and eliminating the need for additional logic to handle 'zero' encodings. The interaction between dielectric properties and water within materials like concrete has crucial implications for various industrial applications, particularly in regards to monitoring the status of concrete structures through NDT methods. Although the link between concrete's moisture content and its dielectric properties is well-documented, generating precise predictions using non-destructive testing data poses a significant challenge. The model, which is inducted using scanning laser imaging and local job measurement of water content, demonstrates high accuracy and robustness, even when confronted with diverse concrete compositions and ages. The model's versatility is further illustrated through successful applications in various concrete types. The model's capabilities are summarized in detail, along with a step-by-step description of its training and validation processes. The results of this research have important implications for developing non-destructive testing methods to assess the condition and monitor various material properties in complex materials like concrete. A model, the key to heavy-heavy hadronic molecule physics being the rectification of the constraints of the parton model, is suggested.  Utilizing the known spectrum of the parton model, the model can predict various heavy-heavy hadronic molecules, such as $D\bar{D}^*$ pairs, the tetraquarks in the conventional sense, the X, Y, Z particles as well as the R and Y states demonstrated in the BESIII experiments.  A linear potential is established among the bound states of the parton model, which is consistent with the observations in the Landau levels of the QCD constituents.  A fundamental aspect of the model is the method used to establish the bound state problem, which does not rely on the uncertain nonperturbative QCD effects but rather solves the bound state problem within the parton model in a predictable and certain manner. Furthermore, the model is applicable not only to the study of heavy-heavy hadronic molecules but also the entire range of light and heavy mesons and bosons. Research on pedestrian trajectory prediction has gained significant momentum in recent years, but existing studies have limitations due to their simplified state space and assumptions. Unlike single-agent dynamics which works well for isolated trajectories, it poorly predicts concurrent pedestrian movements. This study adapts the single-agent method to accommodate multiple agents, however, this still doesn't work well for the more complex real-world scenarios it attempts to model. A possible reason for these shortcomings is the oversimplification of interaction between agents. A new approach, multi-agent Lagrangian dynamics, has been developed to address these challenges. It views the movement of multiple agents as parts of interconnected fluid dynamics systems. By representing each agent's position relative to its neighbors, the new method can leverage variational autoencoders and generate more accurate trajectory predictions. The effectiveness of this approach has been supported in experiments across the challenging DAIM, ARGOS, and UCF data sets. Additionally, when combined with existing trajectory predictors, the new method resulted in notable performance enhancements, especially in cases involving close-range interactions among agents. A self-supervised co-training framework has also been proposed to further improve the accuracy of trajectory prediction. This approach involves utilizing two Lagrangian networks to model the movement of two groups of agents within the same video, and demonstrating that the networks can learn to handle a broader range of scenarios than the single-agent method alone. The new approach has several advantages over previous trajectory prediction techniques. Firstly, it requires minimal supervision and can learn from unlabelled data. Secondly, it doesn't need to threshold the density of agents within a certain area to separate concurrent trajectories. Thirdly, it doesn't need to employ probabilistic models, which can be computationally expensive and complicated to train. A Python implementation of the new method has been provided on GitHub. In our research, we investigate the emergence of coherence in Boltzmann machines through the lens of quantum information theory. As the time evolution of the network and its parameters shift from classical to quantum dynamics, the machine's computational complexity undergoes a analogous transformation, increasing in line with the scale of its classical-to-quantum transition. Focusing on the most efficient algorithms currently available, we evaluate the optimal parameter counting method and demonstrate that, upon reaching a certain threshold, further data collection necessitates exponentially increasing amounts of both time and memory. It is precisely at this point that the advantages offered by quantum dynamics become fully apparent. In order to facilitate a comprehensive understanding of the issue, we have further developed three distinct approaches to visualize the results: first, by utilizing a systematic numerical examination; second, by providing an in-depth, step-by-step numerical analysis of the most telling parameters; and third, by offering an innovative means of representing the most efficient parameter searching strategy through the use of fractals. Ultimately, our research forecasts that widespread adoption of quantum dynamics by Boltzmann machine developers may be hindered by a considerable barrier stemming from inherent algorithmic limitations. Interestingly, this restriction is reminiscent of a fundamental principle within quantum mechanics itself, raising intriguing questions about the potential for research in this area to uncover novel insights into the nature of reality. Automating the analysis of blood test results enhances healthcare by streamlining measurements, increasing efficiency, and enabling large-scale data tracking. Although extensive medical knowledge is required to accurately interpret laboratory results, experts often provide qualitative analyses without detailing the underlying reasoning due to time and knowledge constraints. Developing more precise automation systems for analyzing blood tests, however, relies on understanding the decision-making processes of medical experts. To close this knowledge gap, we present a framework for explaining qualitative medical diagnoses, focusing on the properties of blood-related measurements as identified by medical specialists. To demonstrate this explanation framework's potential, we automated the analysis of neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio results using deep learning techniques, then created a qualitative diagnosis model based on the identified characteristics. Ultimately, this approach enabled us to determine the specific characteristics used by medical experts to create their diagnoses, thereby facilitating the black-box automation of complex medical analysis processes, including the interpretation of neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio laboratory results. The framework and explanation methods described are freely available online. Please visit the following link to access the code: https://github.com/danierv/ExTAL-BNL.

Chromatic aberration, a function of lens geometry, separates light into its component colors, delaying the red wavelengths the most, a phenomenon with significant photographic implications. While commonly viewed as a distortion, it has historically received less attention than other optical defects. In imagery, chromatic aberration's impact is largely overlooked, despite its inherent nature that can be compensated for in cameras. In reality, cameras cannot fully correct this defect; instead, it reappears in the image capture process, an phenomenon that remains unexplained. A theory suggests a biological advantage in compensating for this defect could exist. If this were the case, it would also lead to a preservation of chromatic aberration in works that feature warm colors, as these are most prevalent in artworks. In contrast, cool colors are less affected and therefore less likely to be retained. To test this, a database of 81,651 image regions from the Image Tagging Heritage (ITH) dataset, characterized by prominent chromatic aberration due to distance between subject and camera, was used. Analysis showed that artworks featuring warm colors tend to retain chromatic aberration, an effect that is not observed in those with cool colors. This retention of chromatic aberration in artworks with warm colors may indicate a deliberate intent to emphasize these colors, an advantage in their rendition and perception. Conversely, retention of chromatic aberration in these colors may also be the result of an inadvertent effect due to artist preference. To distinguish these two scenarios, a new classifier was designed to identify images featuring warm colors in their peripheral areas from those with cool colors. If the preference for warm colors is genuine, it should be characterized by features that are far from the camera's viewpoint. Conversely, if retention of chromatic aberration is the result of accident, it should be positively correlated with features that are in the camera's vicinity of view. As it turns out, images featuring warm colors in their peripheral areas, likely to retain chromatic aberration, should be positively correlated with this defect and also with features within these areas. Conversely, images featuring cool colors in their peripheral areas, likely to discard chromatic aberration, should be negatively correlated with this defect and also with features within these areas. Researchers proposing the nuclear break-up mechanism for the photoinjection of electrons in laser-wakefield accelerators have developed a novel electron beam production technique. A picosecond-scale nuclear breakdown, induced by a short pulse from a chirped-regenerative amplifier, yields a high-energy electron beam matching the laser's trajectory. This beam's intensity can be manipulated by adjusting parameters like laser duration and electron kinematic energy to provide nanocurrent-level particle beams with extremely low emittances, suitable for protein crystal structures analysis. This technique offers an innovative pathway for a wide range of applications to leverage the capabilities of tabletop laser-wakefield accelerators. Unlike the SASE scheme, this technology doesn't demand sophisticated, laser-injection setups or extensive, on-wax photon storage. Instead, it leverages the natural, self-injection processes of the plasma focus to offer high-quality electron beams with very little investment. We present findings from our recent studies of the SSBU NLPCA facility, detailing how its short pulses and high power can generate electron beams compatible with cutting-edge structural biology. We demonstrate that the local plasma focus in this setup provides nanocurrent-level particle beams with extremely low emittances due to its inherent, sharp focusing fields. We examine the theoretical constraints of this technique, transposing ideas from conventional accelerators to explore their full potential and predicting that better beam quality can be attained with longer laser pulses in two areas of research: crystal structures analysis and bio-medical applications. We present a detailed, theoretical comparison between the present setup and two different free-electron X-ray sources: the STRETCH technique and the laser backflow scheme. We show that our technique offers an attractive middle ground between these competing technologies, providing an independent pathway to achieve cutting-edge sample damage reduction and sample diffraction limits with laser pulses produced by typical, chirped-regenerative amplifiers. Conversely, for the medical community, it offers an independent pathway to deliver high doses and treatment levels against conventional radioresistance. Consequently, this technique represents an innovative, underinvested option for the vast majority of users in the fields of biology and medicine. We also outline future research goals, listing the primary aims of starting a new R&D program aimed at further developing this technique. These initiatives include establishing collaborative projects and programs to explore the physics behind local nuclear break-ups under the influence of very intense, ultrashort laser fields. We introduce pyStoNED, a Python package that offers a new generation of multivariate regression techniques based on statistical network modeling. It provides both classical and machine learning approaches to tackle challenges that traditional statistics cannot handle efficiently. PyStoNED offers a robust platform for analyzing complex datasets and visualizing results, and its scalable algorithms allow it to handle large datasets that exceed the limitations of existing statistical methods. We discuss the underlying principles of statistical network modeling, specifically normalization and differential equation networks, and demonstrate the package's capabilities through a series of educational examples. PyStoNED is compatible with popular statistical data analysis tools and integrates well with other Python libraries, including scikit-learn, Biopython, and Graph-tool. It maintains strong connections to underlying statistical theories and is always willing to adapt to emerging fields like deep learning. PyStoNED offers an intuitive user interface for complex network objects, allowing for the integration of various metadata through its node and edge data structure. It provides comprehensive documentation for each function, and the source code is accessible through the pyStoNED GitHub repository. PyStoNED offers feature-rich functionality for regression tasks, time-series analysis, and network generation, and its integration with other Python libraries facilitates the integration of statistical network modeling into existing data analysis pipelines. PyStoNED stands for "statistical network modeling and dynamic analysis," and it offers a new generation of multivariate regression tools based on statistical network modeling. PyStoNED aims to strengthen its connections to various applications and establish itself as a leading package for statistical network modeling in Python. Over the past decade, neural networks in computer vision have become increasingly complex, making them difficult to understand and diagnose. This limitation hinders software testing from being a reliable method for ensuring the validity of visual outcomes. We developed and present a novel, open-source technique that emulates neural networks using kernels, specifically neural tangent kernels. This approach not only facilitates faster testing due to a reduction in the number of computations required (by eliminating the need for network training), but also enhances interpretability. We contrast this method with traditional, fully connected neural networks and experimentally verify that models based on neural tangent kernels effectively replicate their counterparts' performance in classifying diverse image datasets. This contrasts with tangent kernels, which fell short in this regard. We also explored the implementation and validation of NTKs in the context of image classification. Our results demonstrate that neural tangent kernels tailored to specific tasks can be learned from scratch, outperforming networks in some cases. This breakthrough comes at the expense of a significantly increased memory storage needs and training time for learning these kernels. We propose an optimized algorithm for decreasing the NTK resolution's impact on memory consumption. We utilize our kernel-based framework to propose a unique method for diagnosing failures in object recognition. In line with public datasets, we generate and describe a set of failure scenarios not accounted for in existing datasets. The code for the kernel-based technique is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ufo-orl/ntk-vision. Our testing framework, which utilizes the kernel-based technique, is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ufo-orl/nl-vision. We anticipate that neural tangent kernels will contribute to achieving true automation in image recognition, a goal that may also lead to the development of more resilient and adaptable machine learning systems across image and signal processing domains. Publicly accessible resources for replicating our research include Jupyter Notebooks for training and testing purposes (https://github.com/ufo-orl/nl-orl/tree/master/ntk-vision), as well as planning and automation scripts written in Python and WTL (https://github.com/ufo-orl/nl-orl/tree/master/ntl-vision). Further advancements in understanding neural tangent kernels and understanding deep learning models in general rely on the collaboration of the vision and machine learning research communities. Capturing panoramic images with a single lens is technically complex and has been complicated by the need for costly equipment such as turntables and external positioning sensors like GPS. Recent advancements in wearable technology have made it possible to use inertial monitoring units (IMUs) to track the movement of a camera, allowing for efficient panoramic image capture through simply taking pictures while moving the IMU along a predetermined path. Although IMUs can be an affordable solution, the accuracy of the calculated camera positions remains a concern. This study proposes an innovative method that uses IMU data to calculate the position and orientation of a camera with high precision by combining calibration data, minimizing distortion in position measurements, and estimating camera orientation. Based on this theory, a prototype was developed, and its effectiveness was tested by analyzing the method's ability to calculate the position and orientation of a camera with high precision. Chimeras stability has been studied in networks of coupled oscillators, however previous research often considered a homogenous group of oscillators which does not accurately represent real-world scenarios. In this study, we relaxed this assumption by investigating a phase oscillator dynamical model that allows for varying parameter values across the network, building upon existing theory which showed that increasing group heterogeneity leads to more unstable chimeras. Using the extension of the stability matrix method via commutator, we confirmed that for any pair of groups the largest stability factor is bounded by a specific expression containing the difference between group oscillation frequencies, and it tends to zero when this difference approaches zero. This result was further validated numerically in a 5-node network, where we observed that for a Zettl-Martin pair it is not only the difference in frequencies but also in parameters that determines the stability factor, and increasing group heterogeneity does not always lead to more unstable chimeras. On the contrary, in a three-node network we found that chimeras emerge only when a specific condition related to group parameters is met, and this condition depends on the difference in frequencies. Importantly, our analysis revealed that for small networks it is possible to stabilize a chimeric state by adjusting the parameters within a group, however this is not the case for larger networks. Lastly, we observed that increasing heterogeneity may also lead to the emergence of multiple stable chimeras in a group.} \\[0.5cm] \text{Keywords: Chimera stability, Phase oscillators, Topological influence.} \\[0.5cm] \text{References:} \\end{document} \begin{enumerate} \item E.M. The vast potential of sim-to-real scenarios has highlighted the significance of developing versatile and robust controllers that generalize effectively to real-world conditions despite accounting for inevitable uncertainties in dynamic models. Often, maximum likelihood estimation tends to overlook the potential discrepancies between model outcomes and observational data, which may lead to the learning of imprecise models that compromise the reliability of controllers based on model-predictive control. Therefore, introducing a lower bound on the model's likelihood errors using adversarial training could enhance the robustness of the learned controller. However, traditional methods based on maximum likelihood may fail to capitalize on this advantage. This paper suggests an approach where we combine adversarial training with a novel method of learning based on likelihood-free statistics, where the univariate cumulative distribution function is applied to the sum of instantaneous errors. This novel approach can utilize the empirically derived distribution of summed errors to construct a robust MPC that is more resilient to uncertainty and better equipped to generalize to unseen initial conditions. Focusing on the difficult case of imposing a lower bound on short-term likelihood noise, we have developed specialized CDFormulations for both unimodal and bimodal low-velocity impacts in planar dynamics, which can be utilized in adversarial training. Our method of enforcing a robust likelihood noise (RLN) model has been validated by simulating impacts at various locations on a basic planar pendulum and a more complex V-2 rocket, as well as in real-world scenarios, with results showing robust control in numerous initial conditions, with added benefits including the potential for RLN-based black-box optimization and novel physics-based learning outcomes. All simulation code and data, including The Airborne Dynamics Toolbox, are publicly available online. We have successfully demonstrated a controller that passes the "seen as unseen" test in multiple scenarios. This understanding has been applied to random tensor networks and used to develop a method for extracting information about a specific region's bond dimension. A method for efficiently calculating the reflected entanglement spectrum was also developed, which has implications for understanding phases of matter and critical behaviors. This method may be particularly useful for near-term quantum machines, as it is resilient to limited errors. Furthermore, the system was examined under various conditions, including quantum criticality, symmetry-protected topological systems, and lattices composed of multiple Lattice sites. These studies yielded similar results when comparing the reflected entanglement spectrum to the standard R'enyi spectra, suggesting the spectra can be used in tandem to aid in the characterization of the system's phases and critical behaviors. By analyzing the system's behavior, the researchers were able to determine the bond dimension of the reflected region, even under imperfect simulation conditions. This method for calculating the reflected entanglement spectrum, along with its associated extractor, may be applied in the analysis of various quantum systems. Our research demonstrates that for a broad class of dynamic systems, the likelihood of long-term persistence in large subsets can be driven significantly lower by minor alterations to the system dynamics. This phenomenon arises when an abrupt shift in the system's behavior occurs within a large subset, causing the transition area to exhibit unusually high persistence. As a result, small changes in the system's parameters can dramatically impact the overall persistence statistic. Moreover, the statistical power of persistence as a measure to differentiate distinct dynamic systems is shown to be limited. Example cases illustrate that even in systems exhibiting periodicity, the linearity of persistence as a function of parameters can be disrupted. In addition, the analyses provide insight into the underlying mechanisms driving persistence in different scenarios and offer potential avenues to improve the utility of persistence as a metric in various applications. derived from gauge theory, which have been used to model various physical phenomena, 
including the Aharonov-Bohm effect, Dehn twist, and topological superconductors.
Despite their wide range of applications, the notion of holonomy holds distinct meanings 
in gauge theory and general theory of gravity. We aim to provide an in-depth explanation 
of holonomy within both theories, beginning with an introduction to holonomy before applying 
it to the general theory of gravity in a new manner. By extending the Faddeev-Jackiw approach 
and utilizing a new geometric interpretation of holonomy in gravity, our work reveals that 
holonomy may result in gravity holonomy loops contracting to points, a phenomenon dubbed

anomalies. To confirm our theory, we have developed an alternative derivation of the 
geodesic Weyl anomaly, in addition to proposing a thought experiment to verify the 
gravitational holonomy spinhole effect, which may be subject to experimental confirmation.

holonomy spinhole effect, including scanning high-precision gravity maps and testing the 
holonomy spinhole effect in neutron interferometry. If successful, our thought experiment

gravitational holonomy effect, paving the way to a new application of holonomy in

gauge theory, general theory of gravity, and gravitational physics.
