A quantum dot connected to a superconductor can be used as a sensitive device to study the superconductor's quasiparticle energy levels. By analyzing these energy levels, one can gain insight into changes in the superconductor's properties such as its band gap and pairing interactions. While the Landau-Ginzburg theory provides a method for calculating a superconductor's macroscopic properties, this approach proves inadequate for analyzing the fine details of quasiparticle energy levels. A theoretical model known as the BCS theory of superconductivity, however, allows for the determination of the energy levels with the aid of a self-consistent scattering problem. Our work shows that these two theories can be combined to study how a quantum dot embedded within a superconductor responds to variations in its environment. By utilizing this hybrid model, we can determine the temperature at which the superconductor transitions from a normal to a superconducting state as well as assess the impact of this transition on the quantum dot's energy levels. Furthermore, this hybrid model provides a sensitive means of studying the interaction between the quantum dot and the superconductor, allowing for the detection of very small changes in this interaction. Our study also identifies a particular quantum dot parameter range in which its energy levels can be directly related to the superconductor's quasiparticle density of states, thereby enabling their non-local properties to be studied using the quantum dot as an analog sensor. Similar quantum dot and superconductor structures have been previously studied in the context of quantum devices, including tunnel junctions and quantum pumps. Our work demonstrates that these systems can be viewed as specific implementations of our general finding, allowing for the characterization of a superconductor's interaction strength and the complexity of its energy levels. Our research offers a foundation for utilizing quantum dots to study various superconducting properties beyond their macroscopic behavior, such as their band gap and pairing interactions. As an example of this, we investigate how a superconductor's confinement length affects its interaction strength with a quantum dot embedded within it and show that this would result in a change in the quantum dot's Kondo temperature at temperatures at which the superconductor would transition to a normal state. Our findings, therefore, highlight the versatility of quantum dots as sensitive devices to study a wide variety of superconducting properties and their interactions. Furthermore, this approach can be expanded to analyze the impact of quantum dots on a superconductor's properties, allowing for the detection of very small changes in these interactions. A geometric approach to the Euler equations and their relationships with Lagrangian manifolds and group actions are presented in this work. We derive new metrics in Lagrangian space and compare them with their Eulerian counterparts, revealing that the hyperbolic nature of fluid dynamics is not universally inherent. This understanding leads to a new material description, rooted in a group of symplectic transformations, that is applicable to the most general compressible fluids and reduces to well-known forms for fluids with perfect geometry. Furthermore, this new material description is shown to coincide with existing models based on Lagrangian manifolds, ultimately paving the way for a unified geometric description of fluid dynamics across various regimes of material behavior. The work also provides a novel method for deriving thermodynamic laws from a geometric perspective, one that is compatible with various material models, including the Holmgren system. Interestingly, when the new metrics are expressed in the Eulerian space, they yield a mix of hyperbolic and parabolic components that are precisely the components identified by various authors in their attempts to resolve the question of the Euler equations' hyperbolicity. This work is completed by noting that, despite these successes, several key challenges and obstacles remain in the field of fluid dynamics. Firstly, a geometric description of the Rayleigh condition relevant to weakly compressible fluids is not yet known. Secondly, extending the work to fluids with imperfect geometry is not yet possible due to the absence of a well-formulated set of equations for these fluids. Thirdly, elevating the work to the dynamic case for fluids with imperfect geometry is not yet feasible due to the absence of a well-formulated dynamic version of the equations for these fluids. Fourthly, resolving the question of the Euler equations' hyperbolicity is far from being a simple consequence of the work; in fact, several parabolic components remain present even in the Lagrangian space and are therefore cannot be held responsible for the non-hyperbolic nature of the Euler equations. Finally, fifthly and lastly, several key challenges and obstacles are mentioned. These challenges and obstacles include the lack of understanding the geometric description of the Rayleigh condition relevant to weakly compressible fluids, elevating the work to fluids with imperfect geometry, among others. This paper suggests treating duration modeling as a problem within a transfer learning framework. Typically, time series models assume knowledge of the distribution of durations at model setup, but our approach assumes only that durations are drawn from a known family of distributions, without specifying it. As a result, any distribution within this family can be learned without the need for model retraining. By contrast, conventional models that learn distribution parameters must be retrained whenever the distribution changes, although some models can be adapted for different distributions through changes to their hyperparameters. To illustrate the advantages of our method, we compared it to the classic Proportional Odds Model and a neural network approach on synthetic data, and found that our approach outperformed these models when the true distribution differed from that initially assumed. However, when the assumed distribution was correct, the Proportional Odds Model performed best. An implementation of our approach, called Cannonball, is available for comparison purposes. It can be used to model censored durations, and it treats such cases by incorporating the Nelson-Aalen estimator into the model. When durations are censored, the model learns a distribution that accurately fits both the observed times and the patterns of censoring. Examples of this behavior are provided from both real and synthetic data. Moreover, the method can easily extend to any type of time series with taking into account the differences in distribution as the data shifts. Examples of this behavior are provided from both real and synthetic data. When applied to the treatment duration of patients with Lupus, we found that using a transfer learning approach, as implemented in Cannonball, yielded results that matched real-world clinical data. Finally, we demonstrated the method's applicability to various use cases, including both small-sample and large-scale settings. As such, we believe that our approach has the potential to address challenges in duration modeling that are rooted in changes in distribution. This research aims to create predictive models of myocardial infarction survivors who develop various combinations of multiple health conditions over long periods of time. We built this upon previous studies focusing on the occurrence of new health conditions in MI survivors who remained free from the condition for at least five years. By employing Bayesian predictive models to time-to-event data from two large Scottish patient datasets linked with hospital and death records, we found that survivors who experienced MI are at a significantly higher risk of developing new health conditions. An overall analysis of these survivors' patterns of care and their health over time, combined with the socio-demographic data available, revealed distinct trends across different communities and sexes. Consequently, we suggest modifying the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines for patients who have had an MI to prioritize prevention of common post-MI health conditions that also share similar risk factors with cardiovascular disease and vice versa. Furthermore, we propose enhancing public health initiatives to address post-MI health conditions by focusing on heart-healthy measures, especially for at-risk groups, to bridge the health gap between different communities and populations. The Metric Dimension problem, which involves finding the minimum number of vertices required to accurately determine the distance between any two vertices in a graph, has generated significant interest. Parameterized analysis by key graph characteristics such as tree structure, degree maximum, and clustering number has been explored. Contrasting these strategies reveals distinct patterns in algorithmic complexity, particularly where treewidth, which correlates with the number of colors needed in a graph coloring, results in subexponential complexity and a threshold behavior at a specific treewidth value. This is in stark contrast to other parameters where treewidth-based complexities yield polynomial transitions. Experimentally verifying metric dimension values using distance-based algorithms has shown subexponential complexities to be within a factor of at most 2 of optimal solutions. This is confirmed through benchmarking on various graph types. Moreover, a bound on the minimum number of source vertices needed to efficiently calculate distances to any pair of vertices in a graph has been established and implemented. This number of source vertices dictates the number of contraction steps required in a treewidth contraction process. This bound, which holds for trees and randomly uniform graphs, results in complexities that remain sublinear until the parameter reaches a value corresponding to the square root of n, where n is the number of vertices. Implementing an algorithm using this bound has shown that, contrary to previously obtained complexity upper bounds, choosing the treewidth parameter can lead to potentially polynomial complexities, which contradicts previously proposed treewidth-based upper bounds. This highlights a distinct difference in behavior between algorithmically obtained complexities and subexponential upper bounds. This difference is particularly noticeable in complexities obtained using the maximum degree parameter, which exhibit constant upper bound values. This constant values correspond to the maximum degree parameter value. This behavior is observed in experiments across various graph types. Moreover, bounds obtained using this approach are tighter than previously obtained complexity upper bounds. This effectively "closes the gap" between obtained bounds and upper bounds for the Metric Dimension problem parameterized by degree maximum. This has been verified through benchmarking on various graph types. Implementing an algorithm using this bound has shown that, contrary to previously obtained complexity upper bounds, choosing the clustering number parameter can lead to potentially linear complexities. This is in contrast to previously proposed upper bounds, which are generally lower. This effectively "closes the gap" between obtained bounds and upper bounds for the Metric Dimension problem parameterized by clustering number. This has been verified through benchmarking on various graph types. Using a global climate model, we implemented two scenarios: one with all channels unblocked and another with specific channels blocked, mimicking certain circulation patterns that restrict water vapor ascent. In both cases, we observed that low-ocean heat trapping led to distinctive climate responses, characterized by altered latitude-dependent temperature patterns, shifted precipitation patterns, and changes in cloud coverage. Notably, the difference between these scenarios was relatively minor at the equator but became more pronounced at higher latitudes, where altered circulation patterns resulted in increased temperatures, greater precipitation increases, and altered patterns of cloud cover. In general, the effects of low-ocean heat trapping were more pronounced in areas with existing precipitation gaps, where further warming would exacerbate dry spells. This points to an increased likelihood of severe droughts in regions already experiencing precipitation deficits. Furthermore, the research highlights the importance of considering circulation patterns and water vapor circulation when evaluating climate responses, as relying solely on latitudinal temperature trends may significantly underestimate the impacts of low-ocean heat trapping in certain cases. In fact, the research suggests that as much as 40% of the temperature trend difference between models can be attributed to variations in precipitation patterns and cloud cover. These findings emphasize the need for further research in this area, emphasizing the intricate water cycle dynamics that shape climate responses and amplify climate sensitivities in certain instances. Ultimately, the research supports earlier claims that'missing channels' in models can amplify climate responses, as the models in this study showed increased sensitivities in the absence of certain water vapor absorption patterns, with factors such as ocean depth, geostrophic width, and temperature damping contributing to variations in the climate response. The interpolation problem for smooth functions on a regular simplex Qn within the unit cube Qn is explored, with interpolation occurring at its nodes. A regular simplex's symmetry generates an inherent symmetry in the resulting interpolated function, which is also smooth and covariant under the orthogonal group. When dim(Qn) equals n, this symmetry implies the interpolated function's partial derivatives up to the nth order are uniquely determined by the values at the nodes. A function on Qn with this property can be identified as a polynomial of degree n or less, which also explains why such a function's interpolation within Qn occurs exactly when the number of nodes equals n+1 or less. However, this result is not a consequence of the Chebyshev property, which is only true in one-dimensional space (n=1). In all cases where n>1, smooth nondegenerate regular simplices with interpolation nodes will always exist, which answers and contradicts the Pippenger and Shankrova conjecture. A computationally feasible approach exists for determining such a function and its polynomial coefficients through the solution of an orthogonality constraint within the orthogonal group's action on tensor representations. Two correlated random walks, one with transitions A to B and B to A occurring at different rates, can be treated as a special case of a Markov chain with its states represented as pairs (A or B, a specific state value). Using this approach, we investigate correlated random walks with initial preferences in one direction and discuss scenarios where the initial bias is balanced. Additionally, we apply a mathematical method to determine the characteristic polynomial of the transition probability matrix, represented as a polynomial function of variables, and use this approach to calculate higher-order statistics (mean, standard deviation, skewness, and curvature) for the equilibrium distributions of correlated random walks. Furthermore, we validate these findings through derived exact formulas for these statistics and an analysis of error rates in approximations made during the calculation process. Ultimately, we apply our results to examine the properties of Cauchy random variables and normal distributions. Interestingly, we discover that characteristic polynomials of larger Markov matrices with positive values on the main diagonal have close connections with higher-order asymptotic series of expanded integrals, and normal distributions, when considering a specific range of Correlated random walk parameters. The regularity of these statistics also enables construction of efficient approximation tools such as the piecewise linear approximation method (PLAM), a novel technique we've developed which offers rate optimality in the class of piecewise linear methods. The regularity of these statistics further enables construction of efficient approximation tools, and we've developed the polynomial root shifting method (PRM), which offers rate optimality in the class of polynomial-based methods. The newly introduced methods provide significant improvements, and our theoretical findings validate their effectiveness through large classes of examples showing exceptional accuracy and efficiency. In addition to these Markov-based findings, we've also derived exact formulas for the equilibrium distributions of a binary preferred random walk in a fair game with a dependent triangle and proved the regularity of these statistics, and developed the preferred game shifting method (PGM), which offers rate optimality in the class of piecewise linear methods, and provides significant improvements over the standard piecewise linear approximation method (PLAM). Notably, the first preferred game shifting method and polynomial root shifting method do not rely on a preference parameter being balanced, and can handle cases where the parameter is either balanced or imbalanced. The method of preferred game shifting further enables construction of efficient approximation tools, and offers significant improvements, and our theoretical findings feature large classes of examples showcasing the methods' exceptional general applicability and efficiency. In certain cases, the new techniques provide significant improvements over previously proposed methods

Originally, the size-change principle was developed to automatically prove the termination of term rewriting systems. More recently, clocks were introduced to broaden its application to rewriting systems that are not fully convergent. Our study further expands on terminating rewriting systems by introducing evaluation rules to minimize the need for clock values. We introduce a new version of size-change graphs that incorporate clocks with evaluation mechanisms. It has been mathematically proven that the termination proof of a rewriting system can be simplified if the evaluation mechanism is implemented in a size-monomial way. To demonstrate the practical utility of our findings, we applied the size-change graph method to various evaluation strategies, including first-order rewriting and positive and negative nested substitution, for which the necessary monomial definitions have been computationally derived. Moreover, the simplification criterion has been practically verified through its implementation in the Prolog logic system. Our evaluation, involving an benchmark of 13 infinite domains, showed that the size-change graph method significantly reduces the computational burden associated with termination analysis, as it now takes only a few milliseconds instead of more than 10,000 seconds. Our study also highlighted that clock values can be completely eliminated in certain cases where the evaluation strategy itself follows a size-monotonic pattern. Our method has been successfully validated for its applicability to rewriting systems with positive built-in functions, including built-in exponentiation, as illustrated by its successful termination analysis of the pre-implemented code in Prolog. Our findings further show that the evaluation strategy has a significant influence on the simplification of termination analysis. For instance, the termination proof of the pre-implemented code in Prolog is much simpler when using nested substitution than when using first-order rewriting. Our method has also successfully incorporated the evaluation strategy to further simplify the representation of size-change graphs by eliminating the need for equalities among size monomials. Our approach has been validated for its independence of distribution, meaning that the termination analysis can be performed independently for any subset of rules. Our study has shown that the size-change graph method can fail to terminate in some cases where the evaluation strategy itself does not follow a size-monotonic pattern, as illustrated by the examples with built-in division. Our approach has further highlighted that the failure of size-change graph method does not imply the decidable termination of rewriting systems with infinite domains. Our study has been concluded by successfully applying the size-change graph method to termination analysis of evaluation strategies that do not necessarily follow size-monotonic patterns, as illustrated by the examples with built-in division. Our approach has been validated for its practical applicability

We define and calculate the real part of the most unstable mode of a particular phase in the cycle for various hairpin packet aspects but find no consistent pattern that matches the observed fluctuations in the flow's behavior. We also discuss reasons for these discrepancies and explore possible directions for further research. We then compare this model to other existing models for how hairpin packet growth occurs and find that it can be represented in a particular structural form in the context of mathematical modeling. Moreover, we examine which parts of this structure match the predictions of different theories that aim to explain how these packets grow. We discover that theories related to these explanations provide accurate predictions for how these packets grow in a particular environment. Notably, the spectral positions of resonances in these nanoantennas can be individually adjusted through the parameters of paRAMide molecules, and their interactions give rise to unique phenomena including coupling, mode mixing, and the occurrence of diabolical points in paRAMide configurations. These phenomena can serve as foundational elements for advancing paRAMide-based photonics applications. Furthermore, the developed methodology incorporates the incorporation of post-self-assembled monolayers metalization techniques, offering a practical route to realizing these nanoantennas, whose performance is quantified in scattering and near-field simulations. These studies also identify strategies for optimizing the design of paRAMide-based optical nanoantennas, advising against using certain gap configurations that give rise to undesirable spectral interactions and signal cancellations. Notably, the spectral interactions in these nanoantennas fall within the weak coupling regime, thereby satisfying the conditions for unambiguous quantum entanglement generation between the involved electromagnetic modes. In conclusion, the novel designs presented can enhance the performance of paRAMide-based photonics by providing a competitive advantage over existing state-of-the-art nanoantennas. Amorphous materials with varying chemical compositions have become a focus due to their diverse range of applications and intricate mechanical properties. These properties, which cannot be fully explained by traditional models, rely heavily on localized plastic events that occur at various length scales. Each event triggers a force field that disrupts the material's packning and causes damage to nearby bonds. Nevertheless, the model we currently have fails to account for many complex features of amorphous materials. In opposition to this, a new model based on molecular dynamics reveals that the disturbance from these events can lead to variations in the material's elasticity and ultimate strength, depending on the event itself. These plastic events also serve as weak points in the material, making it more prone to fracture when subjected to tension. These phenomena have been observed equally in amorphous and crystalline materials, suggesting that classical fracture theories may not fully apply to amorphous materials. Interestingly, though, the model predicts that the time it takes for cracks to form will follow a universal pattern that is less influenced by the chemical composition of the material. These conclusions were reached after analyzing data from a range of amorphous materials with different packings and chemical features. These findings also highlight the need to update the theory of strength that has been widely accepted until now. These results demonstrate that the mechanical characteristics of amorphous materials rely heavily on localized events such as breakage and the physical structure of the material. Moreover, they struggle to embed human expertise, specifically driver experience, which is pivotal in evaluating driver behavior and skill. In this study, researchers develop a model that not only considers external driving factors but also incorporates human expertise, utilizing advanced reinforcement learning algorithms. They collect safety-relevant data from human drivers in various driving scenarios, including inclement weather, and collect expert knowledge from driving manuals, which they integrate into the model. Initially, the model is tailored to a specific vehicle type and driving location, and it uses its learned knowledge to assess the safety of other vehicles operating in the same location under similar conditions. Experiments show that the model outperforms current vehicle safety assessment models, relying on vehicle sensor data alone, and generates more robust, transferable solutions. Further analysis reveals that the model's learned knowledge corresponds with human expertise, suggesting that the model achieves safe driving states. In general, the model's performance improves when expert knowledge and driver behavior data are combined, and increasing the diversity of expert knowledge enhances the model's transferability. Overall, the research demonstrates that expert knowledge and experience can effectively improve vehicle safety assessment, particularly when driver behavior data is limited. Moreover, the model's utility extends to other automation systems, including those that require safe and knowledge-based decision-making in diverse and uncertain environments. Researchers believe that the model's findings have significant implications for the development of safe automated vehicles, including their ability to collaborate with human drivers and other vehicles on the road. Future research will focus on integrating the model with driver-human interaction interfaces to collaborate with other vehicles on the road. Researchers also propose several potential applications of the model, including vehicle-sharing systems, autonomous delivery systems, and urban mobility systems. Automatically generating labels for an Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) dataset can contribute significantly to the advancement of scene text recognition technologies. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach for generating synthetic data, grounded in language modeling, to produce labeled samples drawn from the probability distributions of words not seen during model training. Notably, our method differs from existing synthetic data techniques such as data augmentation and word embedding-based approaches. Furthermore, we introduce a new framework for generating models in parallel, to leverage the benefits of multi-model ensembles for enhanced accuracy. In evaluations conducted within the context of widely-used scene text datasets, our method was found to outperform existing synthetic data approaches and complement strong encoders and multi-model ensembles with comparable results to state-of-the-art models trained on full vocabularies. The source code for our approach can be found on our GitHub repository. Additionally, the OOV dataset for OmniNet can be accessed here. A related project for generating OOV words can be accessed at https://omnitext.github.io/omni-vocabulary/. The project utilizes language modeling to identify OOV words and to train models in parallel, to leverage the benefits of multi-model ensembles for enhanced accuracy. In evaluations conducted within the context of MS-COCO P, PASCAL-Combined, ICDAR-13, and SDC datasets, our method was found to outperform existing synthetic data approaches and complement strong encoders and multi-model ensembles with comparable results to state-of-the-art models trained on full vocabularies. The project's homepage can be accessed at https://omnitext.github.io/omni-vocabulary/. This research presents a novel method to measure the similarity of two random fields observed in distinct environmental conditions. By using min-max cross-covariance operators, we establish a quantitative approach that identifies any discrepancies in statistical characteristics between fields observed in different settings. This method is analogous to the max f-divergence metric, which evaluates differences in statistical characteristics between fields observed in the same environmental conditions. To showcase its efficacy, we apply our method to data sets obtained from numerical simulations of a material's failure in three scenarios: a central field with varying applied stresses and three analogous fields with stressed regions at distinct intervals. By performing two types of random field summaries, one revealing stress similarity and the other highlighting spatially independent material properties, we were able to recover known linear material characteristics and accurately establish categorical relationships between fields observed at diverse regimes. Ultimately, this work successfully bridges the statistical analysis of central fields with that of fields observed in distinct environmental conditions, providing a comprehensive framework for cross-regime random field analysis. Furthermore, this method is adaptable to data sets of any dimension and can be utilized in various applications beyond the example provided here. A publicly accessible R package, sfsti is available for reproducing the research's results. Further details can be found in a companion paper that demonstrates the practical applications of this method in a material mechanics context. This work builds upon previous research which introduced the min-max cross-covariance operator and was initially used to evaluate similarities in statistical characteristics between fields observed in the same environmental conditions. By extending this theory, we have successfully addressed a more complex challenge that has valuable implications in multiple disciplinary fields. In this context, we provide an annotated example of its effective use within a biomedical application which we will present in detail in a separate publication. In the present paper, we maintain a high level of mathematical abstraction and generality in order to ensure the broad applicability of this method. Consequently, we have employed a relatively abstract and simplified model, which does not itself contain any geometric dependencies, to better isolate and compare the method's performance in the presence of different types of geometric correlations. In the accompanying paper, we use these results to address the particular challenges associated with data sets of a similar nature in a two-dimensional setting. We investigated the dynamics of a magnetically levitated droplet in various atmospheres, consisting of vapour and a liquid phase, which are determined by the droplet's superheating or supersaturation levels. A model based on the Rayleigh--Plesset equation enabled us to simulate the droplet's behaviour in steam environments. In superheated gas conditions, magnetic levitation caused a stabilizing effect that resulted in a decrease to an equilibrium radius with minimal oscillations. Conversely, in supersaturated gas, magnetic levitation led to a dramatic increase in perturbation amplitude, producing large oscillations, and the droplet may eventually become unstable and collapse. These predictions were confirmed through microgravity experiments conducted aboard the 'Cressida' facility in Cyprus. Notably, in the initial stages of droplet formation, magnetic levitation had a stabilizing effect, but as the droplet grew, magnetic forces had a negligible impact on its growth rate. Consequently, to induce instability and collapse, the microgravity conditions were briefly terminated, resulting in a drop in atmospheric pressure that significantly increased superheating and triggered a rapid decrease in the droplet's radius. The findings from these experiments were then incorporated into existing models to refine their accuracy, offering significant potential for further research into magnetically levitated droplets. This could lead to innovative methods for producing novel materials, such as carbon nanotubes, nanodiamonds, and superconductors. A custom-built simulation environment, Magneto-Fluid-Dynamics (MFD), was developed to study the interplay of magnetic forces and fluid dynamics in the droplet, feeding the physical model with simulation data of its thermal, dynamic, and magnetic behaviour. The potential environmental complexities, such as convection in the surroundings, were also evaluated within this framework. As a by-product of this research and in anticipation of future instrumental advancements, an open-source software, 'Droplet-MFD', was developed and released, enabling users to generate and manipulate droplets based on various configurations, and simulate their behavior in static and rotating environments. Furthermore, based on the findings from the open-source software exploration, suggestions were provided to enhance the accuracy of the existing models used in the physical model to achieve greater precision. In the final section, a potential application of magnetic levitation in producing novel materials for quantum technology was explored. This study investigates an extensive range of junctions formed between graphene and conventional metals through simulations using the tight-binding model. Graphene's unique electronic structure, consisting of two Dirac points, causes a distinct variation in transport characteristics within the metal/graphene/metal junctions compared to those with conventional metals. To better understand these unique features, the current-voltage characteristics, conductance, and other transport quantities are calculated and compared over a broad range of graphene-metal interfaces, involving various metal substrates. Moreover, the influence of potential barriers within the sandwich structure on these parameters is also quantified and compared. The results suggest that graphene-metal junctions exhibit distinct behavior that can be adjusted by manipulating the potential barriers and graphene-metal interactions. This finding presents an opportunity for exploring novel devices based on these unique interactions, which can modulate energy transport in different ways. As a result, the proposed metal/graphene/metal junction may find applications in devices requiring non-linear responses, phase coherence, and quantum fluctuations. Furthermore, this research paves the way for exploring other novel interfaces, such as those formed with semiconductors, superconductors, and doped semiconductors to expand device capabilities. The derived simulation code, named salempic, offers a range of controllable parameters that can be used to simulate and compare the behavior of different junctions. The research outcomes are presented in the form of databases, accessible through the hubarx platform, for better understanding and visibility. Traditionally, achieving model reduction for partial differential equations with adjoint-based methods proves to be computationally resource-intensive due to the need for adjoint model implementation and adjoint discretization. Our approach, the SASK method, eliminates these obstacles by utilizing asynchronous vertex resampling on a mesh, bypassing the need for an adjoint model and adjoint discretization. This is made possible by integrating the projection of the adjoint solution into the reduced model's vertex space. We leverage the fact that the reduced model's adjoint can be approximated through the projection of the full model's adjoint solution. Our analysis confirms the preservation of key properties such as data consistency, dual backward error, and stability. Furthermore, when applying the SASK method to nonlinear problems, it demonstrates fast convergence in the reduced model's nonlinear iteration steps. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we present a series of numerical case studies showcasing the SASK method's efficiency and precision in real-world applications. These include rank-truncated flow modeling in reservoir simulation, reduced diffusion wave propagation, and reduced combustion modeling in the context of laser-driven gas dynamics. By comparing the SASK method to other model reduction techniques such as residual-based projection, non-linear least-squares, and residual minimizing integration, we consistently observe significant speed advantages while maintaining precision comparable to linear least-squares methods. Importantly, the SASK method outperforms existing methods in terms of the robustness of the reduced solution's nonlinear convergence and ultimately computation time. By eliminating the requirement for an adjoint model and adjoint discretization, the SASK method offers a more efficient and precise approach to model reduction. By leveraging asynchronous vertex resampling, our approach can potentially utilize parallel computing strategies, further amplifying its benefits. Therefore, we present a newly optimized parallel implementation of the SASK method based on dynamic mesh resampling and demonstrate its potential to seamlessly integrate with existing mesh-based codes without requiring significant modifications. As such, the SASK method has the potential to greatly augment the computational speed and efficiency of partial differential equation solvers in the future. Our results demonstrate that leveraging the SASK method and parallel processing together can result in substantial time savings across various platforms, from dozens of times faster on a laptop to hundreds of times faster on a high-performance server. To facilitate the adoption of the SASK method, we provide a freely available open-source code written in the C++ language that integrates the SASK method with the PETSc C++ framework for high-performance computing. The Sinkhorn algorithm, a method for solving the Schrödinger problem through iterative tensor optimization, relies on a quantum interpretation. It's designed to find the closest negative probability distribution to a given non-negative probability distribution, represented as a matrix. However, the algorithm's convergence has a specific behavior when there's no solution or when the solution results in a zero measure. This paper examines these conditions and reveals that the algorithm converges to either zero or a measure supported by a subset of the original distribution's support points. This result implies that the solution always exists and is unique. Additionally, we compare the algorithm's performance with respect to a different metric that uses the Wasserstein distance for its convergence criteria, and we show that using tensor optimization methods like the one from NumPyro can lead to premature convergence to an incorrect solution, especially when the original distribution has empty spaces within its support. This incorrect solution would be the closest negative probability distribution to the original distribution under the Euclidean metric. Conversely, applying the Sinkhorn algorithm at each iteration prevents early convergence to an incorrect solution and requires fewer iterations to achieve a specified level of precision. Furthermore, we compare the algorithm's performance for solving the Schrödinger problem with respect to its original formulation using Lanczos iterations and a different approach based on finding the square root of the original distribution's negative probability counterparty through Lanczos expansions. Interestingly, direct computation of the square root tends to require fewer iterations but generally takes longer to achieve a specified level of precision, and it's able to reach the exact solution in this case, whereas applying the Sinkhorn algorithm at each iteration results in higher performance but does not guarantee reaching the exact solution. The characteristics of entanglement in randomly ordered, interacting spin systems when constrained within specific spatial areas are examined using quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Unlike free-running spins, the entanglement in such systems displays long-term stability when tied to a central qubit or cavity mode, but not when connected to a central spin. This is due to the loss of coherence within the entanglement when tied to a central qubit or cavity mode, but not when tied to a central spin. Conversely, the entanglement in tie-qubit systems exhibits an increase and fluctuation depending on disorder levels, whereas tie-cavity and tie-spin systems show reduced yet consistent levels. Moreover, the entanglement in tie-cavity systems exhibits loss of coherence due to extra interactions exerting influence over the central cavity mode, an effect not seen in tie-qubit or tie-spin systems. This makes tie-cavity systems particularly suitable for studying long-term entanglement. Furthermore, the findings can be applied to various platforms such as cold atoms, solid-state systems, and trapped ions. Ultimately, the conclusions obtained may also prove valuable in a wide array of quantum technology applications. The unanticipated surge of the COVID-19 pandemic necessitated a sudden and unprecedented shift in the lives of government officials and everyday citizens alike. In a swift response to the emerging public health crisis, local authorities and medical experts devised a series of temporary measures to combat the spread of the virus. These measures included the implementation of universal mask-wearing policies, mass vaccination programs, and stringent restrictions on public gatherings, travel, and personal liberty. Although these measures were meant as a short-term solution, they had a profound and lasting impact on individuals' daily lives and societal dynamics. In a literary and sociological exploration, we seek to understand the COVID-19 pandemic's far-reaching effects on urban life, diversity of human encounter, and community resilience, examining how the virus created a lasting rift between isolated individuals and fostering a society of disparate 'V'-shaped cohorts. Furthermore, we aim to determine whether these disparate groups, distinguished by their exposure and immunization status, will eventually reunite, exploring the potential for long-term societal reintegration through narrative analysis and literary expression. In conclusion, we present original, previously unpublished short stories, including one by our colleague and fellow researcher, Michael May, as well as by ourselves (Stephanie B. Hubbard, Ananya S. Parikh, and Ashwin Parikh), illustrating the pandemic's and post-pandemic realities, highlighting both the isolation and potential reunification of individuals, and examining the distinct ways in which various segments of the population experienced and responded to the crisis. These stories were conceived, written, and compiled over a period of approximately two years during the pandemic, reflecting diverse perspectives and trajectories that are an integral component of urban, communal, and global endeavors. Although an endeavor has been made to diversely represent various story subjects' mask-wearing habits, this representation is not exhaustive and should by no means be regarded as representative of the various mask-distinguishing groups created by the pandemic. The stories were initially presented at a virtual literary conference, titled 'The Pandemic Effect: COVID-19 and the Long-Term Shift in Urban, Communal, and Global Realities,' which took place on October 9, 2021, and were discussed in conjunction with other presentations exploring the pandemic's and post-pandemic realities from various sociological and medical perspectives. These stories were initially published in a collection by Rutgers University Press as part of a forthcoming publication, 'The Pandemic Effect: COVID-19 and Urban, Communal, and Global Realities,' which is due to be released in Spring

We have developed the Fully Implicit Semi-explicit Multi-Scale Numerical Scheme (FSMSN) based on the multi-scale conservative residual smoothing technique. This method diverges from traditional approaches such as the Sequential Fully Implicit method for solving multi-physics problems. The FSMSN algorithm time-step combination ensures accurate momentum equation solutions across different scales, unlike continuous Smoluchowski approximations or sequence-based schemes. To assess its effectiveness, we applied the FSMSN algorithm to simulate single-phase flow in heterogeneous media for continuous and discontinuous flow scenarios. The results demonstrated that using the FSMSN algorithm yielded accurate solutions that aligned with single-scale numerical models for both constant and discontinuous flow cases. Additionally, we evaluated the FSMSN algorithm for non-linear homogenization by simulating adhesive nanofilm peeling off a large substrate, and the resulting solutions showed minimal discrepancy compared to single-scale direct solutions. The FSMSN algorithm thus offers an efficient, accurate, and timely solution for solving multi-physics problems across various scientific and engineering disciplines. By seamlessly integrating different time-step schemes, it can further significantly reduce computational costs. For instance, in the example described above, leveraging the FSMSN algorithm allowed for an ~65.7% reduction in computational costs compared to direct single-scale solutions, and for an ~94.5% reduction in conjunction with the time-step combined scheme. This method therefore represents a simple yet powerful approach to addressing multi-scale complex problems in science and engineering. The corresponding source code for the FSMSN algorithm is available at the public GitHub platform for continuous development and improvement. The specific repository address for the FSMSN algorithm is https://github.com/Liljosedan/FSMSNAlgorithm. Theoretical foundations of the Alcubierre warp drive have been further developed by incorporating modifications to generalize previous work on stable solutions. Our approach builds upon existing research which demonstrated the necessity of exotic matter or energy in negative mass regions to achieve stable solutions. In contrast, we suggest that both exotic matter and energy configurations may be required, particularly to accommodate the varying amounts of necessary negative energy and negative mass. Furthermore, we propose the existence of a critical mass density threshold, beyond which, the amount of required negative mass would need to decrease in order to compensate for the corresponding increase in necessary negative energy. We have also extended previous analyses by taking into account the specific equations of state that define thermodynamic properties for matter and energy. We provide numerical estimates of warp drive speed in units of the speed of light based on our novel framework applied to different scenarios featuring different types of matter and energy. Ultimately, this work highlights additional challenges in creating a warp drive, an idea whose implementation has been shown to require under ideal conditions an unfeasibly large amount of negative mass. Moreover, the necessity of negative energy may need to be complemented by the presence of negative work to make the warp drive effect observable without violating established physical laws. Our work is based on a simplified model of classical space-time that does not take into account quantum effects. However, the amount of negative mass needed for a warp drive makes the idea of recycling matter through space-time likely infeasible, which in turn suggests that any feasible warp drive effect would likely be incompatible with our established understanding of classical and quantum coherences. In particular, the amount of negative mass needed for a warp drive makes the idea of recycling matter through space-time likely infeasible, and the absence of a feasible solution motivates an investigation of the warp drive effect using quantum mechanics and feasibility to be explored in future research. Future research could explore warp drive feasibility from both a classical and quantum mechanics perspective, and focus in particular on the problem of assembling and starting a warp drive, which would need to be able to accumulate and concentrate negative mass in a short amount of time without violating the laws of thermodynamics and the established understanding of causality. An additional concern is the issue of the assembled warp drive ship's mass being so large in comparison to typical ships that it would need to be generated by massive amounts of matter and energy in order to be consistent with established notions of space-time physics. However, the amount of matter and energy needed for such large objects would need to be in conflict with established notions of space-time physics as well

The management of urban underground infrastructure is complicated by the extensive network of interconnected systems like sewer systems, pipes for heating and water, and subway tunnels. Planning and maintenance tasks often require combining expert knowledge from various fields, which proves challenging due to the different paradigms used in each. To improve decision-making for interconnected underground systems, it is essential to integrate decision-making approaches from individual domains. This paper presents the GUIDES framework, which enables the coordination of interconnected underground infrastructure by generating guidelines for decision-making based on specific use cases. The incorporation of multi-agent systems in GUIDES facilitates the aggregation of decision-making policies from separate domains, while the use of microservices ensures the framework can be adapted to various use cases with minimal maintenance. GUIDES encompasses three layers: a synthetic environment for network evolution, a core component for coordination, and an extension for visualizing network states. GUIDES's core component is comprised of multiple agents, each defined by their utility functions, rewards, and updates, which interact within a shared network structure. The combination of these agents' behavior yields a multi-agent coordination that is robust yet legible, meaning it is understandable and traceable. GUIDES includes applications for managing changes to its underlying models, monitoring its performance, and generating visualizations to simplify evaluating complex network dynamics. GUIDES empowers users to define policies for individual domain components and coordinate them through the multi-agent coordination layer. This enables GUIDES to be applied to a variety of use cases, including network planning, simulation, and operation, or any combination of these tasks. By designing GUIDES in this way, it is possible for an user to define mechanisms for coordinating individual domain components without fully understanding the other domains, which are treated as a black box. GUIDES can be applied to a variety of urban underground infrastructure management tasks, including network planning, simulation, operation, or any combination of these tasks. A GUIDES-based application is demonstrated for managing policy coordination between urban underground infrastructure planners and operators. This use case focuses on simultaneously planning, simulating, and operating underground infrastructure using a shared synthetic network structure. However, in practice, the synthetic network structure is generated dynamically and is specific to the task at hand. For this purpose, a multi-agent system is used to define urban use cases, another microservice is used to define infrastructure characteristics, and a core component is used to define utility functions for underground infrastructure management. The temperature of a two-dimensional Coulomb crystal in a Penning trap is determined by analyzing the oscillation modes of its electric quadrupole, which makes it possible to calculate the ambient thermal increase rate.
A formula is developed to identify the crystal's shape as a function of noise intensity levels. This is combined with a calibration method for measuring thermal movement, which is used to calculate the initial temperature conditions.
A mechanism for calculating the ambient heating rate is developed by tracking the crystal's change in shape and its effect on fundamental oscillation frequency, which results in precise thermal energy measurements.
A long-term observation of the ambient thermal increase rate across various experiments allows for the identification and analysis of distinct heating sources within the trap.
A 10 Torr gas pressure trap is found to be influenced by two opposing thermal forces - a cooling effect from nitrogen's negative ionization potential and a heating effect from other ions' collisional energy exchange with trap electrodes.
As a consequence, the ambient thermal increase rate may fluctuate between opposite directions, resulting in an unpredictable outcome.
A comprehensive understanding and management of all heating sources within Penning traps may ensure their predictable thermal performance, which is crucial for maintaining precise charge-to-mass ratio measurements for trapped ions. By implementing this new method for calculating the ambient thermal increase rate, it may also be possible to develop more advanced trap technologies with better thermal performance. This could, for example, allow for the measurement of lighter masses, up to the level of hundreds of keV/$c^2$.
A new development for calculating the ambient thermal increase rate may also make it easier to analyze the electrical properties of materials used in trap construction, particularly the importance of the work function in relation to ionization potential. By identifying and quantifying the characteristics of both trap electrodes and materials, it should be possible to develop more effective trapping methods that take into consideration the inherent thermal performance of ions in Penning traps. By integrating thermal analysis with existing ion applications, it may also be possible to enhance our understanding of the electrical properties of materials used in their construction. By quantifying the ambient thermal increase rate in Penning traps it may also be possible to expand the range of measurable masses from hundreds of $m_e$ to thousands of $m_e$. Penning traps with predictable thermal performance may also be used to explore new areas of solid-state physics such as the identification of thermal instability in Kitaev spin liquids. The combination of Raman and nonlinear Raman spectroscopies on nanoscale samples offers distinct electromagnetic and chemical contributions. A specific Raman scattering type known as surface enhanced Raman scattering or hyper-Raman scattering emerges under intense light stimulation. Researchers can exploit the hyper-Raman effect by utilizing 1.5 O3 785 nm laser light that has an overall power of approximately 60 mW. Such an approach yields noticeable signals even in the presence of 950 nm light that is far-off-resonance with the sample, and these signals are comparable to those produced through surface enhanced Raman scattering or hyper-Raman scattering when excited with 633 nm light. By manipulating the polarization of the gathered light, scientists discovered that there exists a notable difference between the electromagnetic and chemical roles they play in the Raman signal generation process. Specifically, the electromagnetic effect has three primary sub-components that are linked to the center and bended arm electronic resonances and a particular plasmon resonance of the sample's tip. On the other hand, the chemical effect has three other notable sub-components that are centered around the sample's primary resonances. Notably, the largest chemical sub-component has a polarization direction that is symmetrical, while the remaining two have polarizations that can be identified as even and odd with respect to the sample's tip arm. Overall, the gathered data suggests that the electromagnetic effect has a considerable impact on the gathered Raman signals and can, in fact, surpass the chemical effect depending on factors like the sample's orientation and polarization of the gathered light. Additionally, the findings provide insight into the properties and interactions of the sample's electronic and plasmonic excitations. They also enable a precise identification of the sample's chemical structures including carbon-hydrogen, carbon-carbon, and carbon-oxygen bonds, while interacting with water molecules. Finally, the researchers discovered a notable interaction between the sample's residual water molecules and the tip's gold material. The data indicates that the sample's water layer has its own specific resonance frequency near 3.06 eV. Moreover, the findings suggest that the sample's water molecules have a preferential orientation with respect to the sample's surface and an intrinsic asymmetrical property. By interacting with the sample's water molecules, the researchers could also pinpoint the sample's redox events involving the oxidation of hydroxyl groups and a particular transfer of electrons from the sample's gold material. Notably, the data provides insight into the sample's chemical structures including its carbon and oxygen content, while interacting with water molecules

Our research offers a search for Axial Magnetic Fields in the Edge-On Spiral Galaxy UZC J135328.1$+$0430 using STAREX and its novel technology. By employing its 40cm dishes to record broadband spectral correlations from 2 to 10 GHz, STAREX can detect magnetic fields and assess Faraday rotation without relying on signal strength. Although the galaxy's distance of 42 Mpc limits the maximum detectable rotation measure to around 8000 rad/m$^2$, we were unable to identify any sizable magnetic fields within the galaxy's confines. Our observations indicate minimal electron content within the galaxy, and we recommend targeting galaxies with certain characteristics for optimal future searches. These characteristics include a type classification of early spiral galaxies, specific orientation, and a distance of several Mpc. Moreover, searching during periods of low ionization can enhance the visibility of magnetic fields, particularly if the galaxy is positioned near the plane of the galaxy's rotation. Our analysis suggests that future searches should occur during periods when the galaxy is positioned on the opposite side of the plane of the galaxy's rotation and when ionization levels are low. If magnetic fields of Axion-like particles are present, their potential to amplify existing fields makes these a particularly compelling area of study. Our data, recorded over 27 days in December 2021, include 27 frequency-labeled correlation records, each spanning 1 MHz in bandwidth. Our analysis of these records yields detectability limits of 20 $\mu$rad/m at 2 $\sigma$ confidence for Faraday rotation and 0.9 Jy km/s for brightness temperature. These limits are represented in a series of images, including total intensity maps, Faraday rotation maps, and Stokes parameters U and V. Our analysis further includes a search for compact sources, which resulted in a catalog consisting of 16 sources comprising 9 in the galaxy's plane and 7 outside of it. These sources' fluxes range from 6 to 130 Jy at 2 $\sigma$ confidence. Additionally, we found two sources with Faraday rotation values of 420 and 660 rad/m, with a 2 $\sigma$ confidence upper limit of 8000 rad/m for the remaining sources. Corresponding source lists and maps for UZC J135328.1$+$0430 can be accessed via DOIs of 10.24419/astro-ph.GAA3RJ, 10.24419/astro-ph.GAA3RK, 10.24419/

The ferroelectric phase transition in ammonium sulfate, a temperature-driven change from low- and high-temperature crystal structures with different symmetry, is studied using heat capacity measurements and molecular dynamics simulations. These experiments and simulations confirm that the entropy change during this phase transition originates from the anion and cation rearrangements within the ammonium sulfate crystal structure, rather than from the ordering of the ammonium cations as previously suggested. Furthermore, the consistency between simulated and measured heat capacity data provides strong support for these simulation results. Notably, the temperature at which this phase transition occurs remains unchanged across varying simulation speeds, indicating no signs of premature transition at elevated temperatures. Molecular dynamics simulations also reveal that within a few picoseconds following the phase transition, approximately 20% of ammonium ions have not completed their rearrangement, although the time it takes to complete this process decays exponentially as the simulation temperature increases. Furthermore, the MD simulations explain that the previously reported monoclinic symmetry of ammonium sulfate is actually a result of strain-induced distortion due to the slight mismatch between the ammonium sulfate unit cell dimensions, a discrepancy of about one angstrom. A new, more accurate tetrahedral model of the ammonium sulfate unit cell is suggested based on these simulation results and includes cell dimensions of 8.096, 8.848, 3.648 Angstroms. Individual decisions in gambling tasks are frequently explained using risk models, but a more significant factor appears to be people's general tendency to avoid losses by adjusting their decisions after negative outcomes. Although commonly thought to increase avoidance of losses, we discovered substantial individual variability in how losses influence decision-making. Furthermore, we found that the brain's reward-related areas not only respond to rewards but also process the importance of avoiding losses as well as the individual's overall probability of winning. Notably, our results suggest that the brain areas involved in attention and memory integrate negative outcomes to guide decision-making, rather than simply the final outcome of a task. This implies that people learn to make risk-averse or risk-seeking decisions by either weighing final win or loss probabilities or, more likely, the accumulated value of avoided losses which corresponds with the common interpretation of prospection in decision-making. By extending the concept of prospection, our findings help demystify the general tendency for people to match probabilities in decision-making.

The notion that different quantum states might be interlinked, yet generally cannot be simultaneously realized, has driven research into nonlocality and contextuality in quantum mechanics. A key question has arisen about how to define these concepts: do they apply universally to all quantum systems or are they properties of specific groups of systems? To address this, we examined systems composed of two interacting particles with their properties determined by two hidden variables. We discovered that, contrary to previous claims, these systems can be described using classical models, provided that the property of contextuality is redefined to include a wider range of hidden variable settings. Importantly, our results do not negate the possibility that modified versions of nonlocality and contextuality might apply to systems with fewer particles. To explore this further, we considered the property of contextuality in systems with three or more particles and found that, in general, these systems cannot be modeled using classical systems, even when allowing for additional hidden variable settings. Our study thus sheds new light on the concepts of nonlocality and contextuality and raises questions about the extent to which these phenomena occur in the physical world. A natural next step would be to develop methods for directly testing nonlocality and contextuality in systems of different numbers of particles. Such experiments could confirm whether these effects occur universally or if they are confined to specific groups of systems. Ultimately, our research contributes to an ongoing debate about how to interpret quantum mechanics and its applications to understand better the strange and often counterintuitive behavior of quantum systems. In particular, we found that generally commuting distributions of simple probabilities do exist for systems with few particles. To illustrate this, we derived the general forms of these distributions for systems with hidden variables representing two, three, and four properties. Our analysis confirms that these distributions remain stable under certain changes to system properties. Importantly, our results do not rely on specific assumptions and can be applied universally to all systems of the same size. A key implication of our work is that modified versions of nonlocality and contextuality, in which contextuality involves incompatibility of distributions under local operations, exist in systems with few particles. Furthermore, our study sheds new light on how these effects change as systems become more complex, for example, in terms of whether these effects generally allow for contextual deductions from overall system behavior to individual sub-system behaviors. Ultimately, our research contributes to an ongoing debate about quantum references and whether these effects occur universally or if they are confined to specific groups of systems. A natural next step would be to develop methods for directly testing

Recent breakthroughs in using quantum computers for solving critical problems within Euclidean spaces have led to $c_{\epsilon} n^{1-\alpha } $-time algorithms for tasks like approximate nearest neighbor with partial information retrieval, multi-dimensional range search, and robust search with $\alpha < 1$. These achievements offer approximation factors that improve as computing time increases. The results incorporate novel techniques, such as corona sets, fractal property of quantum balls, and a novel hierarchical clustering method, and leverage the concept of quantum balls, whose sublinear dimension leads to the resolution of the collision problem with better efficiency than in the classical case. The collision problem, essential for task solutions, is resolved by sampling quantum balls with a sublinear number of samples, reducing the complexity of subsequent steps. The cluster property of samples within these balls enables efficient computation of their distance to unsampled points, contributing to the resolution of the problem with a potentially faster algorithm. The speedup over the classical case arises from the sublinear dimension of quantum balls, which occurs because their volume is bounded by the sample size, a property not seen in earlier approaches where the ball's volume equals the sample size. A sample size of $n^{\alpha } $ and resulting time complexity of $c_{\epsilon } n^{1-\alpha } $ implies that the value of $\alpha $ must be greater than 0. If $\alpha $ were equal to 0, the time complexity would be linear, contradicting the goal of achieving a sublinear complexity, so the value of $\alpha $ must be greater than 0. The value of $\alpha $ can be further optimized. By optimizing the balance between preprocessing and query times, it is possible to achieve equal values for these two quantities, both being expressed as $c_{\epsilon } n^{\alpha } $. The value of $\alpha $ is thus equal to 0.468, and the time complexity becomes expressed as $c_{\epsilon } n^{0.468}$. The goal of achieving a sublinear complexity, and resulting time complexity of $c_{\epsilon } n^{1-\alpha } $, means that the value of $\alpha $ must be greater than 0. If $\alpha $ were equal to 0.5, the time complexity becomes expressed as $c_{\epsilon } n^{0.5}$. It is possible to achieve a speedup of order $n^{1/3}$ for tasks like approximate nearest neighbor with partial information retrieval, multi-dimensional range search

The rapid advancement of quantum computing has led to the emergence of various hardware platforms, driven primarily by applications in scientific research. Among these platforms, two quantum-based technologies stand out for their scientific significance: quantum computers and quantum sensors. A quantum computer's unique processing capabilities allow for the simulation of complex systems, while a quantum sensor's exceptional sensitivity enables precise measurements. However, both technologies are plagued by errors in their respective cores: quantum computers by hardware-induced inaccuracies and quantum sensors by imperfect readings. To mitigate these issues, unfolding techniques drawn from particle physics research can be applied. Originally designed to handle detector inefficiencies, these techniques have been successfully expanded to utilize Bayesian unfolding. The use of Bayesian unfolding, however, poses a significant challenge: dealing with system errors. Thanks to recent advancements in measurement mitigation technology, it's now feasible to enhance the scalability of Bayesian unfolding by multiple orders of magnitude. The development utilized the CoCo, a 11-qubit quantum processor, and demonstrated its capabilities through a real-world application - the analysis of coherent population transfer experiments. The results showed that the combination of Bayesian unfolding and measurement mitigation significantly improves the accuracy of measurements. The success of the approach highlights the considerable potential for further hardware improvements in this field. The study also explores the implications of further advancements in measurement accuracy for future quantum computing systems and other quantum-based technologies. The investigation reveals that achieving higher measurement accuracy may lead to notable contradictions in the data unless more sophisticated processing techniques, such as Markov chain Monte Carlo analysis, are applied. The study thus sets the stage for the development of more sophisticated tools and techniques to handle and analyze data from quantum computers and other quantum-based technologies. When interacting with a robot, nothing is known about its purpose or functions unless it chooses to disclose the information. There's no research that studies how revealing a robot's purpose affects interactions with it, despite the fact that many studies show benefits from knowing a robot's goals. We conduct a series of studies to explore these issues in educational settings where humans and robots complete tasks together. We found that humans value knowing a robot's purpose and that showing the task options helps humans complete tasks more efficiently. However, it's counterintuitive that also revealing the sequences of task options chosen by the robot actually decreases humans' performance. We suggest that humans feel more confident when they see a robot's chosen task options because it resembles expert behavior, making them reliant on the robot. We also compared the methods robots use to teach humans about their purpose and how this influences humans' trust in robots, finally highlighting the complexities of deciding what information robots should share. In cases where robots have multiple ways to share this information, different revelation strategies can either enhance or decrease human efficiency, suggesting that how robots communicate their purpose can impact performance. We propose that robots should consider sharing their purpose only when it results in better outcomes, otherwise keeping it private. More generally, there's no straightforward answer of what information a robot should share; each case will need to be carefully evaluated. We also believe that robots should consider spreading controlled amounts of false information in order to create a more cooperative environment. In the long run, robots will need to establish clear guidelines on what information to share and why. This might spark a new area of research within AI, distinct from current focus on robots' autonomy, but rather the intelligibility and human-readability of robots. Inconclusively, we raise additional questions such as: Will robots, capable of making mistakes, increase users' efficiency by revealing false task options? Can robots enhance humans' focus on relevant task factors by keeping their purpose hidden? Do humans' expectations of accuracy impact their efficiency when a robot's purpose is kept private? We encourage researchers to explore these questions and others that relate to robots' ability to share their purpose and engage in collaborative settings. In the short term, we suggest conducting more research on how humans interact with robots in isolated environments to gain a deeper understanding of these complex issues. In the future, researchers will have an opportunity to contribute towards creating policies that establish robots' transparency requirements, paving the way for a new human-age of robot responsibility. A new approach, effective gap width, is a broadened optical model that more accurately predicts light behavior in media with sharp boundaries. Unlike the traditional local model, effective gap width effectively simulates the combined effect of multiple parameters that influence light propagation. To establish a standard effective gap width for air, we've developed a high-accuracy procedure that accurately extracts broadband attenuation coefficients from polycrystalline silver halides. Leveraging this method, we've determined the air's effective gap width, finding it to be roughly 0.3 nm at its peak. Consequently, we've developed an optimized expression for describing attenuation patterns and derived a generalized expression for describing optical gaps applicable to broad classes of materials, including air and similar transparent mediums. We have validated our model by comparing its predictions with existing experimental and numerical data on optical gaps in materials like sodium chloride and silver halide crystals. Additionally, we have used our model to calculate the optical gap width in nanoholes and thick crystals of silver halides, gaining insights into the complex interplay between optical gaps and geometric parameters. Our studies have also compared the accuracy of our model with that of a detailed quantum scattering model. Importantly, our results obtained with the optimized expression are comparable to the predictions made by quantum scattering models. Ultimately, we have used our model, expressed as $\frac{\beta^2}{2\lambda^2}-\frac{\beta^4}{4\lambda^4}$, for various wavenumber $\lambda$. This expression implies that air's optical gap is approximately independent of the wavelength at 550 nm. Consequently, we have used our model to calculate the diffusion length in air, observed at around 44 $\mu$m.

This paper addresses the problem of minimizing total energy consumption in a cooperative network consisting of multiple users, multiple relays, and analog receivers. Energy efficiency is enhanced by strategic scheduling of relays in addition to transmission power. We transform the initial constraint-based issue into an optimization problem with jointly optimized power and relay allocation. A two-stage approach is taken, starting with optimization of the first stage (power allocation) to obtain an optimal power load, followed by allocation of the second stage (relays) through a genetic algorithm. Specifically, we use the minimum user capacity maximization method in the second stage. Numerical simulations show that this transformation is effective and offers reduced computational complexity compared to methods based on Lagrange multipliers. We also validate that our approach is suitable for both analog and digital receiver systems. Ultimately, our proposed method outperforms traditional energy-efficient designs that neglect computational complexity. It effectively balances energy consumption and user throughput. This is because the genetic algorithm allows for exhaustive optimization of power allocation and relay scheduling, resulting in optimal performance. Moreover, we observe that relay gain surpasses thermal noise in scenarios with low number of relays, thereby confirming the impact of relay scheduling on overall performance. These findings encourage the integration of analog receivers in existing systems to enhance energy efficiency. Under specific circumstances, like when magnetic adatoms are positioned very close to the Fermi level, spin-orbit coupling could result in broadened YSR state peaks, whereas dimers, even those with highly correlated spins, can only lead to slightly increased splitting. Spin polarization at the adatom or dimer tip is expected to be relatively weak. Notably, spin-orbit coupling significantly influences ferromagnetic YSR state peaks, particularly those that are heavily weighted towards the Fermi level, whereas it has a more considerable effect on the anti-ferromagnetic state peaks, resulting in a more substantial impact on the resulting spectra. A proposed theoretical framework, incorporating a more precise model of the YSR state, is an improvement over existing methods that fail to accurately capture the characteristics of heavily spin-imbalanced fermions. This new framework is versatile, allowing for the analysis of a range of fermionic states, including those with spin-orbit coupling, and is applicable to various magnetic configurations, extending beyond the study of adatoms to include magnetic dimers, and even more complex magnetic entities. A more particular and intriguing case studied here involves a specific type of magnetic entity, where four spin-orbit coupled spins are connected to one superconductor and show anti-ferromagnetic properties, resulting in a very complex and multifaceted spectra with a wide range of possible states, including those with spin polarization. The use of Pauli matrices for the spin-orbit coupled one-dimensional chain allows for a more precise model of the spin density of the magnetic entity, and is particularly notable when the resulting state spectra exhibit a coexistence of two distinct ferromagnetic states, and is applicable to a range of discrete energy splittings.
